listings.title: Understanding the Relationship Between Patterning and Mathematics
listings.summary: Patterning refers to the ability to notice regularities in sequences (e.g. ABABAB, ABAABAAB, where the As and Bs might represent colours or shapes). Recently, patterning has attracted substantial interest because performance on patterning tasks shows robust and significant correlations with mathematics achievement.
listings.description:
Patterning refers to the ability to notice regularities in sequences (e.g. ABABAB, ABAABAAB, where the As and Bs might represent colours or shapes). Recently, patterning has attracted substantial interest because performance on patterning tasks shows robust and significant correlations with mathematics achievement.

However, the patterning literature is fragmented and confused, partly because it is unclear whether patterning is distinct from similar constructs such as analogical reasoning (the ability to infer and work with relations from incomplete information, e.g. “Doctor:Hospital, Teacher:?”) and nonverbal reasoning (e.g. filling in the missing piece of a 3 × 3 matrix of shapes).

Understanding the cognitive processes involved in patterning is key for both theory and practice; for example, should patterning be included in the primary school curriculum? This PhD project will contribute to this goal by investigating the role of patterning and related constructs in mathematics.

The research will make use of existing tasks and methods established in the literature, as well as developing new methods. It will involve analytical approaches that allow us to identify the types of cognitive processes required for different tasks and to understand the relationships between those tasks.

The successful applicant will join the vibrant community of the Centre for Mathematical Cognition one of the world’s leading research centres for the study of mathematics education and numerical thinking.

The Centre for Mathematical Cognition brings together academics who conduct research in three different areas: basic research on mathematical cognition, the design of research-based educational resources, and the evaluation of educational interventions.

listings.title: PhD Studentships: An investigation into the interface material layer created during linear friction welding of Titanium alloys.
listings.summary: Applications are invited for a PhD position at the University of Nottingham addressing the specific engineering details of the contact layer created during the Linear Friction Welding (LFW) of Titanium alloys. The successful candidate will have a first-class or upper second-class honours degree in mechanical…
listings.description:
Applications are invited for a PhD position at the University of Nottingham addressing the specific engineering details of the contact layer created during the Linear Friction Welding (LFW) of Titanium alloys. The successful candidate will have a first-class or upper second-class honours degree in mechanical engineering or a related subject.

This CASE studentship will attract a stipend of £25,000 per annum for four years. The position arises from a long-standing engineering research relationship between the University of Nottingham and Rolls-Royce plc. The University of Nottingham hosts two of the (~30) University Technology Centres (UTCs) used by the company as the main engines of its engineering research and development. Nottingham’s UTC in gas turbine transmissions systems will host this studentship and the candidate will sit within a community of ~20 PhD students at various stages of their study.

The attachment of blades to discs using solid-state joining is a key factor in achieving cost-effective, high performance and low-weight fan and compressor stages in aero-engines. LFW is an established joining process utilised by R-R to manufacture Titanium blisks across a range of engine types. R-Rs strategy requires the continued exploitation of this technology to a wider range of Titanium alloys, including dissimilar joints. The LFW process has been developed to ensure high quality joints are produced over a broad range of welding conditions commensurate with manufacturing capability; however, the quality of joints made in more advanced Titanium alloys and dissimilar material joints is ensured by consistent flash extrusion and flow from the interface contact layer, which is in turn linked to the transient behaviour of the process, process stability and the interaction between the part and the tooling.

This project will develop the fundamental understanding of the thermo-mechanical effects and material flow within the high strain-rate/high temperature interface contact layer created during LFW of Titanium alloys and the links to key process variables and machine/tooling behaviour. This study will be undertaken using computational simulation, supported by experimental investigations using test welds and novel material characterisation methods.

This project is available from 1st October 2026. Applications are accepted until post is filled. Informal inquiries can be made via email to Dr James Rouse (james.rouse@nottingham.ac.uk).

This exciting opportunity is based within the thriving Optics and Photonics Research Group in Faculty of Engineering which conducts cutting edge research spanning exploration to translation, with curiosity driven projects all the way through to application in the clinic.

We are seeking PhD student that is motivated and enthusiastic and keen to push the boundaries of what is currently possible when imaging with an optical microscope. Combing the latest in optical developments with the recent surge in AI, this project aims image the centre of a live intact root for the first time. Something that is currently not possible.

This project will address a long-standing issue in plant biology: the inability to image the centre of live, intact, plant roots. The ability to observe dynamic cellular processes at the centre of a live root for the first time will unlock entirely new lines of biological inquiry, crucial for areas such as sustainable agriculture and food security. Such an imaging system would allow for studies of a plant’s resilience to drought, salinity, and water logging, as well as responses to fungal infections and nanoparticle uptake. It is very common that new optical microscopy techniques are developed to image mammalian tissue, and that these approaches are very slow to translate across to plant biosciences where the impact could be huge and as a result exciting opportunities get missed.

When we use light to image deep into complex samples there is a common problem that occurs – the light gets distorted and scattered by the structures present in the sample and as a result a nice quality focus and hence a nice image cannot be produced at depth into the sample. At Nottingham we have been working on this problem for several years and have developed methods that shape the incoming light with the equal but opposite distortion to that imposed by the sample to produce a high-quality image deep into the sample of interest. Recently we have been using AI and machine learning to predict the distortion present and significantly speed up this correction process.

This PhD project will take the latest in AI-informed wavefront correction techniques and tailor them to imaging deep into plant roots. It will use a range of state-of-the-art optical microscopes based in the Optics and Photonics Research Group in the Faculty of Engineering, plus those housed in Plant Biosciences at the Sutton Bonnington campus. listings.title: Are children’s intuitions about ownership impacted by concerns for human flourishing?
listings.summary: How are children’s intuitions about the ownership of property affected by their understanding of the potential impact of ownership on human flourishing? In other words, when there are several candidate owners, will children attribute ownership to the candidate in greater need?
listings.description:
How are children’s intuitions about the ownership of property affected by their understanding of the potential impact of ownership on human flourishing? In other words, when there are several candidate owners, will children attribute ownership to the candidate in greater need?

Given the importance of ownership to modern societies, it is unsurprising that children’s intuitions about ownership have received considerable attention over the last 10-15 years (see Nancekivell, Friedman, & Gelman, 2019). Children as young as two years of age appear to rely on information about who first possessed an object when deciding who owns it (Freidman & Neary, 2008). Goulding & Friedman (2018) showed that children aged 3-5 years use land ownership as a basis of ownership attribution for found objects. All of this work is based on traditional theories of ownership in legal studies in which owners’ rights are emphasised at the expense of owners’ responsibilities. Interestingly, ‘progressive’ theories of property have emerged in the legal studies literature in which issues of human flourishing are central to questions of ownership (Alexander, 2009; Alexander et al., 2009). Under such accounts, owners have responsibilities or social obligations to ensure that their property promotes human flourishing.

One issue raised by progressive theories of property is whether questions of who would most benefit from ownership of an object should figure in decisions about disputed ownership. If owners have a responsibility to use their possessions to promote flourishing then perhaps, when ownership is in dispute, that decision which is most likely to promote flourishing should be preferred.

The proposed programme of investigation will be comprised of a number of closely related experiments designed to investigate whether concerns for flourishing impact on children’s ownership attributions in contexts similar to those previously studied in the literature. We will examine the role played by human flourishing in children’s attributions of ownership when first possession or land ownership may be used as a basis for decision making. We will also examine both the contextual and developmental factors which influence effects of concerns for flourishing.

As well as having significant implications for psychological theories of ownership, results from this project will shed light on theories of property in legal studies.

listings.title: Lost in Thought: Exploring Children's Awareness of Mind Wandering
listings.summary: This project will investigate how children develop awareness of their own attentional states and learn to recognise moments when their attention lapses. By examining how metacognitive awareness of inattention evolves and relates to learning, this research will clarify when and how such awareness helps children manage…
listings.description:
This project will investigate how children develop awareness of their own attentional states and learn to recognise moments when their attention lapses. By examining how metacognitive awareness of inattention evolves and relates to learning, this research will clarify when and how such awareness helps children manage inattention more effectively. Ultimately, the study aims to reveal how meta-awareness can serve as a protective mechanism against inattention, providing a foundation for strategies that support sustained focus in the classroom.

Mind wandering - when attention drifts from the task at hand to internal thoughts or feelings - is linked to poorer academic outcomes and mental health difficulties in adolescents and adults. However, remarkably little is known about how these patterns emerge during childhood.

This doctoral project will address a key but underexplored issue: how children’s awareness of mind wandering develops alongside their understanding of its impact on learning. The research will investigate how meta-awareness of mind wandering and metacognitive knowledge about attentional processes change across the primary school years, and how these factors relate to individual differences in attention regulation.

Guided by Nelson and Narens’ (1990) influential model, the project distinguishes between metacognitive monitoring (awareness of one’s own cognitive state) and metacognitive control (the regulation of behaviour based on that awareness). While awareness appears to develop relatively steadily throughout childhood, the ability to translate this awareness into strategic self-regulation is more variable and sensitive to individual and environmental factors. By applying this framework to attention, the project will investigate when children can not only detect mind wandering but also act on that awareness to support effective behavioural regulation.

We seek candidates with a strong background in psychology, education, or a related field, and a keen interest in cognitive development and educational psychology. Experience with experimental methods, cognitive assessment, or developmental research would be advantageous.

This project offers an exceptional opportunity to advance understanding of attention and metacognition in childhood. The findings have the potential to inform practical strategies for improving classroom engagement and supporting children’s ability to sustain focus in learning environments.

listings.title: Words for Feelings: Exploring the Development of Emotional Granularity in Children and Adolescents
listings.summary: This project will investigate how children and adolescents develop emotional granularity—the ability to differentiate and label emotions with precision—and the role language will play in shaping this skill. By examining how emotional vocabulary and expression evolve over time, the study will aim to identify critical…
listings.description:
This project will investigate how children and adolescents develop emotional granularity—the ability to differentiate and label emotions with precision—and the role language will play in shaping this skill. By examining how emotional vocabulary and expression evolve over time, the study will aim to identify critical periods for fostering emotional awareness and resilience in young people.

This PhD project will aim to investigate the development of emotional granularity—the ability to differentiate and label emotions with precision—in children and adolescents. The project will use a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative measures like experience sampling with qualitative analyses of children's language use in describing their emotional experiences.

In line with constructionist approaches, emotions are considered mental events shaped by more basic psychological processes, with language playing a crucial role in this construction. This perspective implies that a richer emotional vocabulary can lead to a more nuanced understanding of one's own emotional states as well as those of others. Indeed, existing studies with adults suggest that individuals with higher emotional granularity demonstrate better emotion regulation skills, which are crucial for navigating daily challenges and maintaining well-being. High emotional granularity is also associated with a lower prevalence of certain psychiatric symptoms (e.g., low mood and anxiety) and reduced engagement in harmful health behaviours (e.g., alcohol consumption). Together, these findings suggest that increased emotional granularity may serve as a protective factor against mental and physical health difficulties.

Despite the clear association between emotional granularity for well-being, it remains understudied in younger populations. This research will explore how emotional granularity develops across childhood and adolescence, potentially identifying sensitive periods for intervention. Insights from this study may contribute to the development of educational programs aimed at fostering emotional literacy and well-being in children and adolescents. Identifying early markers of challenges in emotional differentiation could support early interventions to mitigate mental health risks.

In summary, this PhD project holds substantial promise for advancing our understanding of emotional granularity and its developmental trajectory, with applications for both theoretical frameworks and practical intervention

listings.summary: This project examines how children understand and use emotion words, and how emotional vocabulary shapes their emotional development and wellbeing. Focusing on emotional granularity (i.e., how precisely emotions are perceived and labelled) and the range of words children use to describe feelings, it explores the role…
listings.description:
This project examines how children understand and use emotion words, and how emotional vocabulary shapes their emotional development and wellbeing. Focusing on emotional granularity (i.e., how precisely emotions are perceived and labelled) and the range of words children use to describe feelings, it explores the role of language in supporting emotional awareness, expression, and regulation. While adults with richer emotional vocabularies often experience greater self-insight and wellbeing, the impact in children remains largely unknown. This raises a critical question: can enhancing children’s emotional vocabulary meaningfully influence their wellbeing, and if so, how?

This PhD project will investigate how children understand, use, and benefit from emotion words, examining the role of language in emotional development. At its core, the project focuses on emotional granularity (i.e., how precisely children perceive and label emotions) and emotion vocabulary, the range of words they use to describe feelings. While adults with richer emotional vocabularies often show greater self-insight and wellbeing, the evidence for children is limited.

The project will explore how children’s emotional vocabulary relates to their understanding, expression, and regulation of emotions across contexts such as peer interactions, classroom behaviour, and mental health. Many interventions aim to enhance children’s emotional word knowledge, but their impact on wellbeing is not yet well established, creating an important gap this project could address.

The project is deliberately broad, allowing exploration of theoretical, applied, or methodological questions. It offers a unique opportunity to generate novel insights into how language shapes emotional development and wellbeing, informing future interventions and educational strategies.

listings.summary: Freezing of gait (FoG) is a debilitating symptom of Parkinson’s Disease during which individuals feel like their “feet are glued to the floor”. However, the exact cause of this phenomenon is unknown. The goal of this project is to identify the abnormal brain activity that leads to FoG in PD.
listings.description:
Freezing of gait (FoG) is a debilitating symptom of Parkinson’s Disease during which individuals feel like their “feet are glued to the floor”. However, the exact cause of this phenomenon is unknown. The goal of this project is to identify the abnormal brain activity that leads to FoG in PD.

Freezing of gait (FoG) is a major cause of falls and reduced quality of life in Parkinson’s disease, yet its neural basis is poorly understood. This project will use high-density mobile EEG, electromyography, and motion capture to measure brain activity during balance perturbations and clinical gait assessments. By identifying cortical signatures that precede and occur during FoG episodes, we aim to uncover biomarkers of freeze risk. The findings could inform adaptive therapies, such as rehabilitation or closed-loop deep brain stimulation, to improve mobility and independence.

listings.title: Inclusivity in Higher Education: Exploring Contexts, Barriers, and Facilitators of Positive Student Experiences
listings.summary: This PhD Project aims to develop a framework for considering compassionate pedagogy in higher education, which focuses on facilitating learning in a way that includes and interacts caringly with all people. It will explore the diverse experiences of students from under-represented backgrounds studying in Higher…
listings.description:
This PhD Project aims to develop a framework for considering compassionate pedagogy in higher education, which focuses on facilitating learning in a way that includes and interacts caringly with all people. It will explore the diverse experiences of students from under-represented backgrounds studying in Higher Education. The project aims to identify key factors which are important to facilitate positive student experiences and utilise these to develop recommendations for an inclusive curriculum which is driven by compassionate pedagogy.

This PhD project will aim to investigate contexts, barriers, and facilitators of positive student experiences whilst studying in Higher Education. This project will use a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative measures of student experience: sense of belonging, academic self-efficacy, student engagement with qualitative analyses of students’ lived experiences when studying in Higher Education. A two- tiered approach, rooted in pedagogical and psychological theories, will be used to analyse students’ experiences. Specifically, ‘micro’ and ‘macro’ level experiences will be explored. Micro-level experiences relate to students’ day to day experiences of completing their studies and includes: learning environments, peer-peer learning opportunities, engagement at classes, and psychological states. Macro-level experiences encompass students’ experiences more broadly whilst attending Higher Education, for example, academic performance, skill proficiency, psychological traits, and other sociocultural factors.

This project aims to investigate higher education institutions (HEIs) nationally to determine what initiatives they have in place to foster an inclusive curriculum embedded in compassionate pedagogy. This will be considered in accordance with the Universal Design for Learning (UDL; Smith, 2012) framework which is a promising, but underused, framework which assists Higher Education institutions to create learning environments that are accessible to all students. It is expected features of this framework currently exist at the ‘micro-level’, being incorporated by individual members of educators in their teaching with differential impact on student experiences. Therefore, this project will align quantitative and qualitative results from students’ experiences to curriculum design within the UDL framework to provide a novel contribution to curriculum design research.

listings.title: Beyond Labels: Mapping Early Dimensions of Neurodivergence in Infancy
listings.summary: This project investigates how the brain develops along diverse pathways in the first years of life, aiming to reveal the earliest origins of neurodivergence. Moving beyond traditional diagnostic labels, it will use large-scale infant neuroimaging and behavioural datasets (HBCD, BCD) to identify neural and cognitive…
listings.description:
This project investigates how the brain develops along diverse pathways in the first years of life, aiming to reveal the earliest origins of neurodivergence. Moving beyond traditional diagnostic labels, it will use large-scale infant neuroimaging and behavioural datasets (HBCD, BCD) to identify neural and cognitive dimensions that shape early development. By uncovering how these patterns emerge and vary across individuals, the research will advance our understanding of early brain organisation and inform developmentally grounded, non-stigmatizing approaches to supporting neurodivergent children.

Research trying to understand neurodivergence is still much reliant on diagnostic criteria that classify individuals in distinct categories. However, recent findings show these categorical classifications, while currently useful in the clinical setting for want of better strategies, fail to reliably capture variability and complexity both between and within diagnostic groups. In contrast transdiagnostic clustering approaches which focus on uncovering different dimensions of cognitive and brain functioning have shown promise in explaining variability across neurodevelopmental conditions in older children and adolescents (Siugzdaite et al., 2020). However, such models have yet to be applied to infancy, where the earliest origins of divergence lie (Astle et al., 2024). This project will harness large-scale open datasets from the Healthy Brain and Child Development (HBCD; 0-9 months) and Baby Connectome (BCD; 0-5 years) studies, each containing thousands of neuroimaging and behavioural datapoints, to characterise the developmental pathways of neurodivergence in the first years of life. By integrating multimodal data and advanced clustering methods, the research will provide a new framework for identifying early markers of neurodivergence. This work is essential not only for advancing basic science but also for supporting early, non-stigmatizing, and developmentally informed approaches to intervention and policy (Astle et al., 2022, Fletcher-Watson 2022).

listings.title: Two halves make a whole: Exploring the role of the families in caring for police officers with occupational related psychological distress.
listings.summary: This PhD project will focus on spouses / intimate partners who have cared for police officers with occupational related psychological distress. Through survey data collection and in depth interviews we will gain a better understanding of the role of the family and how caring for those with psychological distress has…
listings.description:
This PhD project will focus on spouses / intimate partners who have cared for police officers with occupational related psychological distress. Through survey data collection and in depth interviews we will gain a better understanding of the role of the family and how caring for those with psychological distress has impacted on them and their children. This project will be a mixed methods project utilising both quantitative (survey methodology) and qualitative (respondent interviews) data collection methods.

A wealth of literature has focused on the psychosocial determinants of health and well-being in first responder populations such as police officers. The focus has been placed on these populations as they are often at an increased risk for exposures to traumatic incidents through the nature of their occupational roles and therefore are also at an increased risk of developing adverse posttraumatic outcomes. Less attention has been given in the research literature to the impact that this has on the families of police officers and the caring responsibilities that family members face in times of the development of post-trauma difficulties. Police officers often work in environments which are fast-paced, may require long and sometimes unexpected hours, and which may place them in direct danger. This can disrupt family schedules, upset children, and cause worry and distress in spouses / intimate partners. When psychological difficulties present in police officers due to occupational traumas it is often the family who first notice and have to attend to the distress. They have to care for the police officer and navigate situations which minimise family disruption and at times minimise the potential impact on children.

listings.title: Identifying psychological mechanisms which promote resilience post-trauma.
listings.summary: This PhD project will explore the mechanisms between the trauma and resilience relationship. We are interested in the process of flexible self-regulation, which is a multi-component concept consisting of proficiency in context sensitivity, emotional regulation and having a flexible mindset (see Bonanno et al., 2004;…
listings.description:
This PhD project will explore the mechanisms between the trauma and resilience relationship. We are interested in the process of flexible self-regulation, which is a multi-component concept consisting of proficiency in context sensitivity, emotional regulation and having a flexible mindset (see Bonanno et al., 2004; Bonanno & Burton, 2013; Cheng, Lau, & Chan, 2014; Kashdan & Rottenberg, 2010). The population of interest is those who have experienced traumatic events and remained resilient, for example those who have worked as critical care nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic or those who have experienced occupational related traumas such as emergency responders, police, fire, and/or military. Prospective students can specify their choice of population in their proposal in addition to outlining a plan for access to the population. This will be a mixed methods study requiring a systematic review of the literature, and qualitative and quantitative studies.

Posttraumatic stress disorder was incorporated into the DSM-3 in 1982. An extensive body of literature has since focused on trauma experiences and their corresponding human responses. Of note, the predominant focus has been on negative psychological outcomes post-trauma including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) but also a range of other, often comorbid, psychopathological disorders such as depression and anxiety. The key question being: why is it that when people experience negative life events, they become psychologically unwell? This is an interesting focus given that population estimates of trauma exposure are exceptionally high in comparison to those who go on to develop a posttraumatic stress outcome. Conversely, epidemiological surveys have reported that even when we consider countries with the highest rate of PTSD within the population, this rate equates to approximately 8.8% (this is the rate of PTSD in NI as recorded by the Northern Ireland Study for Health and Stress which was part of the World Mental Health Consortium). So in reality more people who experience trauma remain psychologically well than those who become psychologically unwell. This is referred to as resilience. This concept has arguably received less attention in the academic literature compared to PTSD. In fact, as recent as the early nighties the concept was ignored, denied or at best regarded as a rare form of ‘exceptional emotional strength’ (Casella & Motta, 1990; Shedler, Mayman, & Manis, 1993). listings.summary: Domestic violence and abuse (DVA) is a global concern that is related to poor nutritional outcomes for survivors including binge eating disorder and relatedly, obesity. This may be driven by poor mental health and maladaptive emotions such as shame. This project will use an array of methods to investigate these…
listings.description:
Domestic violence and abuse (DVA) is a global concern that is related to poor nutritional outcomes for survivors including binge eating disorder and relatedly, obesity. This may be driven by poor mental health and maladaptive emotions such as shame. This project will use an array of methods to investigate these relationships.

Domestic violence and abuse (DVA) is a global concern that has deleterious consequences for the physical and psychological health of women and children, often linked to mental ill health outcomes such as Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression and anxiety (Lagdon, Stringer & Armour, 2014). Likewise, evidence has demonstrated a relationship between DVA and poor nutritional outcomes for survivors including binge eating disorder and relatedly, obesity (Mason et al, 2013). Notably, the relationship between DVA and poor nutritional outcomes can be seen when the DVA occurs in childhood, adolescence, and/or adulthood.

Noll et al. (2007) reported that girls who experienced childhood sexual abuse are more likely to be obese in young adulthood than those who were not. In a similar vein, a longitudinal cohort study conducted in the US, demonstrated an increased BMI in maltreated children compared to non-maltreated children in middle to late adolescence (Schneiderman et al. 2012). When adolescent girls are exposed to dating violence, studies have shown that an increased BMI is likely, compared to non-exposed peers (Clark et al., 2014). Marques et al. (2022) further supported the relationship between DVA and elevated BMI in a Brazilian study which focused on the outcomes of rape in adolescents over the age of 13. In a recent systematic review, Schroeder et al (2022) concluded that when assessing a range of adverse childhood experiences, sexual abuse had a greater risk of childhood obesity than any of the other adverse childhood experiences (ACE’s) and again that this was particularly the case for girls.

One mechanism that can explain the link between DVA and obesity is PTSD. Talbott et al (2013) demonstrated that PTSD was associated with emotional eating and that as PTSD severity increased so did the level of emotional eating. The Emotional Eating Theory (ETT: Macht et al., 2011) proposes that emotional eating is a maladaptive response to stressors. listings.title: It all adds up – Supporting children’s arithmetic from the start
listings.summary: Many children experience difficulties with mathematics that can persist into secondary school and adulthood. These difficulties often stem from fragile foundations formed in the early years of schooling, where key concepts are introduced but not always fully understood. One such concept is mathematical…
listings.description:
Many children experience difficulties with mathematics that can persist into secondary school and adulthood. These difficulties often stem from fragile foundations formed in the early years of schooling, where key concepts are introduced but not always fully understood. One such concept is mathematical equivalence—understanding that the equals sign (“=”) means that two quantities have the same value, rather than simply signalling where an answer should appear. Although this idea is fundamental, research shows that many children develop a rigid, procedural view of the equals sign, which later hampers flexible problem-solving and algebraic thinking.

This project aims to strengthen early arithmetic learning by focusing on equivalence as a core building block of mathematical understanding. Drawing on insights from psychology and education, the research will design and evaluate a classroom-based early intervention that exposes children to a wider range of equation formats and explicitly teaches the relational meaning of mathematical symbols. Rather than relying on remediation after misconceptions have already formed, the project targets children at the very start of formal arithmetic instruction, before rigid interpretations become entrenched.

The study will work with young pupils in Northern Ireland and compare an equivalence-focused intervention with an active control condition. By examining pupils’ accuracy, strategies, and common errors over time, the project will assess whether early, targeted instruction can promote more flexible numerical reasoning and support broader arithmetic development.

listings.title: Identifying as “Other”: Disidentification with Traditional Identities in a Divided Society
listings.summary: A bipartite system of categorisation and identification has been the traditional lens through which intergroup relations within Northern Ireland have been viewed, due to the wealth of evidence indicating that the Catholic and Protestant community identities underpin the division and conflict (Moxon-Browne, 1991).…
listings.description:
A bipartite system of categorisation and identification has been the traditional lens through which intergroup relations within Northern Ireland have been viewed, due to the wealth of evidence indicating that the Catholic and Protestant community identities underpin the division and conflict (Moxon-Browne, 1991). However, large-scale surveys have found a consistent increase in the percentage of individuals who identify as belonging to neither the Catholic nor the Protestant community, percentages which vastly outnumber the estimates of ethnic minority populations, suggesting that a growing number of respondents are making a conscious decision to move away from the traditional community identities which may define the area in which they are raised and the identity which their family may still hold. Guided by the social identity approach, this PhD project will explore self-categorisation as “Other” as two distinct processes, disidentification with traditional community backgrounds and identification and sense of belonging with a new, distinct social group. Through focus groups, secondary data-analysis, and cross-sectional research, the project will explore the motivational factors underpinning disidentification, the demographic profile of those choosing to identify as “Other”, and the relationship between the perceived entitativity and collective mobilisation in the form of support for peacebuilding efforts.

listings.title: Transgenerational Contact: Exploring how a Child’s Positive Intergroup Relationships Improves Parental Intergroup Attitudes and Behaviours
listings.summary: The extended contact hypothesis (Wright et al., 1997) predicts that knowing an ingroup member has cross-group friends improves intergroup attitudes. This varies as a function of the relationship with the ingroup member, with closer ingroup relationships resulting in stronger impacts on intergroup attitudes (Tausch, et…
listings.description:
The extended contact hypothesis (Wright et al., 1997) predicts that knowing an ingroup member has cross-group friends improves intergroup attitudes. This varies as a function of the relationship with the ingroup member, with closer ingroup relationships resulting in stronger impacts on intergroup attitudes (Tausch, et al., 2011). The current project explores this premise within the unique relationship of parent and child by exploring how contact interventions with children appear to facilitate transgenerational contact - parent’s indirect exposure to those of other ethnic and religious groups via their children's direct exposure. This PhD project will explore the power of transgenerational contact to mitigate divisive social attitudes and to influence indicators of positive peace through cross-sectional and longitudinal studies. Participants (child and parent(s)) will be accessed via the Northern Ireland school system where sampling will occur via shared education as opposed to planned integrated education, so that parental choice in educational setting, can be removed from the equation.

listings.description:
This project examines the contested role of single-identity work in Northern Ireland. Building on a novel psychological pathway, we posit that a secure social identity is a necessary precursor for sustained, high-quality intergroup contact. This subsequent contact directly challenges sectarian prejudices and fosters the agency required to resist paramilitary narratives. The project provides the first rigorous test of this model to inform government peacebuilding policy.

This doctoral research addresses a central theoretical conundrum in social psychology and peacebuilding: the relationship between intra-group strengthening and intergroup harmony. It critically engages with Social Identity Theory (SIT) and the tenets of Intergroup Contact Theory, challenging the implicit assumption that focusing on in-group identity is inherently antagonistic to successful contact.

The project is driven by a novel, sequential psychological model that specifies the conditions under which in-group focus can benefit intergroup relations. The model posits that effective single-identity work first cultivates a robust and secure social identity within the group, which is notably independent from the negation of the "other." This internal group security is then translated into heightened confidence in contact—the necessary social self-efficacy and readiness to approach challenging intergroup interactions without the threat of identity loss or acute intergroup anxiety.

This crucial precondition ultimately facilitates the formation of high-quality, sustained contact, which acts as the direct mechanism for reducing prejudice. The entire sequence culminates in the development of agency to resist divisive narratives and sectarianism.

The research design will be defined by the student in consultation with the supervisory team, but is expected to feature a robust mixed-methods approach. This will include quantitative analysis, likely featuring a longitudinal design to explore causal dynamics within the context of ongoing community interventions. Crucially, in-depth qualitative work (e.g., interviews and focus groups) will be essential to provide rich psychological detail regarding the emergent constructs of secure social identity and contact confidence, particularly among individuals with more fragile or reactive identities. The student will also be encouraged to integrate participatory research or co-design principles when engaging with young people in community settings.

listings.description:
This project will focus on trauma appraisals as a possible mediator between potential outcomes of posttraumatic stress, resilience or posttraumatic growth following potentially traumatic life events.

Not everyone that experiences potential traumatic events (PTEs) develops posttraumatic stress or negative mental health consequences. In fact, most people may remain resilient or even develop posttraumatic growth following these PTEs.

Ehlers and Clark's (2000) cognitive model of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) highlights the importance of negative appraisals in maintaining posttraumatic stress and these ‘trauma appraisals’ may be an important factor in helping to explain people’s reaction following PTEs.

listings.description:
This PhD project will investigate the prevalence, psychological impact, and support needs of bereaved university students in Northern Ireland, addressing a critical gap in evidence that limits how universities design effective wellbeing support. In Phase 1, the student will recruit a large cohort of bereaved students to examine how grief affects wellbeing, academic functioning, help-seeking, and service use, generating the first contemporary regional dataset in this area. In Phase 2, these findings will inform the co-design and evaluation of an AI-enhanced digital Student Grief Portal, integrating practical university guidance with a psychologically informed conversational agent to support early identification, personalised signposting, and scalable support delivery. The project offers strong opportunities for high-impact publications, digital innovation, policy engagement, and interdisciplinary funding development.

Bereavement is a near-universal human experience - almost everyone will, at some point, experience the death of someone close - yet the psychological impact of loss is shaped by complex individual, social, cultural, and structural forces. Despite this, bereavement in higher education remains critically under-researched. A recent systematic review of bereavement support in UK and Irish universities highlights limited visibility, fragmented provision, and a lack of evidence-based, student-informed pathways to care (Graham et al., 2025). It is estimated that approximately one-third of students experience the death of a close relative or friend during their studies, yet universities lack coordinated or accessible support structures (Balk et al., 2010). Kaplow et al. (2010) found that bereaved students are 40% more likely to show significant depressive symptoms than their non-bereaved peers, illustrating that grief is not only an emotional experience but one that significantly disrupts students’ academic functioning and wellbeing. Recent research suggests that 35–55% of students have experienced a death in the past two years (Hay et al., 2024), and while many adapt, up to 10% experience prolonged or complicated grief with substantial impacts on mental health, academic continuity, and retention (Hay et al., 2024). Although bereavement is widely studied in clinical and social psychology, there is a notable gap in research specifically addressing university students, particularly in Northern Ireland. listings.summary: In 2022 it was estimated that globally more than 1.9 billion adults live with overweight, 650 million live with obesity, and 38.2 million children live with overweight or obesity. Obesity and inactivity have been linked to a range of comorbidities including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension (high blood…
listings.description:
In 2022 it was estimated that globally more than 1.9 billion adults live with overweight, 650 million live with obesity, and 38.2 million children live with overweight or obesity. Obesity and inactivity have been linked to a range of comorbidities including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension (high blood pressure), depression and cancers. Thus, reductions in obesity and inactivity through physical activity intervention can reduce illness risk and improve quality of life. The Daily Mile (TDM) is a popular initiative that has increased children’s physical activity, yet adherence has not been assessed and the quality of the research evaluating the daily mile has been limited. The main addition of the proposed study is to address shortcomings raised in a systematic review to better support TDM initiative as it shows so much potential to improve children's health. With support from the Daily Mile Foundation, our participant involvement group and evidence from our recent systematic review we will make changes to TDM to better support teachers provide autonomy-based instructional techniques that include more choice to children undertaking TDM.

Based on the COM-B model we aims to assess an evidenced informed version of an autonomy-supported daily mile initiative to cognitive function and wellbeing of children aged 10-11 years, and assess adherence to taking part. A second aim is to assess the fidelity of the intervention. The final aim is to determine the health economic benefits of taking part in the revised daily mile and establish how a low cost, scalable initiative can benefit health.

listings.title: The Development of Psychologically Informed Mental Health Guidelines for Community Sport
listings.summary: Several international consensus and position statements on mental health in sport have been published by academics, international societies, and sporting bodies (e.g., International Olympic Committee). Yet, the focus of the majority of these statements has been on elite athlete provision who represent less than 6% of…
listings.description:
Several international consensus and position statements on mental health in sport have been published by academics, international societies, and sporting bodies (e.g., International Olympic Committee). Yet, the focus of the majority of these statements has been on elite athlete provision who represent less than 6% of sporting participants (Breslin et al., 2019). Moreover, recommendations within such statements typically represent top-down, evidence-based guidance, to help policy makers and organisational bodies develop and write tailored mental health guidelines for their respective associations (Vella et al., 2021). Yet, the actioning of this guidance has not been comprehensively forthcoming in the community sports sector, including within the UK and Ireland, and it is likely sports bodies and policy makers require further practical direction (Vella & Swann, 2021; Prior et al., 2022). In the UK and Ireland, a series of welcomed Mental Health in Sport Charters, Wellbeing in Sport Action Plans and campaigns have been published by the Sport and Recreation Alliance, Sport Ireland, Sport Northern Ireland among others, with support and signatories from charities, national governing bodies of sport and prominent athletes. Such commitment represents an excellent starting point to enact the development of evidence-based mental health guidelines for community sports sector that can help improve mental health awareness, education and psychological safety on a national scale.

Phase 2: will include, (i) a Delphi study on a review of existing mental health guidance, and (ii) focus groups with key sport stakeholder groups (players, coaches, club officers and volunteers, officials, mental health experts by experience, sport association representatives, sport governing bodies, policy makers) to determine their understanding and views of mental health guidelines.

This PhD project will explore the ethical, economic, and political justifications for democratizing workplaces and economic relationships more broadly. The PhD candidate will research the political theory and organizational literature on democracy and workplace democracy, and will also investigate the practice of workplace democratization and democracy in various countries and sectors. The purpose of the project is to determine whether there is an ethical, economic, and political case for democratizing workplaces and, if so, whether this is possible under contemporary conditions.

This project will last for 3 years and will run alongside cognate research conducted by the political theory group within the School of History, Anthropology, Philosophy, and Politics. The PhD candidate will be mentored by academic staff with specialisms in democracy and workplace democracy and in wider political theory and philosophy. The ultimate goal of the project is to determine whether workplace democracy is desirable and feasible in contemporary economies, and how these economies might need to be changed to accommodate democratic practices. The candidate will have the space to develop the project as best they see fit under supportive supervision. It is expected that the candidate will work closely with colleagues in the political theory group in organizing seminars and producing publications on the project topic.

Dr Keith Breen’s research areas are political and social theory, his focus being questions of political ethics and philosophies of work and economic organization.

listings.title: Understanding the Roots of Polarization: How Children Form and Revise Beliefs
listings.summary: This PhD project investigates how and why polarized beliefs emerge, persist, or change across middle childhood. Building on the global Developing Belief Network, it explores the cognitive and social mechanisms through which children form, transmit, and revise beliefs about contested issues such as science, religion,…
listings.description:
This PhD project investigates how and why polarized beliefs emerge, persist, or change across middle childhood. Building on the global Developing Belief Network, it explores the cognitive and social mechanisms through which children form, transmit, and revise beliefs about contested issues such as science, religion, and morality. By comparing children in culturally and politically diverse societies—including Northern Ireland, the United States, Indonesia, South Africa, Singapore, and Greece—the project seeks to uncover how social context, identity, and trust in information sources shape belief rigidity or openness. The findings will provide critical insight into how early interventions can foster intellectual humility, empathy, and social cohesion—laying the groundwork for depolarization and peacebuilding.

This PhD forms part of the international Changing Minds research project, a longitudinal, cross-cultural investigation of how children develop, sustain, and revise their beliefs in polarized societies. While most polarization research focuses on adults, this project targets the developmental roots of these processes—examining how cognitive, social, and cultural factors interact to shape children’s belief systems from ages 8 to 12.

Drawing on data from the Developing Belief Network (DBN)—a global consortium of 50+ researchers across 19 countries—the project adopts a socio-ecological approach to study polarisation at multiple levels: individual cognition, family and peer dynamics, and broader cultural and political contexts. Using mixed-methods designs (structured interviews, longitudinal surveys, and experimental tasks), the project will:

• Identify cognitive and contextual predictors of belief rigidity and revision, including reasoning skills, identity salience, and exposure to diverse viewpoints.

• Examine children’s attitudes toward others with differing beliefs, linking epistemic polarization (diverging views of truth) to affective polarization (ingroup/outgroup bias).

The PhD student will have scope to focus on one or more sites (e.g., Northern Ireland and the USA) to examine how local histories of division, education systems, and parental belief transmission shape children’s reasoning about contested issues. The project will use longitudinal and comparative analyses to test when and how belief revision is most likely to occur, and what developmental or contextual factors foster depolarisation.

listings.title: How human perceptual and motor abilities shape human-robot interactions
listings.summary: With the advent of robot and AI technologies, many industries (including manufacturing) are starting embed robotic systems into the workplace. Rather than robots replacing humans, the current trend (Industry 5.0) is towards solutions that place humans at the core, in which humans and robots collaborate. Solutions are…
listings.description:
With the advent of robot and AI technologies, many industries (including manufacturing) are starting embed robotic systems into the workplace. Rather than robots replacing humans, the current trend (Industry 5.0) is towards solutions that place humans at the core, in which humans and robots collaborate. Solutions are foreseen in which task performance is optimized by capitalizing on the respective strengths of robots and humans. Lots of progress has been made over the past years in this context, but an outstanding challenge for human-robot interactions is to leverage human perceptual and motor abilities and preferences in designing robots and their control systems. Knowledge of human psychology and movement behaviour are key to addressing this challenge.

This PhD project examines how human performance in assembly-related actions depends on the design (i.e., the look and configuration of the robot arm) and control of the robot arm (i.e., how it moves, possibly as a function of movements of its human counterpart). The use of a virtual reality simulator for human-robot interactions affords studying aspects that are currently restricted in real robots based on safety constraints. The project is embedded in an ongoing collaboration with staff from QUB’s School of EEECS; the findings may inform the development of control algorithms for real-life human-robot systems.

listings.description:
Manual interception (such as catching and hitting) involves the continuous processing of information about the target (e.g., ball) and body – position and motion – to achieve accurate spatiotemporal control of hand movements. While a wealth of research has examined the mechanism by humans achieve this, many questions remain. This project aims to examine how visual information about target motion is combined with visual and proprioceptive information about the hand to achieve effective spatiotemporal motor control of interception movements.

In this project, we will manipulate what people see while they are asked to intercept a moving target, either presented in game-like experiments on a computer screen or in virtual reality. Detailed analyses of the interception movements will be used to examine what sensorimotor mechanisms best explain human behaviour.

listings.title: Reading the kicker: how goalkeeper’s rely on opponent movements to improve performance for penalties and free kicks
listings.summary: Penalties and free kicks are important components of football matches. In this project we will use virtual reality to examine how goalkeepers in both scenarios rely on the kicker’s movements to give themselves a bigger chance of blocking the shot.
listings.description:
Penalties and free kicks are important components of football matches. In this project we will use virtual reality to examine how goalkeepers in both scenarios rely on the kicker’s movements to give themselves a bigger chance of blocking the shot.

Penalties and free kicks are important during football matches. Well-taken penalties force goalkeepers to focus on the visible movements of the kicker, given that waiting for the ball to be kicked leaves insufficient time to reach the edge of the goal. In free kicks, goalkeepers could purely rely on visual ball motion, but they will also (attempt to) benefit from the visible kicker movements, for instance to anticipate the curve (which we know is visually harder to perceive). In this project, we aim to examine how goalkeepers rely on visible kicker kinematics in both situations and whether they can be trained to improve their use of this information, with a focus on the use of virtual reality (VR). To create a VR simulator, a database of kicking motions will be created; this will concern so-called independent kicks, in which the kicker does not alter their movement based on how the goalkeeper moves. The simulator will afford basic studies into goalkeeper behaviour as well as studies into the potential for training goalkeepers to read the kicker. The database is also intended to serve as training data for novel AI algorithms aimed at accurately replicating human full body movements. This project uses fundamental science and methods to examine a practical scenario and should be expected to yield both scientific and practical insights.

listings.title: Communicating Truth: Consumption and transmission of polarised information amongst young people in a divided society
listings.summary: This programme of research will investigate how young people evaluate the credibility of information in divided societies, including how they seek and share information.
listings.description:
This programme of research will investigate how young people evaluate the credibility of information in divided societies, including how they seek and share information.

We use mixed-methods to explore dynamic influences within broader socio-ecological systems. This is an opportunity for a researcher interested in developing an original and exciting programme of mixed-method empirical research related to the development of social cognition amidst polarisation. The student will lead on designing, conducting and disseminating rigorous research with young people. The project activities may include any of the following components: 1) computational text-mining to examine how narratives on identity and polarisation affect social learning; 2) diffusion chains, similar to an experimental game of telephone, to test biases in the transmission and consumption of polarised information across young people; and 3) qualitative interviews to elucidate the role of culture and social context, as well as thought processes around information consumption, transmission, and belief revision. Read more about the project here: Is ‘Truth’ as Objective as We Think? | Templeton World Charity Foundation, Inc.

listings.summary: Presenteeism refers to attending work while ill (Lohaus & Habermann, 2019; Johns, 2010). listings.description:
Presenteeism refers to attending work while ill (Lohaus & Habermann, 2019; Johns, 2010). The prevalence of presenteeism has intensified in recent years, driven by factors such as job insecurity, competitive work environments, and increasing workplace demands (Nath et al., 2024; Schmidt & Pförtner, 2020; McGregor et al., 2016). While scholars have documented the substantial costs of presenteeism, including decreased productivity, increased error rates, and potential health deterioration, our understanding of its leadership-related antecedents remains surprisingly limited (Vänni, 2017; Brooks, 2010; Goetzel et al., 2004). This gap is particularly concerning given the important role leaders play in shaping employee behaviors and decision-making processes.

Prior research has demonstrated that leadership significantly influences the reasons behind employee attendance. Leaders can affect attendance through various means: exerting authority to require presence, using their charisma to inspire voluntary attendance, offering incentives such as promotions or bonuses, or employing punitive measures (e.g., threatening punishment for non-attendance) (Atwater et al., 1997). While past studies have primarily explored consistent leadership styles like transformational and authentic leadership (Nielsen & Daniels, 2016; Dietz et al., 2020), the motivations and mechanisms driving presenteeism remain less understood. An emerging area of interest is leader behavioural inconsistency—discrepancies between leaders' words and actions or variations in behaviour across similar situations (Schilling et al., 2023; Priester & Petty, 1996; Suurd Ralph & Barling, 2023). This inconsistency can create ambiguity and uncertainty among employees. Although recent research has begun to investigate its effects on employee attitudes and general work behaviours (Suurd Ralph & Barling, 2023), there is still limited understanding of how and when such inconsistency influences employees' decisions to work while ill. Drawing on Psychological Safety Theory (Kahn, 1990; Frazier, 2017; Edmondson & Bransby, 2023), leader behavioural inconsistency may fundamentally undermine employees' sense of psychological safety, leading to increased presenteeism as a self-protective response. When leaders behave inconsistently, employees may experience heightened uncertainty about organizational expectations and fear potential negative consequences of taking sick leave, ultimately choosing to work while ill. listings.summary: The main objective of the project to investigate the neural basis (using fNIRS) underlying the relation between antagonistic personality traits, music listening and cognitive performance (executive functions and mathematical ability) in conditions of stress.
listings.description:
The main objective of the project to investigate the neural basis (using fNIRS) underlying the relation between antagonistic personality traits, music listening and cognitive performance (executive functions and mathematical ability) in conditions of stress.

The literature on the neural basis of antagonistic personality traits such as narcissism and psychopathy is very limited. Recently an ambitious study explored whether brain circuits captured with MRI could explain antagonistic personality trait scores (Bakiaj, Munoz, Bizzego, & Grecucci, 2025). Of the brain networks studied, four were associated with antagonistic personality traits. The first component comprises areas within the reward network, including the thalamus, caudate, anterior cingulate and prefrontal regions. The second component encompasses regions within the executive network, predominantly involving prefrontal and posterior areas. The third component includes regions within the default mode network (DMN), such as the angular gyrus, the precuneus and the posterior cingulate cortex. Lastly, the fourth component overlaps with areas of the visual network, primarily located in the occipital and temporal lobes. Within these networks, the reward related component correlated with narcissism, suggesting an association with the need for constant interpersonal rewards to enhance self-esteem and grandiosity in narcissistic individuals. Conversely, the DM-related component correlated with Machiavellianism, potentially reflecting the heightened strategic thinking employed by Machiavellian individuals for manipulation purposes (Bakiaj et al., 2025). While this was an important attempt to understand some of the mechanisms that underlie variation in antagonistic personality traits, the study had some important limitations. For example, antagonistic traits were assessed as unidimensional traits. In addition, brain networks were used only as predictors of antagonistic traits as opposed to studying how brain activity in prefrontal brain areas changes dynamically in conditions that simulate real-life situations (e.g., where one needs to perform under stress) and as a function of variation in antagonistic personality traits.

listings.title: Embracing Individuality in Complex Skill Learning: Variability, Adaptability, and Embodiment
listings.summary: Learning of movement-based skills has typically been treated in both research and practice as progression towards a single, optimal movement solution for a task. This can be seen in approaches to sports coaching, or neurological rehabilitation, for example. However, there are often many possible ways to move to…
listings.description:
Learning of movement-based skills has typically been treated in both research and practice as progression towards a single, optimal movement solution for a task. This can be seen in approaches to sports coaching, or neurological rehabilitation, for example. However, there are often many possible ways to move to achieve a task, and people can make use of these possibilities to find adaptive and even creative ways to perform action goals. This project will investigate complex skill learning as a process of individualisation of movement variability, taking seriously the different routes that learners with differing capabilities take to acquire new skills. It will also look at how training and practice can be enhanced to support these processes.

How do humans develop complex skills in ways that reflect their individual capabilities, constraints, and contexts? Traditional models of motor learning often aim toward a single, optimal movement pattern — an approach commonly found in domains such as sports coaching or neurorehabilitation. Yet emerging perspectives in cognitive science, including ecological psychology and 4E cognition (embodied, embedded, enactive, and extended), highlight a richer, more adaptive view of human skill acquisition. This PhD project will take the latter approach to investigate complex skill learning as a dynamic, individualised process, where movement variability is not noise to be eliminated, but a resource for exploration, flexibility, and creativity. By combining experimental methods with novel digital technologies, the project aims to understand how learners discover and refine personalised movement solutions — and how training interventions and/or environments can support this process.

The project will use experimental paradigms rooted in ecological psychology and dynamical systems theory, applying motion capture, audio/visual interfaces, and other signal-based data collection methods to capture the nuances of skill development. Through carefully designed action tasks, these experiments will explore how learners navigate a landscape of possible movement solutions, and how feedback or task constraints can guide this process.

Findings from this project have the potential to inform inclusive and flexible approaches to training and rehabilitation, supporting individuals in developing skills that suit their bodies, contexts, and goals — rather than conforming to a one-size-fits-all model.

listings.description:
Thermal cracking in the structural concrete of foundations, bridges, tunnel linings and other medium-sized elements has become an increasing problem in the past decades. Previous methods of predicting thermal cracking and stresses in concrete structures have until now relied entirely on empirical knowledge of previous construction. Now, with the advent of powerful computer processing capabilities, it is proposed that a more rigorous and theoretically validated approach needs to be adopted. Equipment has been developed together with practical experimental procedures for determining the heat of hydration and early age mechanical properties of concrete specimens undergoing the same temperature cycles as they would in a real structure in a separate project.

This project will simulate heat conduction and moisture migration, and conduct stress analysis using constitutive theory of concrete and predict thermal cracks using the finite element method and COMSOL software. The effects of concrete strength, i.e. normal and high, binder type and content, size of structural element, casting and ambient temperatures, formwork type and time of removal on the maximum temperature rise and magnitude of the thermal stresses will be investigated and the FE model and methods will be validated using the experimental data gathered from an already funded EPSRC research project.

This research involves several disciplines and can lead to good publications and practical recommendations when well conducted.

listings.description:
Ultra High Strength Fibre Reinforced Concrete (UHPFRC) has been developed which has enhanced homogeneity, enhanced microstructure, and enhanced ductility. The inclusion of fibres improves tensile strength, and also makes it possible to obtain the required level of ductility. The compressive strengths of UHPFRCs without application of pressure before and during setting are likely to be between 170 to 230 MPa depending on the post-set heat treatment (20 to 900C). Fracture energies are between 20,000 and 40,000 J.m-2 and moduli of elasticity between 50 to 60 GPa. UHPFRC appears to be a promising new material not only because of its enhanced ductility but also because the mixing and casting procedures are no different to existing procedures for normal and high strength concretes. UHPFRC has, however, a substantial increase in cost over and above that of conventional and even High Performance Concrete and it is therefore appropriate to identify applications which fully utilize UHPFRC’s mechanical properties and performance characteristics. Research therefore needs to be conducted to develop and commercialize types of precast products which utilize many of the enhanced properties of UHPFRC. listings.title: Structural Behaviour of Concrete Block Pavements: Finite Element Modelling of the effect of construction pattern and unit interlock
listings.summary: The maintenance or even replacement of cracked pavements requires considerable financial resources and puts a large burden on the budgets of local councils. In addition to these costs, local councils also face liability claims arising from uneven or cracked pedestrian pavements. These currently cost the Manchester…
listings.description:
The maintenance or even replacement of cracked pavements requires considerable financial resources and puts a large burden on the budgets of local councils. In addition to these costs, local councils also face liability claims arising from uneven or cracked pedestrian pavements. These currently cost the Manchester City Council and Preston City Council around £6 million a year each. Design procedures for concrete block pavements are empirical. A considerable amount of research has been directed towards producing design charts relating thickness of base and sub‐base material required based on the properties of the subgrade and the traffic characteristics. The design criteria are based on experience and adjusted, if needed, by means of onsite observation and accelerated trafficking tests. However, the accuracy of these methods is limited due to the fact that they are simplified/empirical procedures that ignore certain parameters such as the discontinuous nature of blocks.

A better understanding of the interaction between paving blocks, bedding sand and sub‐base is necessary in order to determine the mode of failure of pavements under load. Increasing applied stress may mobilize “rotational interlock”, providing increased pavement stiffness and thus increased load dissipation resulting in lower transmitted stress on the sub‐grade. The “rotational interlock” is dependent on the applied stress and this unfortunately is not accounted for in existing mathematical models. It is also dependent on the construction pattern, i.e. basket, stretcher and herringbone, with indications that the paving blocks in herringbone pattern support more load by better interlocking with each other and forming a “flat arch”.

Paving blocks are required to have a compressive strength of 49 N/mm2 and a tensile splitting strength of 3.5 N/mm2. It is the latter that is critical in ensuring good performance of pavements. The high compressive strength of 49 N/mm2 appears to be required for ensuring that the tensile splitting strength of 3.5 N/mm2 is obtained. However, there are also uncertainties as to whether this value of tensile splitting strength is actually needed.

Finite Element Modelling of pavements is needed. However, the complex geometry of concrete block pavements, e.g. discrete and discontinuous units laid in complex paving patterns and connected with jointing sand, still pose problems in achieving accurate predictive modelling of their behaviour under load. listings.summary: The development of sustainable products is necessary for the continued success of the precast concrete industry. The project aims to develop sustainable technologies and products that: (a) reuse discarded materials and reduce the need to use expensive 'natural' materials (whose extraction can destroy natural habitats…
listings.description:
The development of sustainable products is necessary for the continued success of the precast concrete industry. The project aims to develop sustainable technologies and products that: (a) reuse discarded materials and reduce the need to use expensive 'natural' materials (whose extraction can destroy natural habitats and which involve intricate supply chains) (b) have superior qualities compared to current best practice/products and extended lives (c) have a positive ecological and social impact (d) can offer value-added benefits and respond to a market need.

This project will focus on the production of Green Precast Concrete Products by investigating the possibility of completely replacing cement by waste materials of high silicon dioxide content, e.g., incinerator ash, basic oxygen steel slag, disposed ash, from coal-fired thermal power plants, into ash ponds or lagoons, together with waste alkali solutions from the chemical industry. The alkali activated ash may have cementitious properties similar to cement. The reaction has been shown to be possible but selection of materials to successfully achieve compressive strengths similar to cement remains a mystery, i.e. the process is based on trial and error of different combinations of materials. This is even with off the shelf alkali solutions of known concentration combined with ground granulated blast furnace slag (ggbs) that is known to be reactive in this way. Use of ggbs and commercially available alkali solutions make this type of concrete prohibitively expensive. Yet this same concrete can be made with 100% waste materials. There is a clear and urgent market need for cement free concrete products with reduced CO2 footprint. The testing and development will focus initialy on the production of ‘Green/Ecofriendly Paving Products' that use as a binder waste materials and thus do not require the use of cement. Cementless Concrete can use lagoon ash, basic oxygen steel slag, and ash from municipal waste incinerators, combined with waste alkali solutions from the chemical industry (production of one tonne of cement corresponds approximately to one tonne of CO2 released to the atmosphere). Research will concentrate on developing an understanding of the reaction mechanism between waste alkali solutions and industrial siliceous ashes. The mechanism of the reaction between these siliceous ashes and alkalis is not well-established. The work will be jointly supervised with the Earth & Ocean Sciences department

listings.summary: The overall aim of this project is to investigate the properties of the fiber reinforced polymer and how these vary along the length of the wind turbine blade. Laboratory tests on three meter length tips of blades will aim to determine likely failure modes, e.g., bolted connection, flexural and shear failures. Finite…
listings.description:
The overall aim of this project is to investigate the properties of the fiber reinforced polymer and how these vary along the length of the wind turbine blade. Laboratory tests on three meter length tips of blades will aim to determine likely failure modes, e.g., bolted connection, flexural and shear failures. Finite Element analysis will be used to model the behaviour of the whole length of the blade when used as a bridge girder.

A multinational research project entitled “Re-Wind” investigated the use of decommissioned wind turbine blades as girders in bridges. The issue of end-of-life of wind turbine blades is becoming a significant sustainability concern for wind turbine manufacturers, many of whom have committed to the 2030 or 2040 sustainability goals that include zero-waste for their products. Repurposing is the most sustainable end-of-life solution for wind turbine blades from an environmental, economic, and social perspective. The Network has designed and constructed two full-size pedestrian/cycle bridges—one on a greenway in Cork, Ireland and the other in a quarry in Draperstown, Northern Ireland, UK. The Queen’s University Belfast structural and technical support staff team has recently led a successful series of structural tests of the blade bridge constructed in the quarry in Draperstown. The bridge was heavily instrumented and monitored by multiple strain gauges, drone videography and digital image correlation. The bridge withstood an incredible 33 tonnes loading with a mid-span deflection of only 9 mm. The testing was also supported by Re-Wind collaborators from Georgia Tech, Munster Technological University and Brunel University. The tests demonstrated the enormous residual strength of end-of-life wind turbine blades and is expected to open up new structural repurposing applications for decommissioned composite material wind turbine blade. This research is based on work supported by the Department of the Economy (DfE) GRANT USI-116; by Science Foundation Ireland (SFI) GRANT 16/US/3334; and by the US National Science Foundation (NSF) under grant numbers 1701413 and 1701694.
