listings.title: Threats to One Health from global spread of cardiopulmonary nematodes under climate change
listings.summary: Lungworms in the genus Angiostrongylus are linked to emerging diseases in animals and humans, including through pneumonia, bleeding disorders and meningitis. This project will combine advanced modelling and molecular biology methods to understand how climate change is altering transmission pathways and contributing to…
listings.description:
Lungworms in the genus Angiostrongylus are linked to emerging diseases in animals and humans, including through pneumonia, bleeding disorders and meningitis. This project will combine advanced modelling and molecular biology methods to understand how climate change is altering transmission pathways and contributing to global parasite spread and One Health impacts.

Angiostrongylus lungworms cause disease in animals (e.g. A. vasorum in carnivores, causing verminous pneumonia and bleeding disorders) and humans (e.g. A. cantonensis, the rat lungworm, causing zoonotic eosinophilic meningitis). The life cycles are complex, involving a wide range of gastropod mollusc intermediate hosts, which are linked to the final hosts through trophic networks. The behaviour of the hosts in relation to climate is likely to modify direct effects of climate on parasite development, and drive non-linearity in responses to climate change. This project will explore the role of climate change in the global emergence of angiostrongylosis, and develop tools to enable prediction and tracking of infection dynamics in complex ecological systems. Methods used will include climate-driven models of transmission potential, to map predicted global climatic suitability; experiments on captive colonies of major gastropod intermediate host species to elucidate climate response norms in transmission-relevant behaviours; and molecular biology including in situ sequencing to track infection in complex trophic networks, with field data collection from Europe, southern Africa and South-East Asia. Insights will be applied under climate change scenarios to predict how distribution and infection risk will change under future conditions, including through intermediate host behaviour and trophic relationships.

listings.description:
Members of the KDM4A histone demethylase subfamily, which includes KDM4A, B, and C, hold pivotal roles in diverse biological processes. We propose that these enzymes directly and indirectly regulate transcription of key genes involved in stress response and post-stress recovery. This project aims to identify such genes and establish exact mechanism of regulation.

Members of the KDM4A histone demethylase subfamily, which includes KDM4A, B, and C, hold pivotal roles in diverse biological processes such as differentiation, double-strand break repair, proliferation, cell cycle regulation, genome stability, metabolic response, and stress response. Dysregulated expression of these subfamily members is observed across various cancers, including challenging-to-treat pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer, and triple-negative breast cancer, rendering them promising targets for anticancer therapy. However, due to their multifaceted activities, targeting specific oncogenic pathways proves challenging.

Both our research and existing literature suggest that these enzymes function as a master coordinator of diverse cellular processes. We propose that these enzymes directly and indirectly regulate transcription of key genes involved in stress response and post-stress recovery. This project aims to identify such genes and establish exact mechanism of regulation using combination of transcriptomics, chromatin accessibility assay, ChIP and investigation of long range genomic interactions. The identification of vulnerabilities stemming from these interactions could pave the way for novel therapeutic strategies in cancer treatment.

listings.title: The host-parasite-microbiome axis: a new paradigm in animal health
listings.summary: Parasitic helminths are responsible for >55% of livestock diseases and are a major concern for producers worldwide. Whilst it is well known that helminths secrete molecules that manipulate host immune responses to ensure their survival, we are just beginning to explore how helminths interact with microorganisms such…
listings.description:
Parasitic helminths are responsible for >55% of livestock diseases and are a major concern for producers worldwide. Whilst it is well known that helminths secrete molecules that manipulate host immune responses to ensure their survival, we are just beginning to explore how helminths interact with microorganisms such as bacteria.

Bacteria play an important role in ruminant health with “friendly” commensal species aiding digestion whilst pathogenic species can lead to disease. Although co-infection of sheep and cattle with flatworm parasites is extremely common, we know little about their impact on bacteria. The liver fluke, Fasciola hepatica and the rumen fluke, Calicophoron daubneyi, are the major endemic flatworm infections of ruminants in western Europe. Although sharing similar life-cycles, they occupy distinct niches within their ruminant hosts and show different pathology and pathogenicity. As such, they are ideal models for comparative studies. In this project, we will exploit recently generated genome, transcriptome and proteome resources to identify putative antimicrobial and immunomodulatory molecules secreted by these helminth species. These molecules, either secreted as soluble proteins, or packaged into extracellular vesicles, will be investigated in terms of their ability to influence the microbiome via direct antimicrobial action but also via modulation of host innate immune responses to microbial signatures. By studying this tripartite interaction, we will gain a better understanding of how host inflammatory responses play out, in the presence of both helminths and bacteria, and how this influences tolerance to commensal “friendly” microbes or clearance of pathogenic species.

listings.title: Understanding management efficacy towards biological invasions
listings.summary: Invasive species have contributed to the majority of extinction events globally and their economic costs exceed $400 billion annually. Despite these severe impacts, management actions have been delayed and deficient, dominated by unsustainable, reactive measures that often fail to achieve desired outcomes. This…
listings.description:
Invasive species have contributed to the majority of extinction events globally and their economic costs exceed $400 billion annually. Despite these severe impacts, management actions have been delayed and deficient, dominated by unsustainable, reactive measures that often fail to achieve desired outcomes. This project will characterise global management actions towards biological invasions to better understand and predict the drivers of management success.

While the ecological, social, and economic erosion caused by biological invasions continues to escalate, actions addressing invasive species are predominantly inefficient. Current damage costs from invasive species are an order of magnitude higher than management expenditures. Moreover, current management actions are mostly reactionary rather than preventative, with 25-times less invested proactively than reactively. Timely management investments towards invasive species can pay massive dividends by avoiding long-term damage and management costs.

While research has quantified disparities in levels of investment between damages and management, as well as management types, there has been no holistic global assessment of management efficacies. This project will address previously unreachable questions relating to (1) the types of management which have had the greatest effect at mitigating negative impacts, (2) the ideal time windows for management efficacy, (3) environmental, socio-economic, cultural, and political determinants of management success, and (4) combinations of management approaches which synergise to achieve the most effective outcomes. To realise its aim, this project will harness global assessments of economic/ecological impacts and dynamics of biological invasions. Together, these areas address a major knowledge gap in fundamental and applied invasion science within an urgent area surrounding management efficacy.

Facing declining incomes, policy changes market volatility, and rising input costs, farmers struggle to invest in sustainable agricultural technologies and access to finance. This study will examine the socioeconomic, structural, and behavioural factors influencing farmers’ investment decisions and access to finance, taking into consideration the different farm typologies

Farmers are increasingly required to make long-term strategic investment decisions to optimise production capacity, enhance competitiveness, and ensure economically sustainable agricultural practices that both reduce carbon emissions and improve profitability. However, these decisions are often made in the context of significant challenges, ranging from economic constraints and market volatility to rising input costs and evolving policy landscapes, such as changes in inheritance tax in the UK. Beyond economic considerations, non-economic factors, including farmers’ values, attitudes, and behavioural tendencies, also play a crucial role in shaping investment decisions. Sustainable agricultural production hinges not only on investment in physical capital such as machinery, infrastructure, and land improvements, but also on human and social capital, including skills development, knowledge exchange, and adoption of innovative tools such as data-driven decision-making and artificial intelligence. This study aims to examine the multifaceted determinants of farm investment behaviour and access to finance, focusing on the interaction between social, economic, structural, and behavioural factors. The outcomes will provide empirical evidence to inform policy interventions and financial support mechanisms that promote investments in the agricultural sector

listings.title: Capturing oligosaccharides from mammalian milk to determine their microbiological impact
listings.summary: Many mammalian milks contain compounds called oligosaccharides, and can be the third or fourth most abundant milk component. Human milk for example, can contain up to 20 g/L of oligosaccharides with over 200 different structures reported. However, these oligosaccharides are not digestible by the infant and appear to…
listings.description:
Many mammalian milks contain compounds called oligosaccharides, and can be the third or fourth most abundant milk component. Human milk for example, can contain up to 20 g/L of oligosaccharides with over 200 different structures reported. However, these oligosaccharides are not digestible by the infant and appear to serve primarily as a source of prebiotics to microorganisms in the offspring’s developing gastrointestinal microbiome. The importance of milk oligosaccharides and microbiome development has been explored, to date, largely through correlative studies of oligosaccharide composition of milk and microbial communities. In this project, we propose the use of surface capture chemistry to trap oligosaccharides from different mammalian milks onto a surface to accommodate microbiological study. Through this, we aim to achieve a better understanding of how specific milk oligosaccharides interact with different microorganisms, both beneficial and pathogenic species.

This project has interdisciplinarity at its core, and this will be reflected in the offered training. Technical expertise will be developed across microbiology (including anaerobic culture), analytical biochemistry (primarily mass spectrometry for small molecule analysis), and biofabrication for developing surface-capture methodologies for milk oligosaccharides. The student will further have opportunities to undertake public engagement activities within the Northern Ireland Science Festival and Breastival, which works to normalise breastfeeding.

listings.title: Evolution of the commensal microbiome under repeated pathogen exposure
listings.summary: Bacterial pathogens are associated with more than 7 million infection-related deaths per year. listings.description:
Bacterial pathogens are associated with more than 7 million infection-related deaths per year. The spread of antibiotic resistance is threatening our ability to successfully treat infections and is driving increases in mortality and costs across healthcare systems worldwide. In order to infect a host, a bacterial pathogen must first successfully invade the host-associated microbiome. Commensal microbes reside in this microbiome without harming host health and can provide colonisation resistance against pathogens via several direct and indirect mechanisms, including toxin antagonism, nutrient blocking, or through interactions with host immunity.

The goal of this PhD is to investigate the evolution of commensal microbes in response to repeated pathogen exposure, and to understand how the acquisition of antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens impacts the commensal microbes they interact with. This project will help us understand the mechanisms by which commensal microbes can resist pathogen invasion, the impact of antibiotic resistance on these outcomes, and the extent to which pathogen invasion forms a selective pressure in the microbiome. Application of this knowledge could improve our ability to manipulate the microbiome to enhance colonization resistance.

listings.title: Dissecting the molecular aetiology of myeloid neoplasia using targeted protein degradation and chemoproteomics
listings.summary: Cells respond to their environment through networks of interacting proteins that pass information, control behaviour and maintain cellular states. A change in a single protein can alter the behaviour of the whole network however, blocking that protein does not necessarily reverse the change. Cells can redirect signals…
listings.description:
Cells respond to their environment through networks of interacting proteins that pass information, control behaviour and maintain cellular states. A change in a single protein can alter the behaviour of the whole network however, blocking that protein does not necessarily reverse the change. Cells can redirect signals through alternative routes, making it difficult to determine which proteins are essential to the network and which are simply associated with it.

This PhD will use genetically defined blood cell systems as models for investigating how signalling networks are organised and maintained. It will focus on two altered signalling proteins, JAK2 and KIT, which allow the effects of a specific genetic change to be studied within a complex human cellular network. The project will use PROTACs, molecules that recruit the cell’s own protein disposal machinery to remove a selected protein. Unlike conventional inhibitors, PROTACs eliminate the whole protein, including any structural or organisational roles it may perform. The student will establish which proteins can be efficiently removed in living cells, identify degraders for up to two important network components, and compare protein removal with conventional inhibition. This will reveal how catalytic and structural functions contribute to signalling network behaviour and how networks adapt when individual components are removed.

Working across the University of Glasgow’s School of Chemistry and Queen’s University Belfast’s Chemoproteomics Centre of Excellence, the student will combine medicinal chemistry with advanced analysis of proteins and cellular signalling. They will receive training in medicinal chemistry, chemical and quantitative proteomics, cell biology, CRISPR and computational data analysis.

listings.title: Can bio-based additives enhance microbial recruitment and degradation of plastics without compromising performance?
listings.summary: Plastic pollution is a major global challenge, driven by the widespread use of durable plastics that can persist in the environment for decades or centuries after disposal. This project will investigate whether bio-based additives, including materials such as wood flour, algal biomass, and chitin, can enhance the…
listings.description:
Plastic pollution is a major global challenge, driven by the widespread use of durable plastics that can persist in the environment for decades or centuries after disposal. This project will investigate whether bio-based additives, including materials such as wood flour, algal biomass, and chitin, can enhance the biodegradability of common plastics while maintaining the mechanical properties required for practical applications.

This is founded on evidence that microorganisms capable of degrading natural polymers can often degrade synthetic plastics, reflecting structural and chemical similarities between these materials. The project will investigate how bio-based additives influence material performance, microbial colonisation, and biodegradation, and whether they can recruit microbial communities that promote degradation of the underlying plastic polymer.

The project combines environmental microbiology, microbial ecology, and materials science. The student will formulate and characterise composite plastics, assess their performance using a range of mechanical and analytical techniques, and evaluate biodegradation in soil, compost,

freshwater, and marine microcosms. Advanced microbiological approaches will be used to investigate microbial attachment, biofilm formation, and community succession, while identifying microorganisms and synthetic consortia with plastic-degrading potential that could

be exploited in future biotechnological applications. The student will graduate with a highly interdisciplinary skillset spanning materials

characterisation, environmental microbiology, microbial ecology, molecular biology, advanced imaging, microfluidics, data analysis, and scientific communication, preparing them for careers in academia, environmental biotechnology, materials science, industrial R&D, sustainability research, and the bioeconomy sector.

listings.title: Enzyme-responsive self-assembling antimicrobial peptides for the eradication of biofilm-associated persister cells in diabetic foot ulcer infection
listings.summary: Bacteria living in biofilms can survive antibiotics without being genetically resistant. A small group, knownas persister cells, becomes dormant during treatment and starts growing again afterwards. These cells
listings.description:
Bacteria living in biofilms can survive antibiotics without being genetically resistant. A small group, knownas persister cells, becomes dormant during treatment and starts growing again afterwards. These cells

This project will investigate persister cells in diabetic foot ulcer infections, where complex biofilms containing bacteria such as MRSA can make infections difficult to treat. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are

promising because they can kill dormant cells by attacking their membranes. However, enzymes found in chronic wounds can rapidly break them down.

The project will turn this challenge into a new treatment strategy. The student will engineer AMPs that respond to infection-associated enzymes by self-assembling at the wound site, creating a concentrated

antimicrobial material that can penetrate and kill biofilms. Lead candidates will be tested against clinical isolates in multi-species wound biofilms and 3D human skin models, examining both antimicrobial activity and effects on inflammation and wound healing.

The student will gain interdisciplinary training in antimicrobial discovery, peptide engineering, biofilm microbiology and skin immunology.

listings.title: Engineering bioactive peptides for vaginal microbiome restoration and sustained vaginal delivery
listings.summary: The vaginal microbiome plays an important role in urogenital health, but disruption of protective Lactobacillus-associated communities can lead to persistent dysbiosis and biofilm formation. Current antimicrobial approaches can reduce bacterial burden without necessarily restoring beneficial microbiome function.
listings.description:
The vaginal microbiome plays an important role in urogenital health, but disruption of protective Lactobacillus-associated communities can lead to persistent dysbiosis and biofilm formation. Current antimicrobial approaches can reduce bacterial burden without necessarily restoring beneficial microbiome function.

This PhD will investigate whether engineered bioactive peptides can selectively shift disrupted vaginal microbiome models towards a more protective state. The student will establish defined in vitro microbiome models, screen and optimise peptide candidates, and determine how

peptide sequence and physicochemical properties influence microbial selectivity, biofilm behaviour and restoration of Lactobacillus-associated functions. The project will also evaluate selected Bdellovibrio-derived bioactives, alone and in combination with lead peptides, to explore complementary mechanisms for microbiome modulation. Promising strategies will be validated in vaginal epithelial models and assessed for compatibility with local vaginal delivery.

The student will receive interdisciplinary training in peptide design and synthesis, analytical characterisation, microbiology, biofilm science, vaginal microbiome models, epithelial systems and data analysis.

student will also complete an industry placement and gain experience in candidate prioritisation, formulation constraints, local delivery, commercial decision-making and intellectual property awareness.

listings.title: Elucidating the Functional Role of Infection Factors from Entomopathogenic Nematodes
listings.summary: We have recently demonstrated the power of using the Drosophila model to determine novel parasitic nematode infection factors and elucidate the genetic and functional bases of host anti-nematode defense. This project will use omics together with reverse genetics and functional approaches to reveal original…
listings.description:
We have recently demonstrated the power of using the Drosophila model to determine novel parasitic nematode infection factors and elucidate the genetic and functional bases of host anti-nematode defense. This project will use omics together with reverse genetics and functional approaches to reveal original entomopathogenic nematode infection strategies in Drosophila.

We aim to understand the infective process of entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) and the host’s immune response to infection. Our hypothesis is that EPNs produce proteins which interact with the host immune and metabolic responses to promote pathogenicity during the early stages of insect infection.

We have identified three putative virulence factors that are up-regulated early in infection. We will test the hypothesis that these molecules facilitate infection by interfering with the host immune signaling and function and altering its metabolic activity.

First, we will determine the combined action of H. bacteriophora candidate virulence factors and P. luminescens infection on the fly innate immune signaling activity and function. Then, we will perform gene knockdown to explore the role of EPN candidate virulence factors on host survival and interaction with the host anti-nematode response. Finally, we will determine the effect of H. bacteriophora candidate virulence factors on lipid metabolism in D. melanogaster.

Results from this research will provide critical information on the molecular basis of EPN infection and the nature of nematode molecules that compromise the insect host defense. This information can be used to advance efforts in the biocontrol of agricultural insect pests and vectors of plant and human diseases.

listings.title: Engineering Long-Lasting Broad-Spectrum Innate Immune Antivirals
listings.summary: This project seeks to discover and develop novel means to push the temporal limits of innate antiviral immunity of epithelial and immune cells against emerging viruses with pandemic potential through a combination of computational, cellular and molecular approaches.
listings.description:
This project seeks to discover and develop novel means to push the temporal limits of innate antiviral immunity of epithelial and immune cells against emerging viruses with pandemic potential through a combination of computational, cellular and molecular approaches.

Viruses continue to be a major global burden to the health and wellbeing of humans, animals, and ecosystems. Emerging zoonotic viruses that spillover from animals into the human population represent a clear future pandemic threat, particularly for respiratory infections, or vector-borne diseases driven by climate change. The diversity and unpredictability of zoonoses are a massive challenge in developing effective, rapid countermeasures.

One answer to this problem lies in our own innate immune system that has evolved to quickly defend against myriad viruses. However, due to evolutionary and biological constraints such pathways are poorly optimised for sustained, safe activity. Therefore, this project seeks to overcome these challenges and engineer longterm antiviral immunity in both mucosal and systemic tissues against airborne viruses and arboviruses.

You will use cutting-edge computational biology and machine learning tools, combined with molecular genetic manipulation of host cells and viral pathogens like influenza viruses and flaviviruses under high-containment to: i) determine the temporal limits of natural antiviral immune signalling pathways in airway epithelial and immune cells; ii) uncover underlying induced RNA and protein biomarkers of signalling kinetics; and iii) identify genetic and biochemical modifiers of these targets in order to safely enhance their longevity.

listings.title: Beyond antibiotics: the impact of non-antibiotic drugs on the selection of antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
listings.summary: The goal of this PhD project is to investigate how commonly used non-antibiotic drugs in combination with antibiotics can impact the evolution of antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a high priority pathogen and leading cause of severe hospital-acquired infections.
listings.description:
The goal of this PhD project is to investigate how commonly used non-antibiotic drugs in combination with antibiotics can impact the evolution of antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a high priority pathogen and leading cause of severe hospital-acquired infections.

The emergence and spread of multi-drug resistant (MDR) bacterial pathogens, virtually untreatable by antibiotics, poses a fundamental threat to human health. While it has been long-established that treating patients with antibiotics selects for resistant bacteria, recent studies have elucidated that many commonly used non-antibiotic drugs may also have unintended antimicrobial effects, and can impact the development and spread of resistance, despite this not being their intended use. The goal of this PhD project is to investigate how commonly used non-antibiotic drugs in combination with antibiotics can impact the evolution of antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a high priority pathogen and leading cause of severe hospital-acquired infections. The PhD student will develop skills in experimental evolution, high-throughput microbiology, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, whole-genome sequencing and analysis, bacterial genetics, and fitness assays in complex environments.

listings.title: Weed Out the Worms – Exploiting Endocannabinoid Biology for Nematode Parasite Control
listings.summary: Parasitic nematodes cause major global health and economic burdens, and long-term control is increasingly threatened by escalating drug resistance. Endocannabinoid (EC) signalling regulates key physiological processes and has become an established therapeutic target in vertebrates. Parasitic nematodes also possess EC…
listings.description:
Parasitic nematodes cause major global health and economic burdens, and long-term control is increasingly threatened by escalating drug resistance. Endocannabinoid (EC) signalling regulates key physiological processes and has become an established therapeutic target in vertebrates. Parasitic nematodes also possess EC signalling pathways that may be important in parasitism. This project will explore the potential of EC signalling as a novel target pathway for nematode parasite control.

Exogenous cannabinoids, commonly derived from the cannabis plant, alter sensory perception and affect a range of behaviours. Vertebrates also naturally produce endogenous cannabinoids, known as endocannabinoids (ECs), that are responsible for the modulation of important physiological processes including movement, reproduction, and feeding. Indeed, these pathways are now the target of many new treatments for vertebrate diseases. Invertebrates, including the free-living model nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, also possess functional EC signalling systems, but they appear to display key differences from vertebrates. We know little about the functional biology or importance of the EC system in parasitic nematodes however, bioinformatic evidence suggests that these pathways also differ from vertebrate EC signalling and may offer new opportunities for antiparasitic therapy.

This project will exploit genomic resources, functional genomics and tractable parasite models, to define the role and importance of EC signalling in parasitic nematodes. The student will: (i) Identify and prioritise EC signalling candidates in key parasitic nematodes using in silico analyses of genome (BLAST, HMM) and transcriptome (RNASeq analyses) datasets; (ii) functionally interrogate prioritised EC signalling effectors using reverse genetics approaches (RNAi and CRISPR) in tractable nematode parasite models; (iii) validate gene silencing or knockout at the molecular and, where appropriate, proteomic level; (iv) determine the biological consequences of EC signalling disruption using in vitro and in vivo bioassays designed to interrogate nematode behaviour and parasitism. This interdisciplinary project will provide training in bioinformatics, molecular parasitology, functional genomics and experimental biology, while addressing a global challenge. listings.title: Research in Mechanochemistry
listings.summary: Mechanochemistry involves the initiation of chemical reactions through mechanical means. It is currently undergoing a renaissance due to its potential for more sustainable processes (since little or no solvent is needed) as well as the need for greater basic understanding of mechanochemical reactions.
listings.description:
Mechanochemistry involves the initiation of chemical reactions through mechanical means. It is currently undergoing a renaissance due to its potential for more sustainable processes (since little or no solvent is needed) as well as the need for greater basic understanding of mechanochemical reactions.

Typically mechanochemistry involves grinding solid reactants together using ball mills or, more recently, twin screw extruders, which are scalable and continuous. We are currently exploring mechanochemistry in each of these areas, often with industrial collaboration, and PhD projects are continuously available.

listings.description:
The continued emergence of antimicrobial resistance is a major global concern. The rapid development of resistance mechanisms by bacteria, as well as the lack of new structurally and mechanistically distinct classes of antibiotics, means that new antibiotics and antibiotic targets are desperately needed. Non-ribosomally synthesized peptides are a rich source of antimicrobial compounds.

This interdisciplinary project will involve the development of new synthetic methods to access novel antimicrobial peptides and their analogues, as well as the testing of these compounds for antibacterial activity. The synthesis of labelled analogues will also be performed and a combination of biochemical assays used to identify their cellular target(s). Candidates should possess strong abilities in synthetic organic chemistry and will be able to develop new skills in bioactivity assays, genetic engineering and/or protein expression, placing them at the cutting edge of chemistry and biology.

listings.title: Mechanistic Insights into Metal Catalysed Carbene Cross Coupling Reactions
listings.summary: Catalysis is a vital technology underpinning modern chemistry in research as well as chemical manufacturing. However, as often happens in synthetic chemistry, fundamental understanding of reaction mechanism tends to lag far behind reaction scope.
listings.description:
Catalysis is a vital technology underpinning modern chemistry in research as well as chemical manufacturing. However, as often happens in synthetic chemistry, fundamental understanding of reaction mechanism tends to lag far behind reaction scope.

One particularly useful reaction, yet barely studied from a mechanistic perspective, is the metal catalysed carbene cross-coupling. While a relatively broad scope for this transformation exists in the literature, no direct experimental evidence for the widely assumed mechanism exists. Additionally, the field suffers from a number of unsolved problems, such as high catalyst loadings, lengthy reaction times, and poor yields or selectivities. Only by understanding the mechanism of a reactions can we hope to rationally improve reaction conditions. We are a multidisciplinary group with expertise in the experimental monitoring of reaction kinetics as well as theoretical computational modelling. We advocate a kinetics first approach to our investigations, in which determining the reaction kinetics is the first port of call in any study, providing a solid foundation for mechanistic hypotheses and an informed choice for continued experimentation. By combining complimentary experimental and computational approaches from the outset of a study, we aim to provide solutions and understanding to problems in synthetic methodology and catalysis.

The project will begin with the exploration of copper catalysed diazo coupling reactions, where recent computational studies have suggested new mechanistic pathways without experimental verification. The student will receive training in a wide range of laboratory techniques, including in-situ IR, NMR, GC, or HPLC, and their use in modern graphical rate equation methods for performing kinetic investigations. Computational density functional theory investigations using the Gaussian 16 software package will also feature heavily.

listings.title: Modified vaccine adjuvants - synthesis and delivery
listings.summary: The ability of vaccines to generate an immune response can vary considerably depending on a variety of factors including age and whether the person is immunocompromised. Vaccine adjuvants modulate the level of response as they promote innate immunity and were first incorporated into whooping cough vaccines in 1932.…
listings.description:
The ability of vaccines to generate an immune response can vary considerably depending on a variety of factors including age and whether the person is immunocompromised. Vaccine adjuvants modulate the level of response as they promote innate immunity and were first incorporated into whooping cough vaccines in 1932. More recently, a newly-discovered immunogenic form of DNA called CpG-ODNs has been formulated with an anti-viral vaccine which can modulate the effect of delivering Hepatitis antigen in Heplisav-B.

In collaboration with the School of Pharmacy, QUB (Prof. Helen McCarthy), we are seeking MPhil or PhD candidates to prepare immunogenic DNA which will enable its formulation with an amphipathic peptide called RALA to form nanoparticles. RALA-derived nanoparticles are very active at delivering polyanionic cargoes such as mRNA to dendritic cells (required to give an immune response). Using labelled nucleic acids, we will to monitor the formulation, distribution, delivery and endosomal escape of such cargoes including adjuvant CpG-ODNs and mRNA. By facilitating such quantitative analysis, we hope will enable large-scale manufacturing of antiviral mRNA vaccines capable of rapidly being applied in any global pandemic response.

The project will require an approximately 50/50 split between the Chemical synthesis and Pharmaceutical analysis; the student should be trained in either chemistry or pharmacy and be willing to contribute to a multidisciplinary team across these two disciplines.

KEY REFERENCES: Conlon et al. Chem. Sci. 2019, 10, 10948-10957; Udhayakumar et al. Adv. Healthcare Mater. 2017, 6, 1601412

listings.title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Cyclic Vinyl Sulfoximines
listings.summary: Over recent years sulfoximines have emerged as an important motif in the pharmaceutical and crop protection industries, due in no small part to their stability, chirality, unique structure, and chemical versatility.
listings.description:
Over recent years sulfoximines have emerged as an important motif in the pharmaceutical and crop protection industries, due in no small part to their stability, chirality, unique structure, and chemical versatility.

This project will explore the viability, scope, and synthetic potential of an unexplored metal-catalysed approach to cyclic vinyl sulfoximines. Preliminary results have been obtained showing that this reaction is viable, and this project will seek to optimize the initial hit, before expanding the methodology to generate a range of unusual sulfoximine-containing heterocycles. The project will provide training in advanced synthetic skills including handling air- and moisture-sensitive reagents and catalysts, and the use of core analytical techniques including NMR, LCMS and XRD. Regular group meetings, presenting at conferences and writing research and review articles under the supervision of the PI will ensure the student receives a rounded education in scientific communication. QUB also offers a range of training opportunities outside of the lab, available through the award-winning graduate school.

The project involves the construction of macrocycles to build on our recent discovery of shape-switchable cyclophanes which not only capture/release aromatic guests, but they also self-indicate occupancy via fluorescence output (Nat. Commun. 2019, 10, 49). This leads to small-scale integration of memories and combinational logic gates. We anticipate new integrated logic arrays will emerge as various shape-switchable macrocycles are made and investigated in various output channels, e.g. Fluorescence, uv-vis and NMR spectroscopy.

Some experience in organic chemistry laboratory practice is required since multi-step organic synthesis and compound characterization are crucial components of the project. Some knowledge of the principles of computer science and technology would be beneficial.

listings.description:
The valorisation of waste and non-food biomass to sustainable and renewable chemicals and fuels is one of the core targets of Green Chemistry. Cellulose from biomass can be converted by controlled pyrolysis to a range of small molecule anhydrosugars which are useful chemical intermediates for further synthesis. One of the most versatile of these anhydrosugars is levoglucosenone.

This project will look at optimizing the conversion of cellulose to levoglucosenone and exploration of the synthetic applications of the compound, particularly for chiral molecular targets.

listings.title: Breaking BaD
listings.summary: In recent years it has become possible to produce gases of atoms at unimaginable temperatures close to absolute zero or zero degrees Kelvin, the lowest temperature allowed by the laws of physics. Oddly, this is often achieved by using lasers that cool the atoms to temperatures around 100 nanokelvin, a tiny fraction of…
listings.description:
In recent years it has become possible to produce gases of atoms at unimaginable temperatures close to absolute zero or zero degrees Kelvin, the lowest temperature allowed by the laws of physics. Oddly, this is often achieved by using lasers that cool the atoms to temperatures around 100 nanokelvin, a tiny fraction of a degree – there are in fact as many nanokelvin in one degree as there are seconds in a period of 30 years.

Alas some elements are still difficult to cool in this way, mainly because of a lack of suitable lasers or the cooling process is compromised. Hydrogen is particularly difficult but fortunately we have potentially found a unique way of creating a very, very cold gas of hydrogen atoms.

The trick is to actually use the lasers to cool something else, a tiny molecule consisting of two atoms, one of which is the hydrogen required. There are a number of hydrogen containing molecules that can be laser cooled, so the idea is to then gently remove the hydrogen atom from its partner using tweezers of light. Curiously, we have shown that the mass of the companion atom in the molecule influences the final temperature of the hydrogen atoms produced, with a heavier partner leading to a colder gas of hydrogen. Consequently, we wish to study heavy diatomic hydrides such as BaH and YbH.

One exciting application is the creation of a quantum gas of hydrogen atoms called a Bose-Einstein Condensate from the fragmentation of diatomic molecules that are themselves not cold enough to form such as gas. This would allow the creation of this unique phase of matter on demand with nanosecond precision, an ability not usually possible with phase changes. A particular focus will be the production of the heavier isotope deuterium by the fragmentation of BaD as such atoms have so far resisted all attempts to cajole them into a quantum gas by current means.

Happily, the technique could also be used to cool other light elements such as carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, essentially all the elements of life. Such a cold gas of hydrogen could have a number of applications, including testing whether the physical constants of the Universe are really constants after all and as a delicate probe of material surfaces, such as the components of electronic circuits.

listings.title: Selective capture of cancer cells in biological fluids
listings.summary: The proposed project aims to investigate the use of surface molecular imprinting for the selective capture of circulating cancer cells in biological fluids. This interdisciplinary project will address the need for a technique able to capture cancer cells without destroying them, enabling their subsequent molecular…
listings.description:
The proposed project aims to investigate the use of surface molecular imprinting for the selective capture of circulating cancer cells in biological fluids. This interdisciplinary project will address the need for a technique able to capture cancer cells without destroying them, enabling their subsequent molecular characterisation and identification. Such materials will offer enhanced diagnostic power compared to existing analytical techniques and enable rapid detection of metastasis in cancer patients.

Molecular Imprinting is a technique for the generation of specific binding sites within matrix of a synthetic polymer by co-polymerisation of appropriate functional monomers in the presence of a template mould. These sites possess three-dimensional complementarity towards the used template in terms of size, shape and functional group orientation. Such “plastic antibody” materials have been used in the recognition of small molecules such as pharmaceuticals, vitamins and environmental pollutants but also larger structures such as peptides and proteins.

In this project we wish to extend the use of imprinted polymers to the surface recognition of whole cells, in particular circulating cancer cells. This will be achieved by employing a “foot-printing” approach whereby cancer cells will be stamped on the soft surface of a polymer layer, leaving imprints complementary to the size and shape of the target cells. Following polymer curing and template removal, these surfaces should be able to selectively pre-concentrate the target cells from large volumes of biological fluids such as whole blood samples. Using biocompatible polymers, we aim to preserve the viability of the captured cells, so that subsequent culture and molecular identification of the cells is possible. On a second level, we aim to target specific chemical functionality on the cancer cell surface in order to achieve higher specificity and combine the cell capture with electrochemical or mass sensitive detection for near real-time cancer cell monitoring.

listings.summary: The need for novel technologies and processes for ammonia emission mitigation is unquestionable. listings.description:
The need for novel technologies and processes for ammonia emission mitigation is unquestionable. Aim of this project is to approach the problem from a materials chemistry perspective, using our extensive experience in the study of host-guest interactions and supramolecular chemistry. Ammonia behaves as Lewis and Bronsted base, hence by definition, the use of complementary acidic sorbents for its reversible capture under ambient conditions is a commonly employed strategy.

However, in this project we will attempt to achieve this goal using sustainable biopolymers as sorbents, recovered for example from seaweeds and meat production waste. Using the unique mixture of expertise and facilities of our group, we aim to design efficient extraction processes for the recovery of such compounds, characterise them and formulate them in useful sorbents for ammonia capture.

listings.title: Novel functional monomers for polymer-based receptors: a computational approach
listings.summary: The aim of the project will be to use modern molecular modelling packages and computational chemistry to design and optimise novel functional monomers for use in polymer-based receptors, such as molecularly imprinted polymers.
listings.description:
The aim of the project will be to use modern molecular modelling packages and computational chemistry to design and optimise novel functional monomers for use in polymer-based receptors, such as molecularly imprinted polymers.

Recent years have seen a rapid expansion in the applications of smart functional materials in bioanalysis, environmental remediation, sensors, medical devices and beyond. The development of these materials is a costly and time-consuming undertaking, which often results in innovation bottlenecks. However, recent developments in computational chemistry and the wider availability of high-power computing clusters, has enabled accurate modelling or increasingly complex structures, starting from small molecules and ranging to proteins, polymers and composite materials.

In this project, we will focus on the use of such computational packages to model the performance of small molecule polymerisable receptors for anionic species, in particular phosphate and sulphate ions, based on the urea and squaramide functionality. The most promising candidates will be taken forward as part of a complementary project that will evaluate the performance of these receptors in the recognition of anions in aqueous samples. Depending on progress on the project, the modelling of an actual imprinted polymer binding site will also be attempted, in order to propose suitable cross-linking and co-monomers for optimum target binding.

listings.title: Rapid recovery and recycling of valuable homogeneous catalysts using molecularly imprinted polymers as affinity separation phases
listings.summary: Molecularly Imprinted Polymers (MIPs) are highly cross-linked synthetic organic polymers, prepared by co-polymerisation of functional monomers and cross-linking monomers in the presence of a template compound. The resulting materials mimic the behaviour of natural receptors and are able to selectively recognise the…
listings.description:
Molecularly Imprinted Polymers (MIPs) are highly cross-linked synthetic organic polymers, prepared by co-polymerisation of functional monomers and cross-linking monomers in the presence of a template compound. The resulting materials mimic the behaviour of natural receptors and are able to selectively recognise the template in a complex matrix, similarly to antibodies and enzymes binding their specific antigen or substrate respectively. Due to their synthetic and robust nature, MIPs are able to operate in purely organic as well as aqueous media, and have enhanced resistance to pH, ionic strength, pressure and temperature, and an extended shelf-life compared to their natural counterparts. The latter, although they exhibit high specificity and selectivity, they are prone to denaturation in environments outside physiological conditions, such as elevated temperatures, pH, and in organic-rich solutions.

Since the early reports of molecular imprinting within organic polymers in the 1970s, molecular imprinting has matured and is now an established technique, with numerous literature reports on the successful imprinting of a great variety of targets. However, despite the abundance of successful protocols for the capture, separation and detection of small molecules, imprinting of molecules of industrial interest, such as expensive organocatalysts or homogeneous catalysts remains unexplored.

In this project, we aim to address this gap by the combination of our ongoing research on the development of high affinity polymerisable receptors, tailored to the recognition of specific functional groups, such as imides, carboxylic acids, ureas, carboxylate and phosphate anions with scalable polymerisation reactions. Our ultimate goal is to develop novel, inexpensive and robust affinity stationary phases for the rapid recovery and recycling of organocatalysts and organometallic catalysts from catalysed chemical processes.

listings.title: Environmentally friendly preparation of metallodrugs
listings.summary: Pharmaceutical industrial processes use large volumes of solvents which are often toxic and/or highly volatile (i.e., solvent use accounts for 80-90% of mass utilization in a typical pharmaceutical batch chemical operation). Mechanochemistry involves the grinding of solid reagents to instigate a chemical reaction in…
listings.description:
Pharmaceutical industrial processes use large volumes of solvents which are often toxic and/or highly volatile (i.e., solvent use accounts for 80-90% of mass utilization in a typical pharmaceutical batch chemical operation). Mechanochemistry involves the grinding of solid reagents to instigate a chemical reaction in the absence of solvents and, therefore, has the potential to reduce dramatically the environmental impact of the Pharma industry [1]. However, mechanochemical routes to metallodrugs are still largely unexplored. We have shown that metallodrugs, including gold, platinum and copper complexes, can be prepared using mechanochemistry. Furthermore, we have observed that copper complexes prepared mechanochemically have enhanced anti-tumour activity, compared to those prepared using solvent-based methods [2].

This project will further explore the solventless preparation of metal complexes known for their biological activity, in particular their anti-cancer properties. The properties of the mechanochemically synthesised products will be compared to those of the drugs prepared conventionally. Mechanochemical reactions will be initially conducted on small scale in a ball mill, but the synthesis of the more promising metallodrugs will be scaled up using a twin-screw extruder, in a continuous process which is more appropriate for manufacturing. Anticancer properties will be studied in collaboration with the School of Pharmacy at QUB. The student should have some experience in wet synthetic methods as well as in the use of standard purification and analytical techniques (e.g., NMR and IR Spectroscopies, Powder X-Ray Diffraction (PXRD), Mass Spectrometry, TGA). This project will be jointly supervised with Dr D. Crawford (School of Chemistry and Bioscience, University of Bradford), and Prof. S James (QUB).

listings.summary: Biocatalysis is one of the most promising technologies for the development of green and sustainable manufacture processes. listings.description:
Biocatalysis is one of the most promising technologies for the development of green and sustainable manufacture processes. It has gained increasing importance in the synthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients, the building block of biofuels, or biodegradation of the environment pollutants. Biocatalysis employs enzymes as catalysts and demonstrates obvious advantages over chemical routes such as mild reaction conditions, high selectivity while reducing the use of hazardous chemical reagents and the cost involved in treatment of chemical wastes.

The project will develop new computational approaches to redesign enzymes or de novo design new enzymes to catalyze desired chemical reactions for the production of complex molecules. The computer-aided technology combining computational modelling, bioinformatics and machine learning, is aimed to study the relationship between sequence/structure and function of enzymes in order to improve the catalytic efficiency, selectivity and stability of the enzyme catalysts.

The potential students should have 2:1 equivalent degree in Chemistry, Biochemistry, Bioengineering or Pharmaceutical engineering or relevant background, with strong interest in enzyme catalysis and computational chemistry & biology.

listings.title: Enhancing photocatalytic disinfection of water: the importance of bacterial factors and reactor design to enhance disinfection rates
listings.summary: Semiconductor photocatalysis is a novel technology which is very effective in pathogen destruction. When photocatalysts such as TiO2 are illuminated with UV light, powerful oxidising agents capable of destroying bacteria are generated. Great variation exists, however, in the literature with regards to the response…
listings.description:
Semiconductor photocatalysis is a novel technology which is very effective in pathogen destruction. When photocatalysts such as TiO2 are illuminated with UV light, powerful oxidising agents capable of destroying bacteria are generated. Great variation exists, however, in the literature with regards to the response that bacterial pathogens have to photocatalytic treatment. Previous work addressing this issue has focused on standardising experimental parameters such as pH, temperature and photocatalyst loading, however the problem still exists.

This project will address this problem by focusing instead on two other factors which have received more limited attention. Firstly bacterial factors that may influence the efficacy of this water treatment method will be investigated, particularly with how these may result in different effects with different photocatalyst materials. The other area of focus will be on engineering design to ensure any key chemical and biological effects which enhance the photocatalytic degradation process will be maximised within a novel photocatalytic reactor configuration and hence maximise the overall efficacy of the process. The incorporation of hydrodynamic cavitation as a process which may work in symbiosis with the photocatalytic system to maximise disinfection kinetics will also be investigated. This project will be jointly supervised with Dr Jeanette Robertson (School of Biological Sciences).

listings.summary: The use of photocatalysis for energy applications such as water splitting or carbon dioxide reduction has been the subject of extensive research interest for nearly fifty years. Over the past decade, however, this has been expanded to include sustainable materials such as glycerol, cellulose or lignocellulose as…
listings.description:
The use of photocatalysis for energy applications such as water splitting or carbon dioxide reduction has been the subject of extensive research interest for nearly fifty years. Over the past decade, however, this has been expanded to include sustainable materials such as glycerol, cellulose or lignocellulose as potential feedstocks for energy conversion. To date, there have been a number of reports where these feedstocks have been used to generate a range of products including hydrogen and more recently value-added compounds such as carbohydrates.

This project will look at the development of a photocatalytic process for the valorization of biomass to potential fuel products. The main targets will include a range of materials including cellulose, lignocellulosic materials and other biomass materials such as digestate generated from anaerobic digestion. The project will look at the whole process from the fundamental reaction on the photocatalyst surface through to how these mechanisms can be maximized through effective reactor design. This project will be jointly supervised with Dr Gary Sheldrake and Dr Nathan Skillen.

listings.title: Novel 3D printed photocatalytic technologies for continuous flow synthesis
listings.summary: In recent years, continuous flow chemistry has evolved as an enabling technology for manufacturing chemicals and metal nanoparticles. Flow chemistry offers a number of unique advantages over traditional batch processes, which include an increased process safety and environmental sustainability, improved heat, mass and…
listings.description:
In recent years, continuous flow chemistry has evolved as an enabling technology for manufacturing chemicals and metal nanoparticles. Flow chemistry offers a number of unique advantages over traditional batch processes, which include an increased process safety and environmental sustainability, improved heat, mass and photon transfer within the reactors, improved product stability, better control over the size of the nanoparticles, shortened residence times, and decreased foot-print for miniaturization of commercial production. Continuous flow processes offer the ability to optimize the production routes for performing sequential cascade reactions, without needing the separation of intermediate products, thus developing further scope for process intensification. Recently, with the emergence of 3D printed reactors it has been possible to design and 3D print photoreactors to enhance mass and photon transfer within the reactor to improve the performance. In our group at QUB, we have demonstrated several continuous flow photocatalytic processes including photo-reforming, photo-oxidation and photo-degradation reactions.

In this project, we will develop novel 3D printed reactor technologies for photocatalytic processes involving multiple phases of gas/liquid and gas/liquid/solid reactions. By modifying the reactor design using pinched tubular reactors, process intensification of photocatalytic processes would be achieved.

listings.title: Ionic Liquids as a Sustainable Platform for Cascade Engineered Reactions
listings.summary: Ionic liquids (ILs) are a group of salts composed of cations and anions, and they are liquids at ambient temperature. Advanced ILs have shown a unique combination of physicochemical properties that can be tailored by varying cation/anion combinations. The structure and properties of ILs can be tuned as desired for…
listings.description:
Ionic liquids (ILs) are a group of salts composed of cations and anions, and they are liquids at ambient temperature. Advanced ILs have shown a unique combination of physicochemical properties that can be tailored by varying cation/anion combinations. The structure and properties of ILs can be tuned as desired for applications as reaction media as well as catalysts to develop energy efficient processes. Previously, in our group, we have prepared advanced nanofluids by dispersing metal nanoparticles (MNPs) in ILs and shown that such advanced nanofluids possess an excellent catalytic activity in selective hydrogenations in liquid phase.

In this project we will develop dual-functional nanofluids as catalysts using metal nanoparticles (Pt, Ni, Cu) dispersed in Brønsted acidic ionic liquids (MNP-ILs) for application in cascade engineered reactions. Cascade reactions are organic transformations in a chemical process occurring in tandem or in subsequent steps. For eg. one-pot synthesis of raspberry ketone by crossed Aldol condensation of p-hydroxybenzaldehyde with acetone, followed by hydrogenation of resulting p-hydroxybenzalacetone to raspberry ketone. Cascade engineered process would be optimised using Design of Experiments (DoE) approach. Hybrid polymeric materials for API delivery are a fascinating area of research aiming at obtaining the optimal pharmacological responses that require spatial, temporal, and dose control of drug at the site of action. This involves the fabrication of novel porous hybrid polymeric materials or their modification, characterization of materials, and assessments of materials performance.

We are interested in a wide range of materials as the platform for drug delivery, including inorganic/organic polymers (metal organic framework, core shell microstructure, functionalized silica nanoparticles etc). The applicant’s skills/experiences in synthesis and characterization of functional polymeric materials are preferred.

listings.title: Engineering a Bespoke Environment for Biocatalysis Within Ionic Liquid Gels
listings.summary: The methods of synthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients have been undergoing a revolution over the past decade driven by biocatalysis. Biocatalytic methods have become the most efficient method of functional group transformation, completely solving chemo and stereoselectivity issues encountered by purely…
listings.description:
The methods of synthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients have been undergoing a revolution over the past decade driven by biocatalysis. Biocatalytic methods have become the most efficient method of functional group transformation, completely solving chemo and stereoselectivity issues encountered by purely chemical routes. Project partners Almac have been at the forefront of this change.

Proteins still have a drawback however, their stability is often lower in comparison with chemical reagents, particularly when exposed to organic solvents and reagents

In a 4-year-old collaboration QUB and Almac have been looking at the application of entrapment methods1 to protect the protein from poisoning and denaturing. Enzymes are entrapped into ionic liquid gels.2 Ionic liquids are used to tune the environment around the enzyme and to ensure facile diffusion of the substrate and product.3 The result is the production of immobilized biocatalysts that are simple to operate, separate and recycle.4,5

The research is at an exciting stage, and a range of materials and ionic liquids have been shown to support enzymatic activity and recycling. Moving forward, 21st century methods will be explored such as flow biocatalysis, multi-enzyme cascades and 3D printing. It is anticipated that the main enzyme classes studied will be transaminases and ketone reductases.

The well-established collaboration with Almac provides a number of benefits to the student, including placements to receive first-hand experience of researching in industrial laboratories, frequent meetings with industrial partners, advice on analytical and reaction methods, and receipt of libraries of industrial biocatalysts. Plus, and perhaps most excitingly, the possibility to transfer your results directly into the pharmaceutical industry.

[1] Enzyme entrapment, biocatalyst immobilization without covalent attachment, H. T. Imam, P. C. Marr, A. C.Marr, Green Chem., Green Chem., 2021, 23, 4980–5005.

[2] Ionic liquid gel materials: applications in green and sustainable chemistry, P. C. Marr, A. C. Marr, Green Chem., 2016, 18, 105–128.

[3] Applications of Ionic Liquids in Whole-Cell and Isolated Enzyme Biocatalysis, H.T. Imam, V. Krasňan, M. Rebroš, A. C. Marr, Molecules, 2021, 26, 4791.

listings.summary: Scope: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is among the most abundant plastics, used - for example - in beverage bottles and sports clothes. listings.description:
Scope: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is among the most abundant plastics, used - for example - in beverage bottles and sports clothes. Although there is perception that PET is easily recycled by mechanical means, in 2022 only 30% of UK’s PET bottles, and negligible percentage of garments, were recycled. About 75% of PET collected for recycling is rejected before it reaches the processing stage. Within the 25% that reaches recycling, only 17% is returned to bottles, and over 50% ends up in fibres, which are not recycled. While mechanical recycling is an important avenue for extending life cycles of polymers, it yields inferior quality product after each iteration. In contrast, chemical recycling breaks polymers down to building blocks (monomers), which can then be used in the synthesis of recycled polymers of quality equal to virgin products.

PET depolymerisation can be achieved through the reaction with alcohol or water, and is catalysed by a wide range of acids and bases. The challenge is to find a catalyst that enables easy product separation, can be recycled and is inexpensive. Furthermore, it should be robust to handle contaminated waste and polymer blends. Preliminary results for PET alcoholysis have been very promising. This project will focus on the use of inexpensive ionic liquids based on sufluric acid and amines, developed in the Swadzba-Kwasny group, for the chemical recycling of real-life polymeric waste (PET, polyurethanes and spandex) and their composites.

Candidates must possess or expect to obtain, a 2:1 or first-class degree in Chemistry, Chemical Engineering or closely related discipline

listings.title: Using epigenetic modifiers in combination with 5-FU based chemotherapy to elicit tumour specific immune responses and immunogenic cell death in colorectal cancer.
listings.summary: HDAC inhibitors (HDACi) are an emergent class of epigenetic modifying agent (EMA), with multi-modal mechanisms-of-action in both tumour and tumour microenvironment (TME).
listings.description:
HDAC inhibitors (HDACi) are an emergent class of epigenetic modifying agent (EMA), with multi-modal mechanisms-of-action in both tumour and tumour microenvironment (TME).

This project aims to understand how these drugs modulate efficacy of 5-FU-based chemotherapy to counteract transcriptional plasticity and immune evasion that underpins emergence of treatment resistance

Colorectal cancer (CRC) has one of the highest Worldwide incidences and mortality rates (>1.3 million new cases and ~610,000 deaths per annum). While 75% of patients with CRC present with operable disease (stages II and III), at least 40% of these patients still experience disease recurrence. Compared to surgery alone, adjuvant 5-Fluorouracil (5FU)-based Standard-of-Care (SoC) chemotherapy improves 5-year Hence, there is a critical need to develop new molecularly stratified, therapeutic approaches to improve outcomes in the adjuvant and advanced disease settings of CRC.

HDAC inhibitors (HDACi) are an emergent class of epigenetic modifying agent (EMA), that are attracting significant interest due to powerful anti-tumour and immunomodulatory effects. Our published preclinical studies and preliminary data have identified novel therapeutic strategies exploiting BOTH their tumour-intrinsic and immuno-modulatory effects in chemo-refractory CRC subtypes.

This project aims to better understand the mechanisms through which Class-I HDACs (HDAC1, 2 and 3) modulate the efficacy of 5-FU-based SoC to counteract the transcriptional plasticity and immune evasion of drug-tolerant persistor cells that underpins treatment resistance in specific genetic subgroups of CRC (namely MMR-proficient, KRAS mutant tumours that are either wild-type or mutant p53). In doing so, we aim to identify how best to clinically position these agents.

listings.title: Tackling protease-mediated inflammation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
listings.summary: The release of proteases from cells is associated with lung damage and aberrant tissue remodelling. Despite attempts to inhibit some of these proteases very little progress has been made in reversing inflammation and improving lung function in patients treated with protease inhibitors. Proteases are released directly…
listings.description:
The release of proteases from cells is associated with lung damage and aberrant tissue remodelling. Despite attempts to inhibit some of these proteases very little progress has been made in reversing inflammation and improving lung function in patients treated with protease inhibitors. Proteases are released directly into the extracellular milieu where they are thought to overwhelm host antiprotease defences. However, recent data has shown that some of these proteases may remain attached to cells and exosomes. These surface-bound proteases may be more difficult to inhibit as they are bound to exosomes or the cell surface and may explain, in part, the reasons for lack of efficacy of protease inhibitors in clinical trials. In this project, we wish to examine further the role of exosome-bound/packaged proteases using a combination of human and patient derived samples and in vivo experimentation

Our preliminary work has attempted to delineate a potential role for cathepsin S (CTSS) particularly in the setting of acute lung inflammation. We have initially evaluated CTSS activity and levels in the lungs of patients with ARDS and have demonstrated significantly elevated CTSS activity and protein levels in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) of these patients compared to healthy volunteer BALF despite normal levels of endogenous CTSS inhibitor being present. To address these findings, we will analyse exosomes isolated from the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of ARDS patients and ARDS mouse models and test for CTSS activity. Importantly, we will determine if CTSS bound to exosomes is more difficult to inhibit. In addition, we will test CTSS bound to exosome for its ability to induce inflammation and lung damage by directly instilling these exosomes into the lungs of naïve mice. listings.summary: Chronic infection and persistent inflammation in people with cystic fibrosis (PWCF) lead to progressive lung damage. listings.description:
Chronic infection and persistent inflammation in people with cystic fibrosis (PWCF) lead to progressive lung damage. Despite novel therapies to correct the CFTR disfunction chronic antibiotic treatments, compounded with extended life expectancy of PWCF, challenge the ecology of the lung microbiome and gives rise to the emergence of potential new pathogens displaying multidrug antibiotic resistance. Of these, Achromobacter sp. are particularly concerning since they are often the dominant bacteria recovered from sputum samples in an increasing number of PWCF including those with end-stage lung disease and they are also commonly found in the airways' microbiome. We understand little about the association of Achromobacter with lung disease and lack information on pathogenic traits of Achromobacter sp. and their ability to interact with innate immune cells (e.g. macrophages, neutrophils), as well as an overall lack of information on the biology of these bacteria. The overarching objective of this project is to understand the cellular microbiology of Achromobacter infections.

Our group has recently demonstrated that Achromobacter CF isolates can survive and replicate in human monocytic macrophages by surviving in a modified phagolysosome, and also that the intracellular infection results in macrophage pro-inflammatory cell by pyroptosis. The mechanistic details of how this occurs are unknow, and also unknown are the bacterial factors involved in promoting inflammation.

listings.title: Bacterial lipocalins: Novel role in bacterial protection against antibiotic-induced membrane lipid peroxidation
listings.summary: We recently discovered that bacteria can resist antibiotics by mechanisms operating extracellularly in response to near-lethal antibiotic concentrations. This means microbes fight antibiotics even before they reach bacterial cells. Key molecules involved in this mechanism are the polyamine putrescine and lipocalins…
listings.description:
We recently discovered that bacteria can resist antibiotics by mechanisms operating extracellularly in response to near-lethal antibiotic concentrations. This means microbes fight antibiotics even before they reach bacterial cells. Key molecules involved in this mechanism are the polyamine putrescine and lipocalins (LP), a highly conserved group of barrel-shaped proteins of unknown function produced by >6,500 bacterial species. We demonstrated LPs scavenge different classes of antibiotics from the extracellular milieu. Also, LPs bind isoprenoids (e.g. octaprenyl-phosphate) into the interior of the barrel, while low-affinity antibiotic binding occurs at the rim of the molecule. The physiological role of LPs remains unknown.

Bacteria exposed to near-lethal antibiotic concentrations (e.g. during treatment of chronic and biofilm infections), also mount an oxidative response, which in turn stimulates transcription of LP encoding genes. We have now discovered that bacterial mutants defective in LP production display enhanced membrane lipid peroxidation and fail to survive under conditions that stimulate peroxidative stress. This means that LPs may have a novel role in protecting bacteria against toxic byproducts of lipid peroxidation. How bacterial cells overcome lipid peroxidation, especially the double membraned Gram-negatives, is virtually unknown. Our experimental results bridge this knowledge gap and uncover LPs as components of a novel mechanism to protect bacterial cell membranes from lipid peroxidative damage.

This programme will address two questions: (i) What are the structure-function properties of diverse LPs involved in antibiotic binding and protection against lipid peroxidation? and (ii) What other bacterial components are needed for protection against lipid peroxidation? The model bacteria employed are the Gram-negative members of the ESKAPE group, namely Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas and Enterobacter species. This research project combines molecular microbiology, biochemistry, metabolomics, bioinformatics, and infection models to elucidate the role of LPs in antibiotic binding and in maintaining the homeostasis of the bacterial membranes under oxidative stress, commonly found upon exposure to near-lethal doses of antibiotics.

listings.title: How do cancer cells decide to release growth-promoting molecules?
listings.summary: This project aims to define how a molecular machinery important for cell signalling called the ‘sheddase complex’ is regulated. The sheddase complex controls release of signals, including growth factors and inflammatory cytokines that can promote the establishment and proliferation of cancer. The PhD project will…
listings.description:
This project aims to define how a molecular machinery important for cell signalling called the ‘sheddase complex’ is regulated. The sheddase complex controls release of signals, including growth factors and inflammatory cytokines that can promote the establishment and proliferation of cancer. The PhD project will include cellular biochemistry, cell biology and in vivo models to ask how cells decide to release these signalling molecules.

Tumour development is often driven by the deregulated production of signalling proteins called “growth factors”. When released from the cell surface, these activate their corresponding cell surface receptor, promoting cellular proliferation. The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) pathway is a prominent example of such a signalling pathway, whose activity is often upregulated in life-threatening epithelial tumours. The growth factors that activate the EGFR (“EGFR ligands”) are synthesized in inactive, membrane-tethered forms. Crucially, the release of EGFR ligands from the cell surface requires a protease called ADAM17. Work from several laboratories, including ours, has identified a molecular complex, the “sheddase complex”, that controls ADAM17 activity and EGFR ligand release. The sheddase complex includes proteins called iRhoms, that are central cofactors for the trafficking and stimulation of ADAM17 activity. Recently, we identified a protein called iTAP as a novel regulator of the sheddase complex. Our biochemical/in vivo studies showed that iTAP is important to control the cell surface levels of the sheddase complex, to control ADAM17 activity. The project aims to define how iTAP maintains the sheddase complex on the cell surface, to allow it to drive growth factor signalling, leading to cancer progression. For relevant references, see: PMIDs 22246777, 22781900, 23969955, 27378062, 29045841, 29897333, 31918923.

listings.summary: Pre-clinical models, including cell lines, are essential to modelling diseases and treatment response in the laboratory setting. listings.description:
Pre-clinical models, including cell lines, are essential to modelling diseases and treatment response in the laboratory setting. In vitro or vivo model choice can be based on personal preference or laboratory custom. However, there is limited focus as to how well these models characterise their target systems. Yet, models, such as cell lines, can be subject to mislabelling and contamination. This project will develop an online tool that will test and ‘match’ pre-clinical models against selected patient groups.

The first stage of the project will involve the curation of publicly-available datasets of human and pre-clinical cancer models, including both gene expression profiles and clinico-pathological data. A ‘soft’ integration method will be used to identify similarities and determine robustness of matches between pre-clinical models and patient groups. Patient groups will be stratified using different methods, including prognosis, molecular subtypes, pathways and clinico-pathological data. The online tool will present ranked results across multiple datasets using meta-analytical techniques.

listings.summary: Multiple Myeloma (MM) is a haematological neoplasm characterised by the clonal proliferation of malignant plasma cells.
