listings.summary: Excitotoxicity occurs upon brain injury or neurodegenerative diseases and exacerbates associated neuronal damages. The prostaglandin E2 receptor (EP2) has neuroprotective properties against excitotoxicity and novel molecules increasing EP2 activity have been recently discovered. Our project aims to identify the EP2…
listings.description:
Excitotoxicity occurs upon brain injury or neurodegenerative diseases and exacerbates associated neuronal damages. The prostaglandin E2 receptor (EP2) has neuroprotective properties against excitotoxicity and novel molecules increasing EP2 activity have been recently discovered. Our project aims to identify the EP2 allosteric sites of these molecules to enhance their neuroprotective effect.

Following a brain injury or in neurodegenerative diseases, neurons are damaged, promoting the release of an excitatory neurotransmitter called glutamate. Excessive glutamate level is toxic for adjacent neurons, a phenomenon termed as excitotoxicity. To limit the extent of neuronal damage upon injury, the neuroprotective prostaglandin E2 receptor 2 (EP2) is activated by the neurons.

Recently, molecules potentiating the activity of EP2 were discovered and reported to reduce excitotoxic damage to neurons. However, the region of EP2 where these molecules bind is unknown. The identification of the EP2 residues binding to these molecules can facilitate optimisation of these compounds to potentiate even more their neuroprotective potential.

The student in charge of this project will use cutting-edge computational approaches to predict EP2 binding sites. Then, using site-directed mutagenesis and bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET)-based biosensors, the student will validate the predictions in a heterologous cellular model. Finally, using CRISPR/Cas9 technology, the student will validate in a physiologically relevant neuronal cellular model the EP2 binding sites by functional assays monitoring neuronal excitotoxicity.

This hybrid dry/wet lab approach will stimulate the development of strong computational and experimental skills required for drug design research, which are highly desirable assets in both academia and industry.

listings.title: Investigating the importance of where we live on dementia risk and brain health using novel geospatial, satellite and multi-omic data sources and technologies
listings.summary: The number of people living with dementia and cognitive impairment is increasing, so we want to figure out how where we live affects dementia and brain health as we get older. Some research suggests that where we live might influence our brain health. It is important that the environment where we live is…
listings.description:
The number of people living with dementia and cognitive impairment is increasing, so we want to figure out how where we live affects dementia and brain health as we get older. Some research suggests that where we live might influence our brain health. It is important that the environment where we live is scientifically designed and improved to maximise our brain health.

This PhD project will use state-of-the-art approaches to explore how a person’s outdoor environment (i.e. the built and physical environment characteristics) impacts their risk of dementia. This PhD project will explore how the urban environment influences our brain health. By analysing data about where we live, such as the amount of air pollution, the toxins in soil, or how walkable the neighbourhoods are, we will explore how different environmental factors relate to brain health. The project also captures data using GPS and physical activity devices, as well as a range of multi-omic data sources to explore the biological responses to where we live.

We welcome applicants from those interested in a wide range of areas such as public health, geography, healthy ageing, urban planning, computer science, data science, epigenetics. The successful applicant will have the opportunity to co-develop their PhD research programme with members of the interdisciplinary SPACE team.

listings.title: Development of novel small molecule inhibitors of Gremlin1, a pathogenic driver of diabetic kidney disease
listings.summary: Gremlin1 is a secreted protein antagonist of bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) that regulated developmental processes such as limb and kidney formation. Gremlin1 also plays key roles in diabetic kidney disease, lung fibrosis and colorectal cancer. This project will develop small molecule inhibitors of Gremlin1 as…
listings.description:
Gremlin1 is a secreted protein antagonist of bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) that regulated developmental processes such as limb and kidney formation. Gremlin1 also plays key roles in diabetic kidney disease, lung fibrosis and colorectal cancer. This project will develop small molecule inhibitors of Gremlin1 as potential future drugs to enhance the treatment of diabetic kidney disease and improve patient outcomes.

Gremlin1 (GREM1) is a secreted glycoprotein member of the DAN family of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) antagonists that form part of the TGFb superfamily. Physiological interactions between GREM1 and BMP2/4 regulate kidney formation and lower limb formation. Perturbations in GREM1-BMP signalling leads to developmental defects such as renal agenesis and abnormal digit formation. Overexpression of GREM1 is implicated in the pathogenesis of kidney and lung fibrosis, chronic pancreatitis and cancers of the colon, lung and cervix. The molecular mechanisms of GREM1-mediated pathology in CRC and other diseases have not yet been fully elucidated.

Given the wealth of evidence implicating GREM1 in human cancer, we hypothesised that small molecule inhibitors of GREM1 would have potential as novel anti-cancer drugs. We have also developed a mass spectrometry based assay to detect GREM1 in plasma as a novel prognostic/diagnostic test for patients.

Successful completion of this project will provide the student with in-depth experience in molecular pharmacology, cell biology, mass spectrometry and biomarker development.

listings.title: Identifying medications associated with cancer risk
listings.summary: In our previous research we systematically investigated 250 prescription medications to identify medications associated with cancer risk using a Scottish General Practice database. In this project we will attempt to replicate some of the findings from our screening study.
listings.description:
In our previous research we systematically investigated 250 prescription medications to identify medications associated with cancer risk using a Scottish General Practice database. In this project we will attempt to replicate some of the findings from our screening study.

In this study we will determine whether associations identified between medications and cancer risk from an earlier screening study are apparent in an independent dataset. The project will involve statistical analysis of routinely collected patient data. A nested case-control study will be conducted to estimate the association between a candidate medication and cancer risk. Cases with cancer will be identified. Controls will be matched to cases using age, gender, year and GP practice. Prescription usage will be determined for both cases and controls. Conditional logistic regression will be used to calculate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (95%CIs) comparing the risk of cancer among users with non-users adjusting for comorbidity and lifestyle confounders. The study has the potential to identify medications which increase cancer risk and consequently alter licensing and usage of these medications.

listings.title: How does heterogeneity in HPV expression influence the tumour microenvironment of oropharyngeal cancers?
listings.summary: Thereis an unmet clinical need to identify oropharyngeal cancer patients who are likely torecur following curative treatment. Here we propose to understand to what extent HPV heterogeneity influences cancer-specific outcomes, the influence this has on the tumour microenvironment and how this mightlead to recurrent…
listings.description:
Thereis an unmet clinical need to identify oropharyngeal cancer patients who are likely torecur following curative treatment. Here we propose to understand to what extent HPV heterogeneity influences cancer-specific outcomes, the influence this has on the tumour microenvironment and how this mightlead to recurrent disease.

Cancers of the head and neck are the 8th most commonly diagnosed cancer in the UK. Despite improvements to clinical practice and the recognition of HPV-related disease as a separate entity, predicted five-year survival is often less than 50% (PMID: 33243986). HPV-positive disease has been shown to respond favourably to standard of care, however, research from our group has previously demonstrated how use of a surrogate biomarker can influence patient staging and outcome in oropharyngeal cancers when definitive HPV testing is not carried out (PMID:30890775and 31666283). Understanding a patient’s HPV status may become clinically relevant for treatment stratification in the future,as it has been speculated that patients with HPV-related disease may benefit from treatment de-escalation to minimise long-term side effects, however, to date there has been limited successin these patientsdue to disease recurrence. Therefore,there is an unmet clinical need to characterise HPV heterogeneity within oropharyngeal cancer patients who are likely torecur following curative treatment. This study aims to understand to what extent HPV heterogeneityinfluences cancer-specific outcomes, the influence this has on the tumour microenvironment and how this might lead to recurrent disease.

listings.title: Understanding factors associated with childhood vaccine coverage: a population-based data linkage study
listings.summary: Childhood vaccines protect children from a number of potentially serious diseases. It is known that vaccine uptake is decreasing across certain programmes. The decision to get a child vaccinated is typically taken by a parent / main carer, and therefore understanding how uptake varies by parental factors might help…
listings.description:
Childhood vaccines protect children from a number of potentially serious diseases. It is known that vaccine uptake is decreasing across certain programmes. The decision to get a child vaccinated is typically taken by a parent / main carer, and therefore understanding how uptake varies by parental factors might help identify opportunities to target Public Health interventions

This PhD project will link a number of population-based datasets to examine maternal factors associated with vaccine uptake among children. To build a sound knowledge base and understand interventions that have been used to improve childhood vaccine uptake, the student will initially conduct a systematic review. The student will then use the child health system to identify vaccine uptake among the population of children in Northern Ireland. Using unique identifiers and data linkage, which will be facilitated by the honest broker service, the student will advise on the creation of an anonymised digital cohort which will contain information about the child’s vaccine status and additional maternal socio-demographic factors. By analysing this dataset, the student will identify factors associated with vaccine uptake and as a member of a multi-disciplinary team will help inform the design of the programme in NI going forward.

This project is suited to an individual who likes working with data, and understands the basic principles of quantitative data analysis, for example, how to produce descriptive tables with numbers and percentages. The individual should have a willingness to learn new software, such as R, and statistical methods to test for associations, for which training will be supported.

listings.title: Investigation of the role of the Formyl Peptide Receptor 2 in diabetic retinopathy
listings.summary: Diabetic retinopathy causes blindness in diabetic patients. The upregulation of formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2) by retinal Müller glial cells (MGCs) is involved. The project aims to identify FPR2 subcellular location in MGCs and to study the role of its location in the cellular responses associated to diabetic…
listings.description:
Diabetic retinopathy causes blindness in diabetic patients. The upregulation of formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2) by retinal Müller glial cells (MGCs) is involved. The project aims to identify FPR2 subcellular location in MGCs and to study the role of its location in the cellular responses associated to diabetic retinopathy.

Diabetic retinopathy is one of the leading causes of irreversible blindness in diabetic patients. One important factor contributing to this condition is the transcriptional and biosynthetic changes occurring in the retina Müller glial cells (MGCs) exposed to higher concentrations of glucose. Under normal conditions, MGCs form architectural support structures for the retina, control the extracellular milieu and retinal blood flow. However, when exposed to a high glucose environment, they become a major source of inflammatory and angiogenic factors contributing to the pathological condition. Importantly, these changes are mediated in part by an upregulation of expression of the chemoattractant formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2), a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), by the MGCs. As opposed to most of GPCRs which are mostly expressed at the plasma membrane, FPR2 has been reported to be located instead at the nucleus, where it robustly signals in cancer cell lines. The proposed project aims to identify the subcellular location of FPR2 and its main site of signalling in the context of MGCs and to better understand the relationship between its location and transcriptional activity driving cellular responses contributing to diabetic retinopathy.

listings.title: Remote assessment for clinical trials and healthcare: Exploring the usefulness of remote spirometry
listings.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic and pressure on healthcare systems has increased use of remote spirometry for monitoring of respiratory patients. These portable spirometers have been advocated by healthcare providers and positively received by patients, however, no conclusive evidence that measurements from remote spirometry…
listings.description:
The COVID-19 pandemic and pressure on healthcare systems has increased use of remote spirometry for monitoring of respiratory patients. These portable spirometers have been advocated by healthcare providers and positively received by patients, however, no conclusive evidence that measurements from remote spirometry are valid and reliable. This project seeks to investigate the validity and reliability of remote spirometry.

The aim of this PhD project is to investigate the validity and reliability of remote spirometry and explore its usefulness in supporting clinical trials and healthcare services.

Traditionally, patients perform spirometry in a clinic setting supervised by a trained professional under standardised conditions (1, 2). Spirometry is used extensively for diagnosis and monitoring patients with respiratory conditions, where measurements are used to assess disease severity and control (3-5). It is crucial to know whether remote spirometry measurements are valid and reliable before mass uptake. listings.title: Establishing and validating a human 3D stem-cell derived brain culture system for neuro-immune research
listings.summary: There is a gap in readily available 3D human brain cell culture systems for neuroscience and neuroimmunology research that do not require specialist resources and will generate reproducible results.
listings.description:
There is a gap in readily available 3D human brain cell culture systems for neuroscience and neuroimmunology research that do not require specialist resources and will generate reproducible results.

This project will establish and validate a human brain culture system using stem cells. The model could serve as a link between early pre-clinical and clinical studies and as a (semi-)high throughput screening tool for potential targets for neurological research.

Mixed brain cell cultures are powerful tools for neuroscience and related fields. They contain glia such as astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, progenitors, and neurons and grow in a three-dimensional layer. The presence of these different cell types enables the investigation of mechanistic interactions and the study of biological processes on molecular and cellular levels.

Challenges arise when translating findings from lab models to humans. Primary human mixed brain cell cultures are limited to researchers with access to brain surgery tissue, are difficult to grow, and yield highly variable results. Induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cultures (iPSC) are used to generate specific glial cell types but are rarely employed in a mixed glia setting with other relevant brain cells. Moreover, these cultures often lack standardisation across laboratories due to variations in iPSC sources and methodology, leading to inconsistent outcomes and low reproducibility.

listings.summary: Bacterial infections are one of the top threats to global human health. Understanding how pathogens overcome immune defences is key to develop new antimicrobials. listings.description:
Bacterial infections are one of the top threats to global human health. Understanding how pathogens overcome immune defences is key to develop new antimicrobials. Our projects aim to dissect how bacteria and host use protein glycosylation, an abundant post-translational modification, in the fight for control over host resources and immune defence.

Macrophages are the first line of defence against bacterial pathogens and successful infection is closely linked to a pathogen’s ability to subvert antibacterial mechanisms. Adaptation of the macrophage’s metabolism, “immunometabolism”, is critical in this battle (Galli & Saleh, 2021).

Protein glycosylation is an abundant post-translational modification (Schjoldager, 2020) that regulates metabolism and signalling, governing cell physiology and defences. Glycosylation is highjacked by bacteria such as Legionella pneumophila, cause of the potentially fatal pneumonia Legionnaires’ disease (Lockwood, 2022).

However, the roles of host and pathogen-mediated protein glycosylation during infection remain poorly understood and their potential as target for new antibacterial drugs underexplored.

Extending our BBSRC-funded research on Legionella-glycosyltransferase effectors, we are looking for highly-motivated PhD candidates for projects aiming to characterise new bacterial glycosyltransferase toxins, to determine the role of host glycosylation machineries and glycans in cell-intrinsic and adaptive host defences and to exploit this knowledge to design new treatments.

Projects are highly interdisciplinary involving a wide spectrum of cutting-edge techniques, from microbiology, cell and immune biology to biochemistry, proteomics and super resolution microscopy. You will join a dynamic, multi-cultural team and, in addition to technical training, develop skills for experimental design, project management, data analysis and scientific writing and communication.

listings.description:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a clinical syndrome of diffuse lung inflammation and oedema that commonly causes acute respiratory failure. ARDS has a high mortality rate of about 30-40%, and there is no specific treatment for it, about 2M of patients in the world would die from ARDS annually, therefore there is an urgent unmet clinical need to find treatments for this condition. Reduced lung regeneration capacity is a key factor contributing to inefficient recovery after lung injury (e.g. following infections, like influenza or COVID-19 or inflammatory insult). Therefore, it is fundamentally important to understand the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving the process of lung repair and regeneration in the human lung. Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSC) are a novel potential therapy for this syndrome. Accumulating evidence suggests that MSCs act primarily through their secretome, key components of which are extracellular vesicles (EVs). These membrane-bound compartments carry multiple different molecules including proteins and different species of RNA as well as whole organelles such as functionally active mitochondria. To effectively and safely translate EVs into clinical application as alternative to whole cell therapy, there is a need for a better understanding of their mechanisms of action. It is imperative to investigate how EVs modulate epithelial regenerative capacity in the ARDS environment. In this project, we propose to establish the role of MSC EVs in regulation of the lung epithelium regeneration in ARDS using human iPSC-derived alveolar epithelial cells.

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a major cause of mortality in the critically ill patients with no effective pharmacological treatment. We previously reported that mitochondrial dysfunction and associated oxidative stress significantly contribute to pathophysiology of ARDS. Although

transplantation of healthy mitochondria is increasingly recognised as a promising approach for treatment of conditions underpinned by mitochondrial dysfunction, therapeutic potential of mitochondrial transplantation in ARDS is not sufficiently investigated. We already have demonstrated that mitochondrial (Mt) transfer by Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (MSCs) via tunneling nanotubes or extracellular vesicles is key for the protective effects of MSC in lung injury in vivo and in vitro. Isolation of MSC Mt is feasible and efficient process, and isolated Mt would represent relatively uniform advanced therapy medicinal product compared to whole cell therapy or MSC extracellular vesicles which are difficult to accurately characterise due to heterogeneity and absence of the unique markers. In this project we wish to optimise the procedure of isolation and buffer formulation of MSC Mt product and explore if isolated MSC Mt will be able to have therapeutic effects in the mouse model of acute lung injury in vivo. Human bone marrow derived will be cultured in the bioreactor . Mt will be isolated from MSC using protocol by Lampl et al, J

Vis Exp. 2015;(97):52076. doi: 10.3791/52076) or using commercially available mitochondria isolation kit (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA) or sucrose gradient density centrifugation and resuspened in a range of buffers (at least 3) known to support mitochondrial respiration. listings.description:
Our Team has a strong track record identifying novel biomarkers associated with kidney disease. Opportunities exist to explore single-omic biomarkers or integrating genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, exposomics, demographic and clinical data. The goal is to enhance understanding of disease mechanisms, improve early detection, and develop personalized treatment strategies.

Chronic kidney disease is a global public health problem, affecting almost a quarter of adults over the age of 35 with nearly half of adults 75 years of age and older having CKD1. Treating kidney disease consumes more than 3% of the UK national health service with costs expected to double within the next decade2.

We urgently need improved methods to identify people at risk of developing CKD, biomarkers to enable earlier detection of kidney disease, and novel treatment strategies. Our team explores big data sets such as UK Biobank, AllOfUs, and Our Future Health, international kidney-focused bioresources with associated registry data, and population-based resources such as NICOLA, TILDA, HRS, Generation Scotland, performing wet-lab and computer-based analyses. Our team’s particular expertise is focused on molecular biomarkers, working with expert colleagues to integrate diverse datatypes and derive robust scientific outcomes from complex analyses.

Its diverse postgraduate student population comprises both basic and clinical scientists from across the globe engaged in wide-ranging research projects spanning the breadth of the School’s research portfolio from traditional population-based epidemiology to 'big data' science and bioinformatics, through molecular and cell biology to clinical trials. Age-related diseases increase in prevalence as populations get older. They are expected to bankrupt the UK national health service if the current rates continue. There is an urgent need to identify biomarkers that predict health and disease across the lifecourse, with a focus on enabling identification of persons most a risk of developing disease, earlier detection of disease, and improved understanding of how diseases develop considering inherited features alongside the impact of where each person is born, lives, and works. We know that people who are poorer, less educated, and who experience more adverse life circumstances experience accelerated biological ageing that is associated with an earlier onset of age-related diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and kidney disease.

This studentship leverages existing large-scale datasets to identify multiomic signatures associated with healthy ageing and diseases that are common in in older populations. There is scope for the successful student to generate new laboratory data, learning both wet-lab and complementary in silico analytical approaches, or to focus purely on an artificial intelligence training track that will enable them to be competitive employment in a range of fields.

listings.description:
More than 450 million people live with rare diseases (RDs). Opportunities exist for research improving diagnosis, using rare disease registry data, analysing real-world evidence, establishing a virtual community of practice, developing patient reported outcomes, supporting participation in clinical trials, or focusing on research that enables access to orphan drugs.

On average, RD patients in the UK experience three misdiagnoses, attend multiple medical specialities, with many never obtaining a diagnosis. Many RDs are chronic, complex conditions; ~70% of RDs affect children; >60% of children who die  10 years to market so re-purposing of drugs already licensed for use in another disease is an attractive option. New approaches are also required to optimise trials in children, managing severely life limiting rare conditions where there are a restricted number of participants and limited molecular diagnoses or natural history information. Emerging options such as adaptive and / or decentralised clinical trials, using biomarkers and real-world data offer promising opportunities for rare disease researchers and patients .

listings.title: Understanding antigen uptake and processing for improved immune responses
listings.summary: We are interested in the steps leading to an effective immune response against infectious agents – antigen recognition, uptake, processing and presentation. Infectious diseases cause over 6 million deaths a year worldwide with significant number of newly emerging or highly mutating pathogens.
listings.description:
We are interested in the steps leading to an effective immune response against infectious agents – antigen recognition, uptake, processing and presentation. Infectious diseases cause over 6 million deaths a year worldwide with significant number of newly emerging or highly mutating pathogens.

One of our main defences against infectious disease is a strong neutralising antibody response against the foreign pathogens. Such responses are initiated when antigen presenting cells internalise foreign antigens and process and present these on MHCII for optimal T cell activation. This antigen endocytosis determines both the amount and repertoire of antigen presented and is critical for establishing long-term immunity. In addition to initiating effective antibody responses, antigen presentation has implications for both autoimmune diseases and malignancy, where our ability to modulate antigen presentation can promote tumour recognition.

Using a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen we have identified a number of novel regulators of antigen uptake and the project will characterise these with the aim of defining new pathways with therapeutic potential for improving antigen presentation.

The project will involve cell culture, flow cytometry, molecular biology and imaging techniques to quantify protein localisation, interactions, effect of deletion on antigen processing and antibody response upon immunisation. This will help us to understand the role of novel regulators both in vitro and in vivo.

listings.title: Human Bronchial Epithelium-Bacteria Interactions In Cystic Fibrosis Using A Novel Opportunistic Bacterium Achromobacter
listings.summary: Chronic infection and persistent inflammation in people with cystic fibrosis (PWCF) lead to progressive lung damage. Despite novel therapies to correct the CFTR disfunction chronic antibiotic treatments, compounded with extended life expectancy of PWCF, challenge the ecology of the lung microbiome and gives rise to…
listings.description:
Chronic infection and persistent inflammation in people with cystic fibrosis (PWCF) lead to progressive lung damage. Despite novel therapies to correct the CFTR disfunction chronic antibiotic treatments, compounded with extended life expectancy of PWCF, challenge the ecology of the lung microbiome and gives rise to the emergence of potential new pathogens displaying multidrug antibiotic resistance. Of these, Achromobacter sp. are particularly concerning since they are often the dominant bacteria recovered from sputum samples in an increasing number of PWCF including those with end-stage lung disease and they are also commonly found in the airways' microbiome. We understand little about the association of Achromobacter with lung disease and lack information on pathogenic traits of Achromobacter sp. and their ability to interact with innate immune cells (e.g. macrophages, neutrophils), as well as an overall lack of information on the biology of these bacteria. The overarching objective of this project is to understand the cellular microbiology of Achromobacter infections.

Our group has recently demonstrated that Achromobacter CF isolates can cross the human bronchial epithelium by inducing the formation of gaps between epithelial cells. We hypothesize these gaps allow the bacteria to reach the underlying mucosal tissue. Epithelial gap formation requires a functional type-6 secretion system (T6SS) and production of flagellin. This project will investigate how the T6SS subverts human bronchial epithelial cells to allow the passage of Achromobacter across the epithelium.

(i) to test the working hypothesis that A. xylosoxidans T6SS effectors induce the formation of gaps in the bronchial epithelial cell barrier.

(ii) to test the working hypothesis that the T6SS targets cellular pathways involved in remodeling epithelial cell adhesion molecules.

To address aim (i) the PhD student will use complementary strategies involving a top-down candidate-based approach, and two bottom-up approaches based on proteomics and high-saturation mutagenesis. The candidate-based approach involves constructing and functionally characterizing gene deletions in suspected T6SS effector candidates of eukaryotic activity. The other approaches involve defining the T6SS secretome by mass spectrometry and constructing a library of transposon mutants to identify genes required for gap formation using high content microscopy approaches. listings.description:
Enterobacter species are opportunistic Gram-negative bacteria associated with morbidity and mortality worldwide due to multiple antibiotic resistance that also extends to last-resort antibiotics; they belong to the ESKAPE pathogens, a group of bacterial species highlighted by the WHO as the most dangerous pathogens worldwide. Surprisingly, very little is known about the infection biology of Enterobacter species. To bridge this knowledge gap, we have investigated the intracellular trafficking of a subset of Enterobacter clinical isolates, including colistin-resistant strains, within human macrophages, and determined the macrophage response to the intracellular infection. We discovered that the Enterobacter isolates do not replicate in human macrophages but exhibit long-term survival within a modiﬁed late phagolysosome compartment. Survival does not correlate with colistin resistance, lipopolysaccharide modiﬁcations, or bacterial pathogenicity in the Galleria mellonella infection model. Remarkably, intracellular bacteria induce low levels of macrophage cytotoxicity that correlates with absence of cleavage of proinflammatory markers in infected macrophages. Since clinical isolates from Enterobacter species isolates can persist without replication inside human macrophages with minimal effects on cell viability and inflammation, we hypothesise that these bacteria can hideout within macrophages to escape innate immune responses and antibiotics.

(i) detailed characterisation of the Enterobacter-containing vacuole (EcV) in macrophages by state-of-the-art confocal microscopy.

(ii) identification of genes required for intramacrophage survival by high-throughput screens (TnSeq) and a candidate gene-based approach by targeted gene deletions and functional analyses.

(iii) elucidating how macrophages respond to intracellular Enterobacter infection and how is their cell death downregulated using metabolic analyses, FACS and global transcriptomics.

All experiments will involve relevant clinical isolates of different Enterobacter species obtained from the UK and primary human macrophages from blood donors.

listings.description:
Computer-based testing (CBT) has now become an accepted standard testing method. This project will study the keystroke data created during computer-delivered assessments in the Medical School. Using this data, the project will develop resources for both staff and students which make the best use of this rich information.

"The COVID-19 pandemic led to a significant shift in the way that training and assessment is delivered. Following the successful move to computer-based testing (CBT) there is a need to better understand the rich data produced during CBT.

This project will utilise CBT keystroke information to provide valuable insights into how students interact with both individual questions and assessments as a whole. In real time, via keystroke logs, it is possible to see which actions were selected, when and what paths students took through questions before providing their final answer. By making use of this information, we can gain important insights into student certainty, stress-behaviours, and behavioural approaches to written assessment papers.

Furthermore, in the ongoing drive towards ‘assessment for learning’, feedback plays a crucial role. Feedback can be used to reinforce and encourage areas of good performance whilst also identifying and correcting areas of poor performance.

The 2022 National Student Survey (NSS) results showed that Queen’s University Belfast was ranked 1st for Assessment and Feedback in the UK. Utilising keystroke data to produce ClickMap feedback would be a crucial contribution to the existing feedback students receive post assessment, meaning that this project would actively contribute to current practice."

listings.description:
Fungal infections are a major problem for immunosuppressed individuals or those with underlying health problems. Bloodstream fungal infections cause >2.5M deaths per year. These fungal pathogens (Aspergillus, Candida, Rhizopus) are rapidly developing resistance to antifungal therapies therefore, new anti-fungal therapies, immunotherapies or vaccines are urgently needed. There are still significant gaps in our understanding of the immune response to fungal pathogens that need to be addressed to aid in the development of novel anti-fungal immunotherapies.

Fungal infections including aspergillosis, candidiasis and mucormycosis cause >2.5M deaths per year. Fungal infections are a major problem for immunosuppressed individuals (eg. patients with organ/bone marrow transplant, chemotherapy patients) or those with underlying health problems (eg. chronic lung disease, diabetes mellitus). Infections with fungal pathogens (Aspergillus, Candida, Rhizopus) have also recently emerged as a major problem for patients post-SARS-CoV2/COVID-19 infection. These fungal pathogens were included on the recently published World Health Organisation (WHO) list of critical and high priority fungal pathogens that pose the greatest public health threat and urgently require further research to address gaps in our knowledge. These fungal pathogens are rapidly developing resistance to antifungal therapies which leads to prolonged therapy and hospital stays, increased used of highly toxic second-line antifungal therapies and increased mortality. Due to many similarities between fungal cells and human cells, there are a very limited number of anti-fungal drugs and some fungal strains are resistant to one or all available anti-fungal drugs. This is a very serious problem and many more deaths will occur in the coming years unless new anti-fungal therapies, immunotherapies or vaccines are developed. However, as recently highlighted by the WHO there are still significant gaps in our understanding of the immune response to fungal pathogens that need to be addressed to aid in the development of novel anti-fungal immunotherapies.

listings.description:
This project involves the detection of novel cancer biomarkers in blood, specifically the presence of circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) fragments. PCR-based tests will be developed capable of detecting ctDNA traces in blood, facilitating the improved diagnosis and monitoring of aggressive cancer types (Pancreatic, Ovarian, Triple Negative Breast and Lung).

Tissue/surgical biopsies are the current mainstay for diagnosing most solid tumours, but they have several key limitations, such as complex invasive procedures, limited options for repeat sampling and high costs. ‘Liquid Biopsies’ or blood sampling could serve as a non-invasive alternative to surgical biopsies, through the detection of circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA). Liquid Biopsies are now seen as an exciting new area of cancer research, offering the possibility to improve several areas of cancer management, including earlier detection, screening, diagnosis, and cancer monitoring during and after treatments.

DNA methylation (DNAme) is a normal process in all cell types, and it is important for normal cell function. However, dysregulated DNAme is an early event which occurs in most cancer types, often before the emergence of other cancer-associated events such as mutations. It is also known that even early cancers secrete low levels of tumour DNA into the bloodstream, referred to as circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA). We will identify novel DNAme markers, and evaluate their diagnostic potential, through the development of PCR-based tests capable of detecting ctDNA in blood. Through Liquid Biopsy testing, we aim to improve the diagnosis, monitoring, and patient survival rates, of cancers currently associated with poor clinical outcomes.

listings.title: Understanding the biophysical basis of FLASH radiotherapy
listings.summary: FLASH is a novel radiotherapy delivery technique which delivers radiation treatments in less than a second. listings.description:
FLASH is a novel radiotherapy delivery technique which delivers radiation treatments in less than a second. FLASH has been shown to reduce normal tissue side-effects, but how this occurs is unclear. This project will explore the fundamental mechanisms of radiation interactions at these short timescales, to better understand this effect.

Delivery of radiotherapy at ultra-high dose rates, known as “FLASH” radiotherapy, gained renewed focus a decade ago when experiments showed that it produced marked normal tissue sparing, while maintaining anti-tumour efficacy. This offered a significant new way to improve therapeutic outcomes in radiotherapy, and has been the subject of intense research.

However, while there is now clear evidence for the effect, its underlying cause remains unclear. A number of mechanisms have been proposed relating to changes in the chemical composition of cells during these radiation exposures, such as oxygen consumption, but there remains a lack of consistent datasets and models with which to explain these effects. This poses a significant challenge to the optimisation and translation of FLASH radiotherapy in the clinic.

This project will seek to map out the initial physical and chemical impacts of FLASH radiotherapy. This will be explored in successively more complex systems, beginning from isolated DNA in water, before adding further complexity by introducing components mimicking different aspects of the cellular environment. This will be used to build a model of the role of different processes in the FLASH effect, culminating in a predictions which will be validated against response studies in cancer and normal cells.

listings.title: Targeting the mRNA translation machinery to improve the efficacy of the anti-cancer treatments
listings.summary: This project aims to enhance the effectiveness of anti-cancer therapies by targeting the mRNA translation machinery. By understanding how cancer cells regulate protein synthesis, we seek to identify vulnerabilities that can be exploited to improve drug responses and overcome resistance, ultimately leading to more…
listings.description:
This project aims to enhance the effectiveness of anti-cancer therapies by targeting the mRNA translation machinery. By understanding how cancer cells regulate protein synthesis, we seek to identify vulnerabilities that can be exploited to improve drug responses and overcome resistance, ultimately leading to more effective treatment strategies. This project explores how targeting the mRNA translation machinery can enhance the efficacy of anti-cancer therapies. Protein synthesis is tightly regulated, and its disruption is a common feature of cancer. Many chemotherapeutic agents exert their effects by interfering with RNA metabolism, thereby impairing translation. Cancer cells can counteract this stress through pathways such as ribosome quality control (RQC), which resolves stalled ribosomes and limits proteotoxicity (Chatterjee et al, Nucleic Acid Research 2024). Our research aims to uncover how cancer cells leverage translation regulation and RQC to survive chemotherapeutic challenges. We are particularly interested in identifying how these adaptive responses contribute to drug resistance and how they can be targeted to improve treatment outcomes. By dissecting the molecular mechanisms linking mRNA translation and drug sensitivity, this work seeks to inform the development of more effective and durable cancer therapies. As a PhD student on this project, you will gain expertise in cutting-edge techniques including CRISPR gene editing, RNA-Seq, Ribo-Seq, proteomics, and drug screening. You will be part of a collaborative and interdisciplinary research environment at the forefront of RNA and cancer biology, with opportunities to contribute to high-impact research and develop a strong foundation in molecular oncology.

listings.title: Enhancing Blood Vessel Stability to Reduce Vein Graft Disease in CABG Patients
listings.summary: Coronary heart disease causes 10 million deaths annually, often treated with bypass surgery using patient blood vessels. However, 75% of grafts fail within 10 years due to vein graft disease, with unclear causes. This project explores novel therapeutic targets to improve graft longevity, offering advanced training in…
listings.description:
Coronary heart disease causes 10 million deaths annually, often treated with bypass surgery using patient blood vessels. However, 75% of grafts fail within 10 years due to vein graft disease, with unclear causes. This project explores novel therapeutic targets to improve graft longevity, offering advanced training in cell and molecular biology.

Coronary heart disease (CHD) is the most prevalent form of cardiovascular disease and causes around 10 million deaths globally each year. It results from the blockage of coronary arteries by blood clots, leading to reduced blood flow, tissue ischaemia, and permanent damage to heart muscle cells (cardiomyocytes). Current treatments include stenting or coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, where blood vessels from the leg (saphenous vein), chest (internal mammary artery), or arm (radial artery) are used to restore blood flow to the heart. Although CABG is effective, its long-term success is limited by vein graft disease—accelerated atherosclerosis that results in 75% of grafts failing within 10 years. The underlying mechanisms of this rapid disease progression are not fully understood.

Our research has identified promising new molecular targets that may improve blood vessel stability and reduce graft failure. Collaborations with local cardiac surgeons provide access to valuable human tissue samples, enhancing the clinical relevance of this work.

This project offers the opportunity to explore these novel therapeutic strategies and will provide the student with advanced training in cell and molecular biology, equipping them with highly transferable skills applicable across many areas of biomedical research.

listings.title: Oxidative Regulation of Protein Stability in Retinal Endothelial Cells: A Novel Approach to Early ROP Intervention
listings.summary: This project explores how oxidative stress affects de-ubiquitin specific proteases (USPs) and protein stability in retinal endothelial cells. By targeting early molecular disruptions in Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP), it aims to develop therapies that preserve vascular integrity and prevent disease progression,…
listings.description:
This project explores how oxidative stress affects de-ubiquitin specific proteases (USPs) and protein stability in retinal endothelial cells. By targeting early molecular disruptions in Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP), it aims to develop therapies that preserve vascular integrity and prevent disease progression, offering a new approach to managing this vision-threatening condition.

Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP) is a serious complication of premature birth and a leading cause of childhood blindness worldwide. The disease arises when oxygen therapy, essential for survival, disrupts normal retinal vascular development, leading to vessel degeneration followed by abnormal neovascularization. Current treatments target this later neovascular phase and are often costly, only partially effective, and associated with irreversible side effects.

This project shifts focus to the under-researched early, vaso-degenerative stage of ROP, where oxidative stress plays a key role in endothelial cell dysfunction. The central hypothesis is that oxidative stress alters the function of de-ubiquitin specific proteases (USPs), affecting the stability of Fbxw7—a crucial protein involved in regulating endothelial growth and differentiation. The research aims to (1) identify USPs that modulate Fbxw7 under varying oxygen conditions, and (2) develop a cellular screening system to discover compounds that enhance Fbxw7 stability in oxidative environments.

By integrating in vitro, in vivo, and human samples, the project seeks to uncover molecular targets that protect retinal vasculature during early disease. This approach may lead to innovative therapeutic strategies that prevent progression to advanced ROP, addressing a critical gap in current neonatal care.

listings.title: Evaluation of Parasite-Derived Peptides as Host Directed Therapeutics
listings.summary: The research team have been evaluating a number of host defence molecules (HDMs) derived from parasites to determine the effects of these peptides on cellular responses by macrophages to bacterial stimulation. We have demonstrated a significant inhibitory effect of some of these peptides to kill bacteria in a…
listings.description:
The research team have been evaluating a number of host defence molecules (HDMs) derived from parasites to determine the effects of these peptides on cellular responses by macrophages to bacterial stimulation. We have demonstrated a significant inhibitory effect of some of these peptides to kill bacteria in a host-directed mechanism of action. Based on these data, selected peptides will be investigated for their mechanism of action and their efficacy in vivo in a model of chronic lung infection.

The development of novel antimicrobial treatments that could directly regulate bacterial load and growth in the lung would revolutionise the lives of patients with lung diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and cystic fibrosis lung disease (CF) by sustaining and maintaining lung function. Additionally, antimicrobial agents that can act by inducing a robust host-derived antibacterial response (host-directed therapeutics) may also circumvent the issue of antimicrobial resistance. Parasites are masters of immune regulation – they can survive for many years in their host by selectively suppressing or modulating specific arms of their host immune systems by secreting specific proteins. We have synthesised and identified a novel derivative of naturally occurring parasite peptide which displays potent antibacterial effects in vitro and in vivo, similar to the parent peptide and with novel IP status. This peptide activates host cells, such as macrophages, to remove bacteria more efficiently by a mechanism that is partly dependent on the activation of macrophage signalling pathways. In this project, we will develop peptides with greater activity to be delivered directly to the lungs of infected mice and retain its antibacterial activity against prominent lung disease-causing bacterial pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Haemophilus influenzae. This study will provide proof of principle data for future studies which will evaluate direct nebulised delivery of these peptide in vivo in collaboration with industry

listings.title: Understanding the machinery of collagen secretion in fibrotic disease
listings.summary: Fibrosis involves the abnormal secretion of collagen, which disrupts tissue architecture in chronic inflammation and cancer, driving debilitating disease. The molecular control of fibrosis remains poorly understood and few effective treatments exist. This PhD project will investigate how cells secrete collagen,…
listings.description:
Fibrosis involves the abnormal secretion of collagen, which disrupts tissue architecture in chronic inflammation and cancer, driving debilitating disease. The molecular control of fibrosis remains poorly understood and few effective treatments exist. This PhD project will investigate how cells secrete collagen, defining the molecular machinery that governs this process.

"Fibrosis is driven by excessive collagen secretion, yet the molecular mechanisms determining collagen biogenesis remain poorly understood. Collagens are the most abundant proteins synthesized by animals and are produced as precursors in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), which are then modified and secreted from fibrotic cells.

Notably, collagen biosynthesis is tightly regulated; failure to attain the correct structure triggers degradation via protein quality control pathways, particularly ER-phagy, which targets aberrant proteins within ER subdomains for lysosomal degradation. Another potential mechanism is ER-associated degradation (ERAD), which eliminates misfolded secretory and membrane proteins via proteasomal degradation. However, the importance of the latter pathway for collagen regulation is much less understood.

In a recent screen, we identified a key ERAD regulator as a potential modulator of collagen biogenesis and potentially ER-phagy, suggesting a previously unrecognized axis of crosstalk between ERAD, ER-phagy and collagen biogenesis.

The project aims to reveal new insights into fibrosis control and identify tractable targets for therapeutic intervention in fibrotic disease.

listings.title: Genomic Dissection of a Novel Midnolin-Mediated, Ubiquitin-Independent proteasomal degradation Pathway in the regulation of Gene expression.
listings.summary: "This project will explore how the adaptor protein midnolin regulates gene expression by promoting proteasomal degradation of transcription factors and chromatin regulators—independently of ubiquitin. Using advanced genomic and proteomic tools, the project will uncover novel mechanisms of protein turnover and…
listings.description:
"This project will explore how the adaptor protein midnolin regulates gene expression by promoting proteasomal degradation of transcription factors and chromatin regulators—independently of ubiquitin. Using advanced genomic and proteomic tools, the project will uncover novel mechanisms of protein turnover and challenge established models of gene regulation in mammalian cells.

"""Gene expression is controlled by chromatin-modifying enzymes, which regulate chromatin accessibility, and transcription factors, which direct the transcriptional machinery. The ubiquitin-proteasome system regulates protein degradation by tagging target proteins with ubiquitin via enzymes called E3 ligases. This ubiquitin code directs proteins to the proteasome, and has long been thought to control gene expression by degrading chromatin regulators and transcription factors

However, emerging evidence challenges this paradigm. A protein called midnolin has recently been identified as an adaptor that promotes the proteasomal degradation of transcription factors and chromatin regulators without requiring ubiquitin or E3 ligases. While midnolin potently drives the degradation of diverse transcriptional regulators and is critical for coordinating gene expression in Drosophila melanogaster, its role in mammalian systems remains poorly understood.

This PhD project will use cutting-edge genomic and proteomic approaches to determine how midnolin influences gene regulation in mammalian cells.

This work will reveal novel insights into protein degradation mechanisms and challenge existing models of gene expression regulation."

listings.title: Microcirculation and cancer survivorship
listings.summary: Patients that overcome cancer or live with managed secondary disease are primarily affected, and often die of, causes independent from the cancer they were diagnosed with. The most common are cardiovascular, pulmonary and neurological diseases, and these appear to correlate with cancer type but also treatment…
listings.description:
Patients that overcome cancer or live with managed secondary disease are primarily affected, and often die of, causes independent from the cancer they were diagnosed with. The most common are cardiovascular, pulmonary and neurological diseases, and these appear to correlate with cancer type but also treatment regimens. This project will investigate the effects of cancer treatment on cancer-free tissues, to understand the long-term effect on quality of life of cancer survivors.

Co-morbidities occur as a result of aggressive diseases, such as cancer, but also aggressive treatments, which are required to eliminate them. These are inevitably systemic, and circulate through our complex circulatory network, reaching every organ in the body, and having different impacts depending on what cells respond to them. Cells lining the blood vasculature encounter cytotoxic compounds first and at the highest concentrations, before such compounds reach their target cells (the tumour cells). Our lab has shown that the functional adaptations of endothelial cells are organ specific, and more severe in some organs than others. Permeability is affected, as is metabolism and the ability to regenerate and repair. In this project we want to investigate if the responses of microvascular endothelial cells are at the root of the most common morbidities seen in survivors. We will evaluate parameters to characterise the endothelial-derived signals contributing to tissue remodelling, the impact on function, the regulatory mechanisms and the reversibility of these effects, to determine if vasculoprotective measures can be used to prevent or mitigate the effects of treatment, not only to prolong life without cancer, but also to enable better quantity of life in cancer survivors.

listings.title: Microvascular cell contributions to metastatic organotropism
listings.summary: Some organs are more likely to harbour secondary tumours than others - lung metastasis are common but some organs, such as kidneys or muscle, very rarely develop metastasis. Our laboratory has shown that microvascular endothelial cells, which are unique to the organs they supply, plan a decisive role in enabling the…
listings.description:
Some organs are more likely to harbour secondary tumours than others - lung metastasis are common but some organs, such as kidneys or muscle, very rarely develop metastasis. Our laboratory has shown that microvascular endothelial cells, which are unique to the organs they supply, plan a decisive role in enabling the establishment of secondary tumours. In this project we will investigate if microvascular integrity can be targeted during cancer and treatment to prevent metastatic disease.

Endothelial cells are gatekeepers of organ function, and responsible to deliver compounds to and from specific organs to meet their metabolic demands. Equally, endothelial cells are in permanent contact with circulating blood and all that it carries: cells, signals, compounds, and respond accordingly to the messages they carry. During cancer progression and treatment, endothelial cells are exposed to tumour-derived signals and treatment induced stress. In this project we will investigate how adaptations and reprogramming of organ-specific endothelial cells affect different organs, and to what extent those changed have implications for where patients are more likely to develop secondary tumours. A combination of in vivo and ex vivo techniques will be used, to characterise the extent and reversibility of the microvascular remodelling, and how these are mirrored in whole organisms.

The aim of this project is to determine whether biomedical informatics solutions can be developed to identify, characterise, and predict adverse and unexpected events derived from the use of Digital Health interventions to ensure patient safety and a safe development of digital health.

Digital therapeutics (DTX) offer patients evidence-based therapeutic interventions that are delivered through high-quality software programs. Similar to drugs or other treatments they aim to cure, manage, or prevent a disease and they are tested on selected volunteers and patients prior to market launch to verify their efficacy and safety. DTX effectiveness of use must be proven through systematic clinical trials that assess the outcome in controlled settings to reduce bias. However, assessment of their potential safety has not been investigated so extensively.

listings.title: Investigating the function of CARD-only proteins and PYD-only proteins in human inflammasome regulation
listings.summary: CARD-only proteins (COPs) and PYD-only proteins (POPs) arose in the primate lineage and regulate inflammasome function. Using new induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) based models we will interrogate their enigmatic function in human inflammasome regulation, potentially identifying new targets for inflammatory…
listings.description:
CARD-only proteins (COPs) and PYD-only proteins (POPs) arose in the primate lineage and regulate inflammasome function. Using new induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) based models we will interrogate their enigmatic function in human inflammasome regulation, potentially identifying new targets for inflammatory diseases.

Inflammasomes are immunological sensors that detect microbial- and host-derived signals and cause inflammation. Inflammasome activation must be tightly controlled as dysregulation contributes to many inflammatory diseases. Inflammasomes can be regulated by decoy proteins known as COPs and POPs, that are thought to inhibit inflammasomes through disruption of CARD-CARD and PYD-PYD interactions. However, conflicting studies suggest that COPs like CARD16 can promote inflammasome activation, so our understanding of these proteins is incomplete. Importantly, COPs and POPs are not expressed in rodents, highlighting the need for human models to study them. We have established human iPSC-derived macrophages (iMacs) as an excellent model for physiological inflammasome studies.

In this project CRISPR/Cas9 mediated gene editing of hiPSCs will be used to define the function of COPs and POPs in inflammasome regulation. COPs and POPs e.g., CARD16, PYD2 will be knocked out in iMacs and inflammasomes will be activated (NLRP3, NLRP1, AIM2, NAIP/NLRC4, non-canonical). Inflammasome activation will be assessed by assays including ELISA (cytokine release), LDH release (pyroptosis), western blotting (caspase activation), and microscopy and flow cytometry for ASC speck formation. COP/POP function will be confirmed by complementing KO iMacs using mRNA transfection. These results may identify novel targets for the treatment of inflammatory diseases.

listings.title: Understanding the evolution of health inequalities
listings.summary: The study will use a series of cross sectional surveys over time to chart changes in health across groups. It will use concentration curve and indices to characterize inequalities, decomposition analysis to understand the changing role of individual characteristics in explaining inequalities and examine, using latent…
listings.description:
The study will use a series of cross sectional surveys over time to chart changes in health across groups. It will use concentration curve and indices to characterize inequalities, decomposition analysis to understand the changing role of individual characteristics in explaining inequalities and examine, using latent class models, to potential to leverage data to gain additional insights.

A significant literature related to health inequalities in a variety of environments exists. An analysis that examines these issues using empirical data over a variety of jurisdictions over time has the potential to provide additional insights on commonalities of experience and the evolution of experiences that may not be available within a more fragmented approach. The study will use data from surveys conducted in the US and UK to characterize and measure inequalities in health and how these change over time. Concentration curves, concentration indices and decomposition techniques will be used to describe inequalities and the role of specific variables in explaining these. Changes over time will be examined and interpreted with the broader context of societal changes. Latent class models, specifically finite mixture models will be explored to ascertain what additional insights these might afford in understanding inequalities and what might constitute appropriate policy responses. Data used will examine both self-reported and objectively measured aspects of health. Data will be taken from repositories that allow public access to data.

listings.title: Can we protect the urinary bladder from radiation toxicity?
listings.summary: Radiation therapy for pelvic malignancies unavoidably impacts healthy bladder tissue. This can lead to acute/chronic urinary symptoms due to radiation-induced bladder toxicity. Understanding the impact of radiation on the bladder’s microvasculature is particularly important as ischaemia underpins pathophysiology. This…
listings.description:
Radiation therapy for pelvic malignancies unavoidably impacts healthy bladder tissue. This can lead to acute/chronic urinary symptoms due to radiation-induced bladder toxicity. Understanding the impact of radiation on the bladder’s microvasculature is particularly important as ischaemia underpins pathophysiology. This project will investigate the impact of radiation on bladder microvascular physiology.

Radiation therapy is commonly used in cancer treatment and aims to maximise tumour kill with minimal normal tissue toxicity. The mechanisms underlying this are incompletely understood and are likely to involve many cell types in the bladder wall. The literature indicates that ischaemia is an important factor and that the bladder microvasculature may be particularly radiation-sensitive.

This project will investigate the impact of radiation on bladder microvascular physiology and aims to: (1) characterise the effect of radiation on gene and protein expression of key ion channel/receptors responsible for endothelial cell-vascular smooth muscle cell signalling (EC-VSM); (2) investigate the impact of radiation on EC-VSM physiological mechanisms; (3) examine the effect of radiation on blood flow in the bladder wall and test the potential for toxicity rescue by pharmacological modulators.

The PhD student will join an enthusiastic research team in the Patrick G Johnston Centre for Cancer Research and will receive full training in the relevant techniques. PhD students in the group typically present their work at national and international conferences and develop professional networks with early-career and established scientists both locally and across the world.

listings.title: Competing Drivers of Visual Decline: A Longitudinal Analysis of Pathology Interaction using Real-World Data
listings.summary: Many patients have more than one eye condition but care often focuses on a single disease. This project uses clinic data to understand how different conditions interact, which ones drive vision loss over time, and how this can support more personalised care.
listings.description:
Many patients have more than one eye condition but care often focuses on a single disease. This project uses clinic data to understand how different conditions interact, which ones drive vision loss over time, and how this can support more personalised care.

Patients attending hospital eye services frequently present with multiple coexisting ocular pathologies, yet most research and clinical decision-making frameworks remain focused on single-disease models. This PhD project will investigate how different eye conditions interact over time to influence visual outcomes, using a large longitudinal electronic medical record dataset.

The study will adopt a competing risks and multimorbidity framework to identify which conditions act as dominant drivers of visual decline at different stages of disease. By modelling visual acuity trajectories alongside recorded diagnoses and treatment patterns, the project will explore whether the impact of individual conditions is modified by the presence of others, and whether these interactions change over time. Particular attention will be given to transitions in dominance, such as shifts from treatable causes of vision loss (e.g. neovascular activity) to irreversible structural damage (e.g. fibrosis or atrophy).

Advanced statistical approaches, including mixed-effects models and competing risk analyses, will be used to characterise these relationships. The outputs will include clinically interpretable models of disease interaction and progression, with the potential to inform more holistic patient management strategies that reflect real-world complexity.

listings.title: ImPACT Stroke: Improving psychological wellbeing among stroke survivors
listings.summary: This is a programme of work to adapt existing psychological therapies so that they are accessible for stroke survivors, including those with cognitive impairments, through the investigation and application of alternative delivery methods, involvement of carers, and appropriate outcome measurement.
listings.description:
This is a programme of work to adapt existing psychological therapies so that they are accessible for stroke survivors, including those with cognitive impairments, through the investigation and application of alternative delivery methods, involvement of carers, and appropriate outcome measurement.

Up to 75% of stroke survivors will experience some form of cognitive difficulty and consequently are less able to access psychological therapies and other interventions. This situation can compound poor psychological wellbeing, quality of life, and social isolation for stroke survivors and their families. Our research team has designed a brief psychological intervention, called ImpACT Stroke, with significant input from stakeholders, specifically tailored for stroke survivors with cognitive impairment, delivered remotely in a small group involving the stroke survivor and using family members as support persons to help achieve therapeutic goals. This PhD programme will investigate how best to deliver this intervention in an accessible and acceptable format, and how to evaluate its impact.

listings.summary: The successful applicant will investigate associations between multiomic signatures and healthy ageing from participants of the Northern Ireland Cohort for the Longitudinal study of Ageing (NICOLA) study (https://www.qub.ac.uk/sites/NICOLA/).
listings.description:
The successful applicant will investigate associations between multiomic signatures and healthy ageing from participants of the Northern Ireland Cohort for the Longitudinal study of Ageing (NICOLA) study (https://www.qub.ac.uk/sites/NICOLA/).

We have longitudinal data for more than 8,000 older community dwelling adults from Northern Ireland. We have genomic, epigenetic, proteomic and metabolomics data for a proportion of these study participants, in additional to lined healthcare data and biomarkers of healthy ageing. The successful applicant will investigate these data to identify associations with healthy ageing and well characterised disease outcomes common among older adults in Northern Ireland.

listings.title: Stepping Beyond Blood Based Biomarker Diagnoses – Characterising Cognitive Impairment With Normal Biomarkers
listings.summary: This study will characterise cognitive impairment observed in participants without dementia-causing disease diagnoses. Correlates of severity and progression will be evaluated.
listings.description:
This study will characterise cognitive impairment observed in participants without dementia-causing disease diagnoses. Correlates of severity and progression will be evaluated.

Approximately one in four people attending memory clinics have disabling cognitive symptoms NOT due to dementia causing diseases. Such symptoms are thought to be due to a combination of factors including sleep deprivation, pain, cognitively deleterious medications, anxiety and depression. People often have a history of trauma too. Socio-economic deprivation is common. It is not clear what role, if any, personality type plays. There is currently insufficient evidence to guide diagnosis, prognosis and treatment. People without positive biomarkers are usually excluded from studies of dementia.

An observational cohort study will collect demographic, clinical and biomarker data. Participants will undergo baseline and follow-up study visits.

Quantitative data collected will include: demographic and autobiographical data, neuropsychiatric questionnaires and assessments, sleep and diet diaries, personality type questionnaires, plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration, epigenetic data eg DNA methylation.

Statistical analysis: Descriptive statistics for the group. Comparison will be made to pre-existing control cohorts where possible e.g. NICOLA.

Blood-based dementia biomarkers and Alzheimer’s disease-modifying drugs will be in routine clinical use in the next five years. People without evidence of dementia-causing diseases will be deprioritised for outpatient memory services. The results of this study will inform policy and service provision for people with cognitive impairment not due to dementia-causing diseases.

listings.title: Standardising outcome measurement in dementia with Lewy bodies
listings.summary: This PhD project will identify and recommend standard outcome measurement tools for dementia with Lewy bodies trials. Building on a newly established Core Outcome Set, it involves a systematic review, tool evaluation using COSMIN criteria, and international consensus to improve consistency and quality in clinical…
listings.description:
This PhD project will identify and recommend standard outcome measurement tools for dementia with Lewy bodies trials. Building on a newly established Core Outcome Set, it involves a systematic review, tool evaluation using COSMIN criteria, and international consensus to improve consistency and quality in clinical research.

Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is the second most common form of neurodegenerative dementia and manifests in many different symptoms. A recently developed Core Outcome Set (COS) has established international consensus on the most important symptom groups to measure in DLB trials. However, there remains no agreement on which outcome measurement tools (OMTs) should be used to do so, limiting consistency in the symptoms measured during clinical trials and impeding data synthesis across studies.

This PhD project aims to identify and recommend suitable OMTs for each outcome in the DLB COS, thereby advancing methodological consistency in DLB research.

By producing a standardised measurement framework, this project will support more rigorous, comparable, and patient-relevant DLB trials, ultimately contributing to better evidence and improved care.

listings.title: The identification and development of blood-based DNA methylation markers to differentiate endometriosis and endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer.
listings.summary: This project aims to develop a non-invasive blood test to improve early diagnosis of endometriosis and endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer (EAOC). Using a novel platform combining in silico machine learning, Enzymatic NGS Methylation Detection and Methylation Sensitive Restriction Enzyme Droplet Digital PCR (MSRE…
listings.description:
This project aims to develop a non-invasive blood test to improve early diagnosis of endometriosis and endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer (EAOC). Using a novel platform combining in silico machine learning, Enzymatic NGS Methylation Detection and Methylation Sensitive Restriction Enzyme Droplet Digital PCR (MSRE ddPCR), we will identify and validate circulating DNA methylation biomarkers to support earlier detection and better clinical outcomes.

Endometriosis is a chronic, debilitating disease affecting 10% of women of reproductive age, often diagnosed after significant delay due to non-specific symptoms and a lack of non-invasive tests. It has been increasingly associated with a heightened risk of developing endometriosis-associated ovarian cancers (EAOC), particularly the endometrioid and clear cell subtypes. The mechanisms underlying this malignant transformation remain unclear, though chronic inflammation and aberrant DNA methylation are thought to play a role.

This project aims to develop a non-invasive blood-based diagnostic test for the early detection and differentiation of endometriosis and EAOC using circulating free DNA (cfDNA) methylation markers. The study will employ a validated biomarker development platform combining in silico machine learning and the TWIST NGS Methylation Detection System with MSRE ddPCR.

The objectives are to: (1) identify DNA methylation signatures specific to endometriosis and EAOC, (2) design and optimise sensitive methylation assays and (3) validate these assays in independent cohorts. Plasma and FFPE samples from women with endometriosis, EAOC and disease-free controls will be analysed.

This work addresses a critical clinical need for earlier diagnosis, improved disease stratification and better long-term outcomes for women with endometriosis and related malignancies.

listings.title: How inflammation becomes fibrosis! investigations into the development of pulmonary fibrosis
listings.summary: Interstitial lung disease (IPF, SSc-ILD) has limited therapeutic options. Using our novel pre-clinical model based on peripheral-blood-derived-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) fibroblasts, epithelial and endothelial cells, we will study the role of the epithelial/endothelial…
listings.description:
Interstitial lung disease (IPF, SSc-ILD) has limited therapeutic options. Using our novel pre-clinical model based on peripheral-blood-derived-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) fibroblasts, epithelial and endothelial cells, we will study the role of the epithelial/endothelial senescence-associated-secretory-phenotype (SASP) in fibrosis and identify already licenced drugs to bring benefits to patients.

Pulmonary fibrosis is a serious, life-limiting lung disease. It causes scarring and thickening of lung tissue over time, making it harder to breathe. There is currently no cure for pulmonary fibrosis.

The most common type of pulmonary fibrosis is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a progressive fibrotic lung disease with unknown cause, affecting approximately 3 million people worldwide. Lung fibrosis is also one of the most common complications in patients with Systemic Sclerosis (SSc). Worldwide 30-50% of SSc patients develop lung fibrosis. The prevalence of SSc-ILD in East Asia is 56% (95% CI 49%-63%) with the highest prevalence occurring in China (72%). Repetitive endothelial and epithelial cell injury is believed to be the first step in the pathological process, which leads to recruitment and activation of fibroblasts and differentiation of fibroblasts to myofibroblasts. Of particular importance is the diseases-specific microenvironment in which fibroblasts are activated. Our work (Fields A et al. 2022) and published data (Schruf E, et al. 2020) show that the microenvironment in SSc-ILD and IPF is highly pro-inflammatory and fibrogenic. Therefore, the source of these microenvironment constituents is a pharmaceutical target to limit pulmonary fibrosis.

Due to the very high mortality rate and the currently limited therapeutic options, there is an unmet need for further research to develop new anti-fibrotic drugs. However, access to patient-derived lung fibroblasts for research is ethically difficult and cells from end stage disease may not accurately reflect disease progression. Therefore, there is also a need for a patient relevant disease model. The project will use a patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) in-vitro cell model of fibroblasts and other lung relevant cells. The proposed project will use patient derived iPSC cells (Vilà-González M et al., 2019).
