listings.title: Aging and senescence in regulation of the angiocrine functions of pulmonary endothelium and therapeutic potential of cell based therapies
listings.summary: Aging impairs lung repair and increases disease risk, partly through vascular dysfunction. This project investigates how endothelial aging affects lung regeneration and evaluates whether cell-based therapies—mesenchymal stromal cells, their extracellular vesicles, or endothelial progenitors—can restore endothelial…
listings.description:
Aging impairs lung repair and increases disease risk, partly through vascular dysfunction. This project investigates how endothelial aging affects lung regeneration and evaluates whether cell-based therapies—mesenchymal stromal cells, their extracellular vesicles, or endothelial progenitors—can restore endothelial function and promote alveolar repair, offering potential interventions for age-related lung injury.

Aging is a major risk factor for many lung diseases. Despite the strong association between aging and disease, few studies have investigated the molecular mechanisms that account for this association.

Growing evidence suggests that vasculature plays important role and, at least in some organs, controls the tissue aging. Blood vessels also provide inductive factors, termed angiocrine signals which, in the lung, has been demonstrated to contribute to alveolar epithelial regeneration.

Cell based therapies such as mesenchymal stromal cells or their extracellular vesicles or early endothelial progenitors are being increasingly recognised as advanced therapeutics and are rapidly moving towards clinical translation.

In this project we will characterise how replicative senescence and age affect functional properties of pulmonary endothelium and its ability to promote lung epithelial repair . We will also test if cell based therapies (MSCs, MSC EVs and ECFCs) can alleviate age-related abnormalities in endothelial cells and reduce severity of lung injury.

listings.title: Advanced Mesenchymal Stem Cell Exosomes for Treating Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
listings.summary: In this project we wish to develop the novel unique next-generation stem cell therapy product based on MSC exosomes. We will test if modifications of MSC exosomes with interference RNA (siRNA) for a specific factor (previously identified by our group) will improve their therapeutic efficacy.
listings.description:
In this project we wish to develop the novel unique next-generation stem cell therapy product based on MSC exosomes. We will test if modifications of MSC exosomes with interference RNA (siRNA) for a specific factor (previously identified by our group) will improve their therapeutic efficacy.

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a major cause of acute respiratory failure in critically ill patients requiring mechanical ventilation and is associated with high mortality and morbidity. ARDS has no specific pharmacological therapy and advanced therapeutics based on mesenchymal stromal cells extracellular vesicles are rapidly moving towards clinical translation.

Recently we have identified a regulatory protein which might be driving development and progression of ARDS. RNA interference (RNAi) has become a primary method for selective gene silencing. Exosomes are natural intercellular transporters of RNAs. Because of their intrinsic features, exosomes can present a more effective means for transferring siRNAs than classic delivery vehicles.

In this project we propose to further investigate the signalling pathway downstream of this regulatory protein and enhance therapeutic potency of MSC exosomes by transfection with siRNA for this specific and/or other downstream regulators and test their efficacy in the in vitro models.

This project investigates how ophthalmic and systemic multimorbidity jointly affect health outcomes, quality of life, and healthcare use in older adults. Using advanced statistical and machine learning techniques on large longitudinal datasets, it aims to inform integrated, person-centred care pathways for individuals living with complex health conditions.

Multimorbidity—the co-occurrence of two or more chronic conditions—is a growing public health concern, particularly in ageing populations. While the impact of systemic multimorbidity (e.g. cardiovascular disease, diabetes) on health outcomes has been well-documented, the intersection with ophthalmic conditions (e.g. age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy) remains poorly understood. Vision impairment is a key contributor to disability and reduced quality of life, yet its synergistic impact when co-existing with systemic disease is under-researched. There is an urgent need to quantify how ophthalmic and systemic multimorbidity interact to affect functional outcomes, care pathways, and patient-reported experiences.

To investigate the longitudinal impact of combined ophthalmic and systemic multimorbidity on health outcomes, care utilisation, and quality of life in older adults.

i) To identify and characterise multimorbidity clusters that include ophthalmic disease using unsupervised machine learning techniques (e.g. hierarchical clustering, latent class analysis) applied to linked population-level health datasets (e.g. NICOLA, UK Biobank, INSIGHT). This will uncover patterns of disease co-occurrence.

ii) To examine the longitudinal association between identified multimorbidity clusters and health outcomes, including all-cause mortality, unplanned hospital admissions, falls, and institutionalisation, using multistate survival models and joint modelling of longitudinal and time-to-event data.

iii) To evaluate the differential impact of multimorbidity clusters on patient-reported outcomes, such as vision-specific and generic quality of life, depression, and functional independence, using validated instruments and mixed-effects regression modelling.

iv) To assess how ophthalmic and systemic multimorbidity influences health service utilisation and care fragmentation, including delays in treatment and access to ophthalmic care, through health economic analysis and sequence analysis of care trajectories.

This project uses high-resolution ANTERION OCT data from the NICOLA study to explore how anterior segment eye structures relate to cataract severity, systemic health, and quality of life in older adults. It aims to inform risk stratification, surgical planning, and integrated care for age-related ocular and systemic conditions.

Cataract remains the leading cause of reversible vision loss in older adults, yet population-level data on its structural ocular correlates and systemic associations are limited. The Heidelberg ANTERION swept-source OCT offers high-resolution imaging of anterior segment structures—such as lens thickness, anterior chamber depth, and axial length—enabling precise quantification of cataract severity and biometric parameters.

This PhD project will utilise cross-sectional data from the NICOLA study, a large, well-characterised cohort of older adults in Northern Ireland, to examine the relationships between anterior segment biometry, cataract severity, and systemic health.

This project will provide novel insights into the interplay between ocular structure, systemic disease, and functional vision in ageing populations, with implications for cataract risk stratification and integrated care.

listings.summary: Approximately 25% patients will develop a symptomatic cardiac event following treatment and resulting hospitalisations and morbidity are detrimental for quality of life during survivorship. listings.description:
Approximately 25% patients will develop a symptomatic cardiac event following treatment and resulting hospitalisations and morbidity are detrimental for quality of life during survivorship. Survival outcomes have improved considerably due to advances in radiotherapy and systemic therapy over the last decade, meaning there is a greater need to lower such risks.

The incidental radiation dose received by several cardiac substructures has been shown to be associated with the incidence of symptomatic cardiac events. eg. we identified that dose to the pulmonary veins is associated with new atrial arrhythmias. Furthermore, we have shown that baseline features of the heart on radiotherapy planning CT scans can be used to identify patients at high risk of several cardiotoxicity subtypes. With the greater availability of autocontouring solutions for cardiac substructures, and a growing evidence base on safe dose limits for these regions, the next step to implementation of cardiac-sparing radiotherapy planning techniques is to demonstrate the feasibility and safety of this approach.

The objective of the PhD project, ""Heart-Optimised Lung Radiotherapy Planning"", is to generate the large-scale feasibility data for sparing the key cardiac substructures in turn, and the dosimetric implications for the tumour, other cardiac substructures and standard organ-at-risk. The Fellow will primarily become adept with technical radiotherapy planning and statistical analysis, but there will also be opportunities to coordinate a Delphi study, conduct resource implication analysis, depending on the Fellow’s interests.

The work will be performed using the NI–HEART dataset and will be co-supervised by Dr Conor McGarry (Radiotherapy Physicist, Queen’s University Belfast).

listings.summary: This project will investigate and develop effective educational approaches for equipping dental undergraduate students with the insight skills and wellbeing strategies to recognise their professional limitations and manage their mental and physical wellbeing, thereby enhancing their preparedness for clinical practice.
listings.description:
This project will investigate and develop effective educational approaches for equipping dental undergraduate students with the insight skills and wellbeing strategies to recognise their professional limitations and manage their mental and physical wellbeing, thereby enhancing their preparedness for clinical practice.

Background: Recently, the General Dental Council have highlighted concerns over newly registered dentists’ preparedness to practice in areas such as recognising their own strengths and limitations and managing and acknowledging their mental health and wellbeing. The GDC’s upcoming Safe Practitioner Framework sets expectations for these ‘insight skills’ in dental professional education, and there are many ways that the proposed learning outcomes and behaviours could be assessed.

Aims: To investigate and develop effective educational approaches for equipping dental undergraduate students with the insight and wellbeing strategies to manage their mental and physical health, recognise their professional limitations, and identify their ongoing learning needs, thereby enhancing their preparedness for clinical practice.

Objectives: A comprehensive review will investigate existing research on dental education, student wellbeing, approaches to developing insight, and reflective practice. Data will be collected via interviews, surveys, focus groups of dental students, educators, and recent graduates, and subsequently analysed. Local educational interventions will also be designed and evaluated using mixed methods. Evidence-based recommendations will be made for pedagogical strategies to enhance dental students’ insight skills.

The promise of AI in medicine will depend on tools being accepted by health care workers (HCW). Understanding the readiness of HCW in different settings will allow leadership on responsible and ethical integration of AI in health systems.

AI for health is rapidly evolving, and will disrupt the way that medicine is delivered and health systems are structured. This requires health leaders and health workers to accept the integration of AI in their working lives. However, the speed of progress risks HCW being left behind, and not taking leadership from within the health sector. On a global level, we risk leaving many populations behind in AI adoption, including HCW, patients and carers. We need to ensure that we do not widen health inequalities with health AI.

Objectives – this mixed methods (qualitative and quantitative) PhD will provide important evidence which could inform integration of AI into health systems, but understanding the attitudes of HCW to this new way of working.

listings.title: Deciphering the epitranscriptomic code: The role of RNA modifications
listings.summary: Cells add or remove chemical modifications to almost all mRNAs to regulate their stability, splicing, localisation and translation efficiency in response to environmental stimuli. This project aims to measure and further elucidate the function of this ‘epitranscriptome’ in a range of model systems.
listings.description:
Cells add or remove chemical modifications to almost all mRNAs to regulate their stability, splicing, localisation and translation efficiency in response to environmental stimuli. This project aims to measure and further elucidate the function of this ‘epitranscriptome’ in a range of model systems.

The epitranscriptome—the collection of chemical modifications on RNA—plays a crucial role in post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression, influencing RNA stability, splicing, translation, and localization. Among these, N6-methyladenosine (m⁶A) is the most prevalent mRNA modification, dynamically regulated by writer, reader, and eraser proteins. Dysregulation of RNA modifications is increasingly implicated in diverse biological processes and diseases, including cancer and neurological disorders. This project aims to investigate how the epitranscriptome regulates gene expression in human cells by identifying and characterizing RNA modifications at single-nucleotide resolution.

The inability to study RNA modifications at a transcriptome-wide scale has recently been overcome with development of nanopore direct RNA sequencing technology, which enables simultaneous detection of RNA sequences and native modifications. Publicly available nanopore datasets will be re-analysed using state-of-the-art modification-calling tools to identify conserved and condition-specific RNA modification sites. Findings will be validated in vitro using human cell culture models, with functional perturbation of RNA modification machinery (e.g., knockdown of m⁶A writer METTL3) to assess consequences on gene expression and RNA fate.

Objectives include mapping the landscape of RNA modifications, linking them to specific regulatory outcomes, and defining epitranscriptomic mechanisms that control transcriptome dynamics under physiological and perturbed conditions.

listings.summary: Streptococcus pneumoniae (StP) is a microorganism significantly associated with pneumonia. listings.description:
Streptococcus pneumoniae (StP) is a microorganism significantly associated with pneumonia. Proteases are released directly into the extracellular milieu where they are thought to contribute significantly to the inflammation and lung damage mediated by bacterial infection. In this study, we will focus on the role of a key protease, known to be upregulated by StP in the lungs of affected individuals, and determine if inhibition of this protease ameliorates the pathogenic effects of StP in vivo.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (StP) is a microorganism significantly associated with pneumonia. Bacterial pneumonia in humans is often accompanied by a pronounced inflammatory response and the recruitment of large numbers of neutrophils to the lung. This neutrophilic response is important for the control of bacterial infection but excessive neutrophilia can also lead to tissue damage in the lung, characterized by disruption of the alveolar barrier, pulmonary edema, and severely compromised lung function. The release of proteases from cells is associated with lung damage and aberrant tissue remodelling and is a feature of many bacterial lung infections. Proteases are released directly into the extracellular milieu where they are thought to contribute significantly to the inflammation and lung damage mediated by bacterial infection. In this study, we will focus on the role of a key protease, known to be upregulated by StP in the lungs of affected individuals, and determine if inhibition of this protease ameliorates the pathogenic effects of StP in vivo. This project represents a significant engagement between academics working at the interface between innate immunity and medicinal chemistry and positive data from this study could lead to significant downstream therapeutic development.

listings.title: Multi-omic analysis of Barrett’s Oesophagus: Insights into the Early Detection of Oesophageal Cancer
listings.summary: Multi-omic integration of RNAseq, methylation and spatial transcriptomic data for the discovery of biomarkers for the early detection of oesophageal cancer.
listings.description:
Multi-omic integration of RNAseq, methylation and spatial transcriptomic data for the discovery of biomarkers for the early detection of oesophageal cancer.

The incidence of oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC), has risen by 50% in the UK in the last 25-30 years and five-year survival is 15%, highlighting the need for better preventative/early diagnosis strategies. Barrett’s oesophagus is the precursor of OAC and new approaches are required to identify lesions at high risk of progression to High Grade Dysplasia (HGD)/OAC to facilitate endoscopic therapy or increased surveillance.

Combined DNA/RNA extraction has been performed on 160 progressor/non-progressor pairs and extracted RNA/DNA has been analysed using RNAseq and the Twist methylome platform. In addition a subset of cases have been profiled by spatial transcriptomics using the Xenium platform. Integrated analysis of the methylation and gene expression data will be carried out to identify pathways and genes associated with progression of non-dysplastic Barrett’s to HGD/OAC. Discovery of these pathways will lead to the development of relevant biomarkers of progression to be used for the early detection of oesophageal cancer.

listings.description:
Chronic kidney disease is a rising public health crisis, with diabetes and certain lifestyle factors driving risk. Our team uses multi-omic and population cohort data to identify novel biomarkers, aiming to detect disease earlier and identify individuals who are at the highest risk of development

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) has been described as a public health emergency with case numbers growing rapidly each year. There is no cure, but life-changing treatments at later stages of the disease help manage the condition. Diabetes is responsible for a large proportion of CKD, accounting for almost half of cases. An individual’s lifestyle behaviours such as diet, exercise, smoking, medication and environment can affect their risk of developing progressive kidney disease.

Our team has experience in identifying novel biomarkers for diabetic kidney disease, combining large population cohort data including lifestyle behaviours, alongside single-omic and multi-omic approaches. Our aim is to identify at-risk individuals and detect disease earlier.

listings.title: Striving for Equity in Ageing: Epigenetic Clocks in Kidney Disease Disparities
listings.summary: Explore whether accelerated epigenetic ageing contributes to kidney health inequalities. Integrate clinical and molecular data to examine how life exposures shape biological ageing and disease risk, aiming to improve risk stratification and inform targeted interventions in ageing populations.
listings.description:
Explore whether accelerated epigenetic ageing contributes to kidney health inequalities. Integrate clinical and molecular data to examine how life exposures shape biological ageing and disease risk, aiming to improve risk stratification and inform targeted interventions in ageing populations.

"Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) represent growing health challenges globally, disproportionately affecting disadvantaged and aging populations.

This PhD project aims to investigate the molecular basis underlying these health inequalities by applying aging biomarkers, particularly epigenetic clocks, to characterise biological aging trajectories.

By integrating clinical, demographic, and molecular data, this project will assess accelerated epigenetic aging in CKD and DKD.

Epigenetic patterns change dynamically over the life course in response to environmental and social exposures, meaning they can act as a molecular record of how factors such as stress, lifestyle, and social factors influence health and disease risk.

Understanding these mechanisms is critical in the context of an aging population and the rising prevalence of diabetes, which together are driving an increasing burden of kidney disease worldwide.

This project seeks to generate insights that could help inform more equitable risk stratification, identify intervention strategies, and ultimately reduce disparities in kidney health."

listings.title: Acknowledging Post-Trial Obligations: Establishing Standards in Dementia Research (APRES)
listings.summary: Post-trial access after dementia trials is ungoverned and ethically inadequate. APRES will develop the first dementia-specific, consensus-based framework for post-trial access obligations, co-produced with people living with dementia, for use by trial sponsors and ethics committees.
listings.description:
Post-trial access after dementia trials is ungoverned and ethically inadequate. APRES will develop the first dementia-specific, consensus-based framework for post-trial access obligations, co-produced with people living with dementia, for use by trial sponsors and ethics committees.

"The Declaration of Helsinki requires that trial sponsors arrange continued access to investigational treatments for participants who have benefited, yet in practice post-trial access (PTA) operates as a discretionary, ungoverned process with no implementation mechanisms and limited ethics committee oversight. This gap is particularly acute in dementia, where trial failure rates are exceptionally high, the path from trial success to accessible treatment is protracted, and progressive cognitive decline may eliminate the opportunity to address consent deficiencies once a trial is underway.

No dementia-specific PTA framework currently exists. APRES addresses this through a three-year mixed methods programme comprising three interconnected work packages: qualitative evidence generation with people living with dementia, care partners, and clinicians; a modified Delphi consensus process to establish minimum PTA standards; and co-production of an implementable governance framework for trial sponsors and research ethics committees.

PPIE is the methodological and ethical foundation of the project. A care partner co-applicant will contribute from inception, and people with dementia and care partners will move across the full spectrum from research participation to framework co-production. Primary outputs will be disseminated through the Health Research Authority and UK research ethics committee networks."

listings.title: Development of a Small Molecule Cathepsin V Inhibitor for Study in Breast Cancer
listings.summary: Cathepsin V (CTSV), is a lysosomal cysteine protease , has emerged as a significant player in the progression of breast cancer, particularly in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) subtypes (Cathepsin V suppresses GATA3 protein expression in luminal A breast cancer - PubMed, Cathepsin V regulates cell cycle progression…
listings.description:
Cathepsin V (CTSV), is a lysosomal cysteine protease , has emerged as a significant player in the progression of breast cancer, particularly in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) subtypes (Cathepsin V suppresses GATA3 protein expression in luminal A breast cancer - PubMed, Cathepsin V regulates cell cycle progression and histone stability in the nucleus of breast cancer cells - PubMed). This cysteine protease is primarily expressed in the thymus, corneal epithelium, and testis under normal conditions. However, in cancer, especially breast cancer, its expression is abnormally elevated. High CTSV expression correlates with poor prognosis in ER+ (especially luminal A) breast cancers but may have a different impact in HER2-enriched or basal-like subtypes. CTSV overexpression is also associated with increased distal metastasis formation. Research conducted at Queen’s, within the Burden lab, has revealed that genetic manipulation of this protease can have a significant impact on the cancer cell signalling pathways and the regulation of GATA3. This data also supported our hypothesis that targeting CSTV with a small molecule inhibitor would be of significant interest for treating ER+ breast cancers.

Project Plan – to date there are no real reported small molecule inhibitors of CTSV. To address this, we aim to develop a novel CTSV inhibitor. This studentship will be focused on (a) synthesizing new small molecule inhibitors and exploring the structural activity relationship (SAR) of this new inhibitor series; (b) testing in cell-based assays to determine impact on biomarkers of CTSV activity; (c) testing lead inhibitor(s) on the hallmarks of breast cancer in cell line models with and without current treatments of care.

listings.title: Functional characterisation of genetic susceptibility loci for breast cancer through post-GWAS enhancer mapping
listings.summary: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of common genetic variants associated with breast cancer risk, most of which lie in non-coding regions of the genome. Understanding how these variants influence gene regulation is essential to reveal new biological pathways and improve risk prediction and…
listings.description:
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of common genetic variants associated with breast cancer risk, most of which lie in non-coding regions of the genome. Understanding how these variants influence gene regulation is essential to reveal new biological pathways and improve risk prediction and prevention strategies.

This project aims to elucidate the functional mechanisms underlying breast cancer susceptibility loci, focusing on regulatory variants that alter enhancer activity. By integrating genetic fine-mapping, epigenomic annotation, and functional assays, the project will identify causal variants, their target genes, and the cell types in which they act.

Experimental work will involve identifying candidate enhancer elements using chromatin accessibility and histone modification datasets (e.g. ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq), assessing allele-specific enhancer activity through luciferase reporter assays and CRISPR-based perturbation, and characterising downstream effects on gene expression and cellular phenotypes. Where relevant, findings will be extended to male breast cancer to explore shared and sex-specific mechanisms of genetic susceptibility.

This research will enhance understanding of how non-coding genetic variation shapes cancer risk and may identify novel regulatory pathways involved in breast carcinogenesis, with potential implications for biomarker discovery and targeted prevention.

listings.title: Uncovering Genetic Determinants of Radionuclide Therapy Response: Enhancing the Efficacy of lead-212 in Prostate Cancer
listings.summary: This project aims to improve the therapeutic potential of targeted alpha radionuclide therapy using lead-212 (212Pb) in prostate cancer. By systematically identifying genes that influence tumour cell sensitivity to 212Pb, this work seeks to reveal the molecular pathways that drive radioresistance and uncover novel…
listings.description:
This project aims to improve the therapeutic potential of targeted alpha radionuclide therapy using lead-212 (212Pb) in prostate cancer. By systematically identifying genes that influence tumour cell sensitivity to 212Pb, this work seeks to reveal the molecular pathways that drive radioresistance and uncover novel strategies to enhance treatment efficacy.

Targeted alpha therapies (TATs) deliver potent, short-range cytotoxic radiation directly to cancer cells and have shown promising clinical results. Lead-212 is an emerging radionuclide with favourable physical properties and established conjugation chemistry for targeted delivery. However, tumour heterogeneity and intrinsic radioresistance limit its therapeutic benefit, and the molecular mechanisms underlying these resistance pathways remain poorly understood.

This project will use a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen in prostate cancer cell lines to identify genes whose loss alters the cellular response to 212Pb exposure. Integrating functional genomics with transcriptomic profiling will uncover key regulators of DNA damage repair, oxidative stress and cell-cycle control that shape therapeutic outcomes. The ultimate goal is to define actionable targets that can be co-inhibited or modulated to enhance the efficacy of 212Pb-based treatments and improve patient outcomes.

As a PhD student, you will gain expertise in CRISPR screening, radiobiology, RNA-Seq, and bioinformatics within an interdisciplinary environment bridging radiochemistry, cancer genomics, and therapeutic development—an ideal platform to build skills at the interface of radiation biology and precision medicine.

listings.title: Characterising the physical parameters and radiobiological mechanisms of responses to photon FLASH radiotherapy
listings.summary: Radiotherapy (RT) is a central pillar of modern cancer care that is used to treat around half of all patients during their treatment journey. RT at ultra-high dose rates has triggered intense interest in the radiation sciences and has led to a new treatment paradigm known as FLASH-RT. This approach has been shown to…
listings.description:
Radiotherapy (RT) is a central pillar of modern cancer care that is used to treat around half of all patients during their treatment journey. RT at ultra-high dose rates has triggered intense interest in the radiation sciences and has led to a new treatment paradigm known as FLASH-RT. This approach has been shown to effectively control tumours while sparing healthy tissues. However, key questions remain concerning the optimum delivery parameters for FLASH-RT and the underlying mechanisms of response to FLASH in tumours and normal tissues.

Our group has recently implemented a photon FLASH cabinet system capable of delivering FLASH dose rates of >80 Gy/s with depth-dose uniformity and field dimensions sufficient for the irradiation of murine models. This system is enabling new lines of research to understand the fundamental principles of FLASH in preclinical models that will support its future translation to clinical practice.

As part of the ongoing development of the FLASH-RT program at Queen’s University Belfast, we seek to explore the ability of FLASH to spare treatment related toxicities in organs at risk during radiotherapy. This work will use preclinical models to identify the key parameters driving FLASH sparing and use omics methods to understand the underlying mechanisms of response.

The PhD student will be part of the Translational Radiobiology Group and gain multidisciplinary experience of radiobiology and radiotherapy physics for advanced experimental studies. This work will develop the evidence base for FLASH-RT by providing critical advances in understanding and contribute to high-impact research, develop a strong foundation in radiation biology.

listings.title: The identification of novel diagnostic markers and druggable targets for Poor Outcome Cancers using differential DNA methylation (DNAme) profiles.
listings.summary: This project aims to discover novel biomarkers and candidate drug targets, based on their differential DNA methylation (DNAme) status in some of the most aggressive cancer types. Poor outcome cancers such as Triple Negative Breast, Ovarian, Pancreatic and Lung Cancers, are often diagnosed in late stages, making…
listings.description:
This project aims to discover novel biomarkers and candidate drug targets, based on their differential DNA methylation (DNAme) status in some of the most aggressive cancer types. Poor outcome cancers such as Triple Negative Breast, Ovarian, Pancreatic and Lung Cancers, are often diagnosed in late stages, making treatments more difficult. Additionally, these cancer types often have limited knowledge around the oncogenic driver pathways responsible for their aggressive traits and poor responses to current therapies.

We have generated DNAme profiles using blood samples from patients with these cancer types. Aberrant DNAme events occur in almost every cancer type, often before the emergence of mutations. Early detection of these cancers would be a major advance in our ability to improve the poor survival rates. DNAme markers could therefore represent reliable starting point for the development of ‘Liquid Biopsy’ assays, capable of detecting circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) in blood. Differential DNAme could also provide insights into tumour suppressor and oncogene regulation, revealing genes/pathways which could targeted using novel therapies.

As a PhD student you will gain valuable experience in cutting edge biomarker and drug development. You will be involved in identifying DNAme markers with the potential to serve as early detection or diagnostic markers, using techniques such as MSRE-PCR, droplet digital PCR technology and fragmentomics approaches. Functional analyses will assess candidate targets, serving as starting points for novel drug development. You will be part of a collaborative team at the forefront of epigenetics, cancer biology, diagnostics and drug development, and be trained in the skillset necessary to pursue a future career in molecular oncology.

listings.title: Targeting apoptosis to overcome resistance to cancer therapy
listings.summary: Cancer therapy resistance remains a significant barrier to successful treatment outcomes across multiple malignancies. Our work and the work of others have elucidated the pivotal role of apoptosis-regulating proteins, such as FLIP and inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs), in controlling cell death pathways central…
listings.description:
Cancer therapy resistance remains a significant barrier to successful treatment outcomes across multiple malignancies. Our work and the work of others have elucidated the pivotal role of apoptosis-regulating proteins, such as FLIP and inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs), in controlling cell death pathways central to therapeutic response. Dysregulation and overexpression of these proteins have been correlated with resistance to chemotherapy, radiation, and immune cell–mediated apoptosis in various cancer types.

This project aims to investigate novel strategies to sensitize resistant cancer cells by pharmacologically targeting FLIP and IAPs, either alone or in combination with existing standard-of-care therapies, such as chemotherapies (e.g. 5-Fluorouracil) and targeted therapies (e.g. KRAS inhibitors). Through preclinical mechanistic evaluation of new small molecule inhibitors and genetic approaches, the project will assess whether and how modulation of apoptotic signaling can restore therapy-induced cell death and overcome resistance. The findings are expected to inform selection of patients who may benefit from apoptosis-targeting agents and accelerate clinical translation of such strategies, offering renewed hope in treating otherwise refractory cancers.​

listings.title: Breaking Resistance: Immune-Driven Therapeutic Advances in Refractory Childhood AML
listings.summary: This project will define how standard-of-care chemotherapeutics and FDA-approved drugs activate immune responses in in vitro and immune-competent in vivo models of paediatric acute myeloid leukaemia (pAML), and provide a rationale for combining them with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) as a new second-line option…
listings.description:
This project will define how standard-of-care chemotherapeutics and FDA-approved drugs activate immune responses in in vitro and immune-competent in vivo models of paediatric acute myeloid leukaemia (pAML), and provide a rationale for combining them with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) as a new second-line option for refractory pAML.

Paediatric AML accounts for nearly one-tenth of cancers diagnosed under age 18 and remains an unmet clinical need. Outcomes are poor, treatments are highly toxic, and ~15% of patients develop refractory disease, reducing survival by up to 40%. Aside from Gemtuzumab and better supportive care, therapy has changed little in three decades. To address gaps in disease biology and therapeutic opportunities, the National Cancer Institute and Children’s Oncology Group established the AML initiative within the TARGET programme, generating extensive multi-omics data from over 1,000 cases.

Our computational analysis of transcriptomic data from refractory pAML samples shows that, after induction failure, an immune response becomes activated compared with matched diagnostic samples. These findings provide a rationale for introducing ICIs as part of second-line therapy rather than simply intensifying chemotherapy, which offers limited benefit in refractory disease.

ICIs have shown limited success in many childhood cancers, often because combinations are not selected based on the immune-priming properties of partner drugs. This study will identify which agents best modulate immune activity in pAML and may inform innovative combination strategies in other childhood cancers.

The successful applicant will gain experience in tissue culture, qRT-PCR, Western blotting, CRISPR/shRNA knockout or depletion, ELISA, CAM assays, RNA-seq, and data analysis.

listings.title: Cutting through Brain Cancer: Understanding Semaphorin Proteolysis in Glioblastoma
listings.summary: Semaphorins are cell-surface signalling proteins central to neural development and also regulate immune function, angiogenesis and tumour invasion. Several semaphorins are overexpressed in glioblastoma, contributing to aggressive growth and poor prognosis. Emerging evidence shows that semaphorins and their receptors…
listings.description:
Semaphorins are cell-surface signalling proteins central to neural development and also regulate immune function, angiogenesis and tumour invasion. Several semaphorins are overexpressed in glioblastoma, contributing to aggressive growth and poor prognosis. Emerging evidence shows that semaphorins and their receptors can be proteolytically cleaved to generate soluble fragments, but the pathophysiological impact of this process is not well defined in brain cancer.

This PhD project will investigate how cell surface proteolysis generates soluble forms of semaphorins and their receptors. We will identify which semaphorins and receptors are cleaved in glioblastoma and determine how this process alters tumour behaviour and the surrounding microenvironment. Using established tools and glioblastoma models, the project will define the proteases responsible for semaphorin shedding and assess how intact versus cleaved forms influence signalling outputs, tumour-cell phenotypes and interactions within the microenvironment.

The project will also examine how chemotherapy affects protease activity and semaphorin shedding and whether cleaved semaphorins contribute to treatment resistance. This work will uncover fundamental principles of semaphorin proteolysis in glioblastoma and highlight potential therapeutic vulnerabilities.

The PhD student will develop expertise in advanced cell and molecular techniques including CRISPR-mediated gene editing, quantitative proteomics, RNA-Seq, live-cell imaging and co-culture systems. The project offers a highly collaborative environment spanning cell surface proteolysis, cancer signalling and tumour biology, providing opportunities to contribute to mechanistic discoveries with direct relevance to brain cancer.

listings.title: How Axon-Guidance Systems Are Redeployed to Regulate Cancer–Neuron Interactions
listings.summary: Semaphorins and their receptors, originally defined as axon-guidance molecules, are increasingly recognised as regulators of tumour invasion and cellular plasticity. Breast tumours exist within a microenvironment enriched in nerve-derived cues that can influence cancer progression, yet the molecular signals…
listings.description:
Semaphorins and their receptors, originally defined as axon-guidance molecules, are increasingly recognised as regulators of tumour invasion and cellular plasticity. Breast tumours exist within a microenvironment enriched in nerve-derived cues that can influence cancer progression, yet the molecular signals coordinating this communication remain incompletely defined. Given their established roles in axon guidance and cancer cell behaviour, semaphorins and their receptors represent compelling candidates for mediating functional interactions between neurons and breast cancer cells.

This PhD project will investigate how semaphorin–receptor signalling shapes the influence of neurons on breast cancer cells. Using tractable co-culture systems combining breast cancer lines with differentiated neuron-like cells, we will determine how manipulating semaphorins or their receptors in either compartment alters cancer-cell invasion, migration, survival and responses to therapy. Signalling outputs in cancer cells will be profiled to identify mechanisms through which neuronal cues reprogramme tumour behaviour.

To capture the broader consequences of this interaction, the project will integrate transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of both cancer cells and neurons, using species-mixed or fluorescence-based separation to resolve cell-specific responses. These datasets will define how semaphorin-dependent cues remodel cancer-cell programmes and reciprocally influence neuronal states. Together, this work will establish how semaphorin signalling contributes to nerve–breast cancer crosstalk and identify potential therapeutic targets. The student will gain expertise in advanced neuronal-cancer cell co-culture models and integrative omics approaches.

listings.title: How does heterogeneity in HPV expression influence the tumour microenvironment of oropharyngeal cancers?
listings.summary: There is an unmet clinical need to identify oropharyngeal cancer patients who are likely to recur following curative treatment. Here we propose to understand to what extent HPV heterogeneity influences cancer-specific outcomes, the influence this has on the tumour microenvironment and how this might lead to recurrent…
listings.description:
There is an unmet clinical need to identify oropharyngeal cancer patients who are likely to recur following curative treatment. Here we propose to understand to what extent HPV heterogeneity influences cancer-specific outcomes, the influence this has on the tumour microenvironment and how this might lead to recurrent disease.

Cancers of the head and neck are the 8th most commonly diagnosed cancer in the UK. Despite improvements to clinical practice and the recognition of HPV-related disease as a separate entity, predicted five-year survival is often less than 50% (PMID: 33243986). HPV-positive disease has been shown to respond favourably to standard of care, however, research from our group has previously demonstrated how use of a surrogate biomarker can influence patient staging and outcome in oropharyngeal cancers when definitive HPV testing is not carried out (PMID:30890775and 31666283). Understanding a patient’s HPV status may become clinically relevant for treatment stratification in the future,as it has been speculated that patients with HPV-related disease may benefit from treatment de-escalation to minimise long-term side effects, however, to date there has been limited success in these patients due to disease recurrence. Therefore,there is an unmet clinical need to characterise HPV heterogeneity within oropharyngeal cancer patients who are likely to recur following curative treatment. This study aims to understand to what extent HPV heterogeneity influences cancer-specific outcomes, the influence this has on the tumour microenvironment and how this might lead to recurrent disease.

listings.title: Abasic DNA Lesions as Targets to Improve Chemotherapy Response
listings.summary: This project aims to improve the effectiveness of thymidylate synthase (TS)-targeting chemotherapies by exploiting cancer cell vulnerabilities in the management of abasic (AP) DNA lesions. AP sites are among the most common and toxic forms of DNA damage and arise at high frequency following misincorporation of uracil…
listings.description:
This project aims to improve the effectiveness of thymidylate synthase (TS)-targeting chemotherapies by exploiting cancer cell vulnerabilities in the management of abasic (AP) DNA lesions. AP sites are among the most common and toxic forms of DNA damage and arise at high frequency following misincorporation of uracil into DNA during TS inhibition. Cancer cells rely on specialised repair complexes to detect, process, and tolerate these repair intermediates, enabling survival despite treatment stress.

This research will investigate how DNA repair pathways—particularly base excision repair (BER)—govern therapy responses, and how rewiring AP site processing can enhance cytotoxicity. By defining the protein machinery that prevents AP-site-induced lethality, this project seeks to identify rational targets to boost current fluoropyrimidine-based regimens and overcome resistance.

As a PhD student, you will receive training in advanced molecular oncology techniques including CRISPR editing, DNA damage and replication stress assays, cellular drug-response profiling, and quantitative imaging, within a collaborative environment focused on translational cancer biology.

listings.title: IL-8/CXCR1/2-Driven Tumour–Immune Interactions in Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer
listings.summary: The IL-8/CXCR1/2 signaling axis is increasingly recognised as a driver of treatment resistance in advanced prostate cancer. Anti-androgen therapies induce IL-8 secretion, promoting recruitment of immunosuppressive myeloid cells, enhancing tumour cell survival, and accelerating progression to castration-resistant…
listings.description:
The IL-8/CXCR1/2 signaling axis is increasingly recognised as a driver of treatment resistance in advanced prostate cancer. Anti-androgen therapies induce IL-8 secretion, promoting recruitment of immunosuppressive myeloid cells, enhancing tumour cell survival, and accelerating progression to castration-resistant disease. Blocking this pathway represents a promising strategy to restore tumour–immune engagement and improve clinical outcomes.

This project will dissect how tumour-derived IL-8 shapes the prostate cancer microenvironment, define the contribution of CXCR1/2-positive neutrophils and MDSCs to therapeutic escape, and assess the potential of clinically relevant CXCR1/2 inhibitors in combination with standard-of-care therapies.

The student will be trained in tumour immunology, cytokine and signalling analysis, immune-cell phenotyping, multiplex pathology, and in vitro/in vivo combination-therapy modelling within a highly collaborative translational research setting.

listings.title: Integrative Functional Genomics of Chemotherapy Response and Resistance in Colorectal Cancer
listings.summary: This PhD project aims to understand and overcome resistance to 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU), a cornerstone therapy for colorectal cancer (CRC), using integrative functional genomics. Despite widespread clinical use, responses to 5-FU are highly variable, with many tumours entering drug-tolerant persister (DTP) states that…
listings.description:
This PhD project aims to understand and overcome resistance to 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU), a cornerstone therapy for colorectal cancer (CRC), using integrative functional genomics. Despite widespread clinical use, responses to 5-FU are highly variable, with many tumours entering drug-tolerant persister (DTP) states that drive treatment failure and relapse.

The project will leverage extensive pre-existing datasets generated within the group, including CRISPR–drug combination screens, longitudinal RNA-seq, clinically annotated patient cohorts, and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. The goal is to define transcriptional and functional programmes that govern sensitivity, tolerance, and resistance to 5-FU.

The project is flexible and open to candidates from wet-lab or computational backgrounds. Computationally focused students will integrate CRISPR and transcriptomic data to model treatment-induced state transitions and prioritise genes capable of steering tumours toward drug sensitivity. Experimentally focused students will validate resistance mechanisms and candidate targets using functional genomics approaches, including CRISPR perturbation and drug-combination assays.

The student will be embedded within the Functional Genomics Group and the multidisciplinary Colorectal Cancer Research group at the Johnston Centre for Cancer Research, gaining interdisciplinary training in functional genomics, RNA-seq analysis, and translational cancer biology with clear relevance to improving therapeutic durability in CRC.

listings.title: Integrative Genomic Mapping of Cetuximab Resistance in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
listings.summary: Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma (HNSCC) has high morbidity and poor outcomes in recurrent or metastatic disease. The anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody cetuximab is widely used, yet patient responses are highly variable and predictive biomarkers of resistance remain poorly defined. Emerging evidence from…
listings.description:
Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma (HNSCC) has high morbidity and poor outcomes in recurrent or metastatic disease. The anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody cetuximab is widely used, yet patient responses are highly variable and predictive biomarkers of resistance remain poorly defined. Emerging evidence from translational models suggests that developmentally regulated signalling pathways may contribute to intrinsic resistance mechanisms.

This PhD project will investigate the molecular basis of cetuximab response and resistance by integrating longitudinal transcriptomic data from patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models with baseline tumour genomics and large patient cohorts. The student will analyse public datasets (e.g. TCGA) alongside in-house HNSCC cohorts with detailed clinical annotation, mapping poor-prognosis patient profiles to matched translational models.

listings.description:
Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) combined with external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) is the standard curative treatment for locally advanced prostate cancer. However, many patients ultimately progress to androgen-independent or castration-resistant disease, limiting long-term treatment success. The molecular programmes driving resistance to ADT-EBRT remain heterogeneous and incompletely understood.

This PhD project aims to define transcriptional and genomic mechanisms underpinning resistance to ADT-EBRT and to identify vulnerabilities that can be exploited through rational combination therapies. The project will integrate longitudinal transcriptomic data from prostate cancer models with CRISPR screens and bulk RNA-seq data from public resources and in-house patient cohorts, including pre- and post-treatment samples.

By embedding these datasets into shared molecular state spaces, the project will identify resistance-associated programmes such as altered androgen receptor signalling, lineage plasticity, and compensatory survival pathways. Candidates may focus on integrative bioinformatics, experimental validation, or both, depending on background.

The student will be embedded within the Functional Genomics Group and ProEx, the philanthropically funded Centre of Excellence for Prostate Cancer Research, gaining training in functional genomics, RNA-seq analysis, and translational prostate cancer biology with direct relevance to therapeutic optimisation.

listings.title: Mutation Specific Cellular States as Vulnerabilities in Acute Myeloid Leukaemia
listings.summary: This project aims to understand how recurrent mutations in blood cancers reshape the internal organisation of cells and create new biological vulnerabilities. In acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), mutations in genes such as NPM1 and components of the spliceosome are among the most common genetic alterations. These…
listings.description:
This project aims to understand how recurrent mutations in blood cancers reshape the internal organisation of cells and create new biological vulnerabilities. In acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), mutations in genes such as NPM1 and components of the spliceosome are among the most common genetic alterations. These mutations do not simply alter gene expression but reorganise how proteins and RNA are distributed and regulated within the cell. In the case of NPM1-mutated AML, the mutant protein accumulates abnormally in the cytoplasm rather than the nucleus, altering protein–protein interactions and regulatory networks. Similarly, spliceosome mutations perturb RNA processing, leading to widespread changes in transcript structure. These alterations can rewire cellular stress responses, differentiation pathways, and survival mechanisms.

This PhD project will investigate how such mutation-driven changes in intracellular organisation influence cancer cell behaviour. A key aim is to determine whether these altered cellular states generate selective vulnerabilities that are absent from normal blood cells. By defining how spatial protein mislocalisation and RNA processing defects reshape cellular networks, the project seeks to uncover new principles of cancer biology and identify opportunities for more selective therapeutic intervention.

As a PhD student on this project, you will gain training in advanced molecular biology and bioinformatic approaches, including CRISPR-based genome engineering, transcriptomics, proteomics, and functional genetic screening. You will join a collaborative research environment focused on fundamental mechanisms of leukaemia biology, with opportunities to contribute to novel therapeutic approaches for blood cancers.

listings.title: Defining FERMT2 as a regulator of tumour cell state plasticity and metastatic stress adaptation in prostate cancer
listings.summary: This project aims to define how FERMT2 regulates tumour cell state plasticity and prostate cancer progression. Patient data show that low FERMT2 expression is associated with poorer survival, is further reduced in metastatic disease, and correlates with hypoxia-associated transcriptional programmes. In contrast, in…
listings.description:
This project aims to define how FERMT2 regulates tumour cell state plasticity and prostate cancer progression. Patient data show that low FERMT2 expression is associated with poorer survival, is further reduced in metastatic disease, and correlates with hypoxia-associated transcriptional programmes. In contrast, in vitro studies often link FERMT2 to proliferation and migration, highlighting a key discrepancy between experimental models and clinical observations.

We hypothesise that FERMT2 is not a simple oncogene, but a context-dependent regulator of tumour cell state. Loss of FERMT2 may promote a stress-adapted, metastasis-prone phenotype that is selectively advantageous under conditions such as hypoxia, detachment, and therapeutic stress.

This project will use isogenic knockout and rescue models in androgen receptor (AR)-dependent and AR-independent prostate cancer systems to define FERMT2-dependent cell states. Functional assays modelling hypoxia, anoikis, and hypoxia–reoxygenation cycling will determine how FERMT2 loss influences survival, recovery, and clonogenic potential, directly testing whether FERMT2-low cells are selected under metastatic bottlenecks.

AR signalling will be modulated using DHT and enzalutamide to determine how lineage context shapes FERMT2-dependent phenotypes. This work will provide mechanistic insight into tumour cell plasticity, resolve discrepancies between patient data and in vitro studies, and identify new vulnerabilities linked to metastasis and therapy resistance.

The student will gain training in CRISPR genome editing, functional genomics, RNA-seq analysis, and advanced models of cancer cell stress and metastasis, within a highly interdisciplinary research environment at the interface of genomics and molecular oncology.

listings.summary: Oxaliplatin combined with 5-FU/leucovorin (FOLFOX) is a common chemotherapy regimen for the treatment of a number of gastro-intestinal (GI) cancers, including colorectal cancer (CRC). listings.description:
Oxaliplatin combined with 5-FU/leucovorin (FOLFOX) is a common chemotherapy regimen for the treatment of a number of gastro-intestinal (GI) cancers, including colorectal cancer (CRC). Oxaliplatin is a third-generation platinum compound, exerting its anti-cancer effect through the formation of DNA inter-and intra-stand and DNA-protein crosslinks, resulting in decreased tumour DNA/mRNA synthesis and cell death. Peripheral neurotoxicity is one of the major and dose-limiting side effects of oxaliplatin and is the main reason for early treatment discontinuation, impacting patient’s quality of life (QOL). Symptoms often include numbness, tingling and pain affecting daily activities and mental well-being. Currently, there are no preventive measures/treatments for oxaliplatin-induced-peripheral-neuropathy (OIPN). This research will underpin mechanism of OIPN and identify drugs that can limit the occurrence of OIPN, thereby improving patient's QOL.

As a PhD student on this proposal, you will be provided with a multidisciplinary training opportunity in both molecular biology and physiology techniques. Notably, specific scientific training will be complemented by providing courses in transferable skills such as in Public and Patient Involvement (PPI) in research, effective science communication and collaboration in research.

listings.title: Can stromal-rich tumours rewire colon cancer metabolism to promote therapy resistance?
listings.summary: This project aims to understand how stromal-rich colon cancers reshape tumour cell metabolism and how this contributes to resistance to chemotherapy.
listings.description:
This project aims to understand how stromal-rich colon cancers reshape tumour cell metabolism and how this contributes to resistance to chemotherapy.

Colorectal cancers with high stromal content are often associated with poor treatment response and worse clinical outcome. These tumours contain complex mixtures of cancer cells, fibroblasts, immune cells and extracellular matrix, which together create a microenvironment that can protect tumour cells from therapy. However, we still do not fully understand how stromal-rich tumour environments alter the metabolic state of colon cancer cells, or if this change in metabolic state supports survival under treatment pressure.

This research will focus on how stromal signals drive metabolic adaptation in colon cancer, particularly in the context of chemotherapy resistance. We are interested in whether stromal-rich tumours promote changes in mitochondrial function and metabolic plasticity, and how these adaptations allow tumour cells to persist during treatment. By studying these mechanisms in clinically relevant colorectal cancer models, this project seeks to identify metabolic vulnerabilities that could be targeted to improve treatment response in stromal-rich disease.

As a PhD student on this project, you will gain experience in advanced colorectal cancer models, including cancer cell and stromal co-culture systems, patient-derived organoids, drug response assays, metabolomics, transcriptomics, imaging and molecular biology techniques. You will join a collaborative translational cancer research environment, with opportunities to develop expertise in cancer metabolism, tumour microenvironment biology, therapy resistance and biomarker-led therapeutic discovery.

listings.title: Investigating the epigenetic plasticity of chemotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer.
listings.summary: Chemotherapy resistance remains a major hurdle in colorectal cancer (CRC) treatment. Recent discoveries highlight a remarkable similarity between chemo-resistant cancer cells and cells found in the early embryo, suggesting that cancer cells can hijack a range of stem, and embryonic programmes to enter a dormant state…
listings.description:
Chemotherapy resistance remains a major hurdle in colorectal cancer (CRC) treatment. Recent discoveries highlight a remarkable similarity between chemo-resistant cancer cells and cells found in the early embryo, suggesting that cancer cells can hijack a range of stem, and embryonic programmes to enter a dormant state that enables them to survive treatment. This drug resistance-persistence state is associated with reversible epigenetic reprogramming allowing cells to reinitiate tumour growth upon drug release. In this project, we aim to identify the reversible epigenetic changes underpinning cell plasticity in response to 5FU treatment, with a particular focus on epigenetic changes. Better understanding of these epigenetic mechanisms will provide new therapeutic approaches to prevent or overcome drug resistance in cancer.

We have recently conducted multiple genomics approaches to understand the epigenetic basis of drug resistance in CRC. Through this research, we have identified several candidate epigenetic regulators that may play key roles in this process. In this project, the PhD student will utilize state-of-the-art CRISPR/Cas9 and genomics approaches to study the role of these candidate epigenetic regulators identified in our genomics screens. This project does not have a pre-defined outcome and both positive and negative results regarding identified epigenetic candidates will be important findings that shed light on the role of epigenetic regulation in drug resistance.

The candidate PhD student will receive training in multi-disciplinary approaches combining genome-wide technologies, stem cell biology, and will also gain experience in computational biology for analysis of genome wide data.

listings.description:
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer among men in the UK, with about 1,400 new cases in Northern Ireland every year. Nearly half of these fall into an ""intermediate-risk"" category—a diverse group where most men do well, but a significant few face a much more aggressive form of the disease. A major challenge lies in identifying those high-risk cases early enough to provide life-saving treatment, while sparing others from the unnecessary side effects of over-treatment.

To address this, we have created a novel study of roughly 400 men with intermediate risk prostate cancer in Northern Ireland. This population-representative study integrates many different types of data, from RNA sequencing and immune phenotyping to digital imaging of tumour biopsy samples, alongside detailed clinical and follow-up data. Our goal is to find biomarkers that can predict how aggressive the cancer is at the moment of diagnosis.

As a PhD student on this project, you will gain expertise in bioinformatics, digital pathology and data analysis techniques within a multi-disciplinary and collaborative team. The research group sits within the QUB Prostate Cancer Centre of Excellence (ProEx), providing additional opportunities for training and collaboration across disciplines.

listings.title: Role Of The Microglia Circadian Clock In Neuroinflammation In Early Diabetic Retinopathy
listings.summary: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss driven in part by microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and vascular dysfunction. In this project the effect of circadian disruption on retina neuroinflammation will be investigated.
listings.description:
Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss driven in part by microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and vascular dysfunction. In this project the effect of circadian disruption on retina neuroinflammation will be investigated.

Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss driven in part by microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and vascular dysfunction. Microglia have robust circadian rhythms that allow optimisation of functions to the daily light/dark cycle. Bmal1 dysregulation, a main circadian clock protein, has been implicated in altered microglial function and exacerbation of neuroinflammation in neurodegenerative diseases. We have preliminary data to suggest that Bmal1 exerts key control over microglia inflammatory status under diabetic stresses. We further know that Bmal1, is elevated throughout the retina in early diabetes (T1D) before vasculopathy appears.

In this project the role of the microglia clock disruption in the context of diabetic retinopathy will be investigated. The contribution of the microglia clock vs the neuroretina clock disruption will be dissected, to understand how circadian disruption impacts neuroinflammation in the diabetic retina.

The candidate will investigate the impact of Bmal1 deletion from microglia vs the neuroretina using tissue specific Bmal1 knockout mouse models. The impact of clock disruption on diabetic retinopathy will be assessed using state of the art retinal imaging, ex vivo fluorescence microscopy, and mRNA sequencing. Finally, evaluation of clock-modulating compounds for their ability to suppress inflammation will be done using both in vitro and in vivo models.

This study will establish a mechanistic link between microglial clock disruption and retina neuroinflammation. It will also identify viable strategies targeting the clock to reprogram microglial behaviour and preserve neurovascular function, paving the way for novel therapies for early DR.

listings.title: Discovering Novel Anti-Angiogenic Strategies With In Vitro Tumour Vessel Models
listings.summary: Tumour angiogenesis drives cancer growth and metastasis but abnormal vessels hinder therapy. This project uses 3D in vitro models to test antisense oligonucleotides for regulating protein expression in endothelial cells to suppress vessel growth and improve vessel normalisation.
listings.description:
Tumour angiogenesis drives cancer growth and metastasis but abnormal vessels hinder therapy. This project uses 3D in vitro models to test antisense oligonucleotides for regulating protein expression in endothelial cells to suppress vessel growth and improve vessel normalisation.

Tumour angiogenesis, a hallmark of cancer, is a critical determinant of disease progression and malignancy. Growing solid tumours have the capacity of remodelling local vasculature to maximise contact with capillaries and thus, enhance diffusion of oxygen and nutrients required to respond to their increasing energy demands. Better access to the vasculature also facilitates the dispersion of tumour cells that can reach distant metastatic sites. On the other hand, the new tumour vessels tend to display abnormal features, which limit drug delivery and further potentiate angiogenesis.

The vascularisation of tumours is triggered by the unbalanced release of tumour-derived pro-angiogenic factors over anti-angiogenic factors, resulting in a so-called “angiogenic switch”. Much attention has been given to key signalling molecules with pro-angiogenic properties as therapeutic targets in cancer treatments. Despite the remarkable advances since the implementation of such approaches, resistance to anti-angiogenic drugs is a major hurdle. Hence, there is a pressing need to identify novel molecular mechanisms that can limit tumour angiogenesis and improve vessel normalisation.

With the rapid development of new and fascinating 3D cell culture systems, it is now possible to recreate key tumorigenic events in artificial environments. Using in vitro models of tumour angiogenesis, this project aims to discover novel ways of regulating protein expression in vascular cells to reduce blood vessel growth.

listings.title: Precision Approaches To Treatment Of Respiratory Viral Infections In Children
listings.summary: We aim to understand and reduce the impact of oral corticosteroids on children’s respiratory health. Using biomarker discovery with genomics and proteomics, we seek to identify which children benefit most, advancing precision medicine and improving respiratory care in early childhood.
listings.description:
We aim to understand and reduce the impact of oral corticosteroids on children’s respiratory health. Using biomarker discovery with genomics and proteomics, we seek to identify which children benefit most, advancing precision medicine and improving respiratory care in early childhood.

In preschool-aged children, oral corticosteroids are commonly prescribed for acute respiratory viral infections, such as virus-associated wheezing. Yet, we know surprisingly little about how these treatments influence children’s long-term respiratory health—especially in those who receive repeated courses of corticosteroids.

What we do know is that even one short course can temporarily alter the immune system, increasing the risk of pneumonia and sepsis in the weeks that follow. However, the underlying mechanisms, and the potential long-term effects on children’s respiratory health, remain a major research gap.

This creates a unique opportunity for discovery. Our research is dedicated to understanding the consequences of corticosteroid use in children and to develop tools that allow clinicians to identify which children will truly benefit from corticosteroid therapy. By improving prescribing practices, we can reduce unnecessary risks while ensuring the right children receive the right treatment.

As part of our team, you will have the chance to contribute to this important work, gaining experience in biomarker discovery and child health research, using powerful multi-omics technologies such as proteomics. Working closely with our multidisciplinary team, you will help pioneer novel methods to phenotype children with acute wheezing and translate these insights into better clinical care.

listings.title: Early Pathogenesis Of Retinal Ischaemic Diseases: Mechanisms And Therapeutic Targets
listings.summary: This PhD will investigate the early cellular and molecular changes driving retinal ischaemic diseases such as diabetic retinopathy. listings.description:
This PhD will investigate the early cellular and molecular changes driving retinal ischaemic diseases such as diabetic retinopathy. Using state-of-the-art cellular and animal models the project aims to identify mechanisms of neurovascular dysfunction and test strategies for early intervention.

Retinal ischaemia underpins many of the world’s most common causes of blindness including diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion and retinopathy of prematurity. These conditions impose a major health and economic burden globally, yet the early stages of disease pathogenesis remain poorly characterised. Current treatments often target advanced disease when irreversible damage has already occurred.

This PhD project will focus on understanding the molecular and cellular events that initiate neurovascular dysfunction in the ischaemic retina. The student will use a combination of in vitro models of endothelial and neuronal cells exposed to hypoxic and inflammatory stimuli together with in vivo experimental models of retinal ischaemia to identify pathways that drive early neurovascular injury. Advanced imaging, transcriptomic profiling and functional assays will be applied to dissect cross-talk between vascular and neural compartments.

This project offers world-class training in vascular biology, ophthalmic disease models and translational science preparing the candidate to contribute to future therapies for blinding eye disease.

listings.title: Comparative Transcriptomic Profiling Of Glymphatic And Gliovascular Cell–Cell Communication In Health And Disease
listings.summary: This project uses transcriptomics to characterise gliovascular communication in the retina and brain. By comparing data across diabetes and Alzheimer’s Disease, we aim to uncover molecular signatures driving neurovascular dysfunction and waste clearance failure in CNS diseases.
listings.description:
This project uses transcriptomics to characterise gliovascular communication in the retina and brain. By comparing data across diabetes and Alzheimer’s Disease, we aim to uncover molecular signatures driving neurovascular dysfunction and waste clearance failure in CNS diseases.

The glymphatic system plays a vital role in brain waste clearance, yet its molecular regulation—particularly via gliovascular interactions—remains poorly understood. This project will use single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to define glymphatic-related cell-cell communication signatures in the human brain, and assess how these networks are altered in aging, Alzheimer’s disease, and diabetes.

The project will also extend this analysis to the retina - an accessible CNS tissue with a similar glymphatic clearance system - comparing human and mouse retinal transcriptomes in health and disease.

This cross-species, cross-tissue systems biology approach will provide novel insight into shared and divergent glymphatic mechanisms, identifying potential therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative and retinal diseases. listings.title: Molecular Mechanisms Of Bacterial Competition In The Gut Microbiome And Their Influence On Chronic Intestinal Inflammation
listings.summary: The gut microbiome contributes to homeostasis and health. However, some strains of bacteria are linked to chronic inflammation and in this project, we want to study this link using state-of the-art genetic techniques to study an inflammation model.
listings.description:
The gut microbiome contributes to homeostasis and health. However, some strains of bacteria are linked to chronic inflammation and in this project, we want to study this link using state-of the-art genetic techniques to study an inflammation model.

Trillions of bacteria comprise the gut microbiome and contribute to human health by producing metabolites that regulate intestinal health and contribute to human metabolism and homeaostasis. Therefore, the microbiome represents an innovative approach to develop new therapies. Our team studies how bacterial competition for nutrients and space shapes the biodiversity of the gut. This is important because gut biodiversity is a determinant of human health. Moreover, few key species can affect biodiversity, by direct competition with other bacteria.

Most microbiome bacteria contribute to homeostasis and contribute to reduce inflammation in the gut. However, like Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, some species called pathobionts have strains associated with cancer and chronic inflammation. Moreover, modern lifestyles contribute to dysregulation of the gut microbiome and establish vicious circles contributing to various metabolic diseases, obesity and cancer.

In this project, we will study genes that allow pathobiont bacterial species to stably colonize the intestinal environment in the first place using state-of-the-art techniques such as microbiome sequencing. Furthermore, we will study how do they affect acute and chronic inflammation in a colitis model. The results of this research will contribute to design strategies to manipulate the microbiome to reduce digestive tract cancer incidence, which in the UK represents ~40,000 new cases per year with an economic cost of £17.1 billion.

The successful candidate will acquire training in cell biology, microbiology, genome editing and high-throughput sequencing. The project should provide experience to pursue industrial or academic R&D in the new field of microbiome therapeutic biologicals, synthetic biology, or biotechnology.

listings.description:
PhD position available in a genetics lab to study bacterial antibiotic resistance. The project explores molecular mechanisms and aims to develop strategies to counter resistance. Applicants should have a strong background in microbiology, genetics, and bioinformatics.

Antibiotic resistance is one of the most pressing challenges in global health today. The rapid emergence and spread of multidrug-resistant bacteria threaten to undermine decades of medical progress, raising the alarming possibility of a post-antibiotic age in which common infections and minor injuries could once again become deadly. Understanding the genetic and molecular mechanisms that drive resistance is critical to developing innovative strategies to counteract it and safeguard the efficacy of existing and future antibiotics.

We are seeking motivated and talented individuals to join our research group at WWIEM to study antimicrobial resistance in bacteria causing intestinal infections.

This project will explore the genetic pathways and regulatory networks that contribute to resistance in clinically relevant bacterial species. Using a combination of molecular genetics, genomics, and bioinformatics, the student will investigate how resistance genes are acquired, expressed, and maintained, and how these processes can be disrupted.
