listings.title: Understanding The Mechanism Of Extracellular Vesicle-Mediated Drug Resistance In Multiple Myeloma
listings.summary: This project will characterise the role of MM-derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) on MM progression and the development of therapeutic resistance, with a focus on alterations to the alterations to the immune microenvironment.
listings.description:
This project will characterise the role of MM-derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) on MM progression and the development of therapeutic resistance, with a focus on alterations to the alterations to the immune microenvironment.

Multiple myeloma (MM) represents around 10% of all blood cancer and while treatment options have drastically improved, almost all patients relapse and develop of drug resistance. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of resistance would provide new therapeutic options and aid precision medicine approaches. The bone marrow microenvironment performs a crucial role in supporting MM pathogenesis and promoting the development of therapeutic resistance. Exosomes, also known as small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), have been identified as a key component of cell-to-cell communication within the bone marrow microenvironment (BMM).

Using CRISPR/Cas9 whole genome screening data we have identified genes related to exosome biogenesis and release as essential for growth specifically in MM cell lines. Furthermore, patients exhibiting increased expression of these genes at relapse have significantly poorer prognosis. Using cell line models of therapy sensitive and resistant MM we have that EV secretion is altered in resistant cells and demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of exosome release blocks MM cell proliferation. Taken together this data points to a strict requirement for exosome biogenesis and a role for this in relapse and development of resistance.

This PhD aims to understand how MM-derived exosomes influence MM pathogenesis and the development of therapeutic resistance. We will use unbiased proteomics approaches to define the molecular mechanisms behind exosome-mediated effects with a focus on alterations to the immune microenvironment. The study will uncover important tools to predict or target drug resistance, representing a significant advance in our move towards personalised medicine.

listings.title: The Role Of Secondary Bile Acids In Lung Infection And Inflammation
listings.summary: This project investigates how bile acids contribute to lung infection and inflammation in respiratory diseases such as CF, COPD, and IPF. It will explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying bile acid–mediated immune responses, using experimental models to clarify their role in respiratory infection and…
listings.description:
This project investigates how bile acids contribute to lung infection and inflammation in respiratory diseases such as CF, COPD, and IPF. It will explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying bile acid–mediated immune responses, using experimental models to clarify their role in respiratory infection and disease progression.

The aspiration of bile acids (BA) into the lungs has been identified as a major co-morbidity of a range of respiratory diseases, and in some cases, has been shown to correlate with a reduction in microbial diversity and an increase in inflammation. Aspiration has been shown to be associated with severe episodes of acute exacerbations of COPD with BA in the lower airways inducing microbiota changes. The presence of BA has been reported in the lungs of patients diagnosed with a range of respiratory conditions, including CF, COPD and IPF. Moreover, BA are also a major contributor to the development of pneumonia in the elderly and have been demonstrated to promote chronic respiratory infections in CF. Despite this, the precise effect of BA on innate immune cell function and response to pathogens associated with respiratory infection currently remains unknown. This project will fulfil this knowledge gap.

listings.title: Prospecting the way forward for systems thinking in Pubic Health
listings.summary: This PhD will explore the future role of systems thinking in public health. It will investigate frameworks, applications, barriers to implementation, and lessons from other disciplines, aiming to inform strategies to strengthen the role of systems thinking in public health research and practice.
listings.description:
This PhD will explore the future role of systems thinking in public health. It will investigate frameworks, applications, barriers to implementation, and lessons from other disciplines, aiming to inform strategies to strengthen the role of systems thinking in public health research and practice.

This PhD will examine how systems thinking can more effectively shape the future of public health research and practice. Public health challenges—such as widening health inequalities, climate related risks, and the growing burden of chronic disease—are increasingly recognised as complex, interconnected, and shaped by dynamic social, environmental, and economic forces. Systems thinking offers tools and perspectives that can help navigate this complexity, and as such has been increasingly adopted in public health. However, significant challenges still exist for a more meaningful adoption and utilization.

The project will explore the evolution of systems thinking within public health, examine barriers that limit broader uptake, and analyse how other disciplines—such as ecology, systems engineering, management science, and behavioural science—have embedded systems thinking in ways that may offer transferable lessons.

The overarching aim is to provide a clearer pathway for strengthening the role of systems thinking in public health. Specific objectives will be discussed with the PhD candidate but may include: map existing approaches and gaps in the application of systems thinking; critically assess capacity, structural, and methodological barriers for wider adoption; describe and compare the evolution of systems thinking in other disciplines, as well as enablers and barriers of its adoption; develop recommendations to enhance adoption of systems thinking in public health.

listings.title: Endothelial Control of Brain Tissue Homeostasis and Degeneration in Systemic Disease
listings.summary: This project will examine how systemic disease and pathophysiological stress alter brain microvascular endothelial cell function and contribute to neurodegeneration. Using in vivo and physiologically relevant models, it will identify pathways regulating metabolic and cell interactions in the brain.
listings.description:
This project will examine how systemic disease and pathophysiological stress alter brain microvascular endothelial cell function and contribute to neurodegeneration. Using in vivo and physiologically relevant models, it will identify pathways regulating metabolic and cell interactions in the brain.

As life expectancy increases, preserving brain health and cognitive function has become a major challenge for ageing societies. Neurovascular dysfunction and dementia are rising in prevalence, reducing quality of life and long-term independence. The brain microvasculature is fundamental in perfusion, metabolism, and cellular interactions, yet how stress-induced endothelial dysfunction contributes to brain degeneration remains unclear.

This PhD project aims to define how brain microvascular endothelial cells maintain tissue homeostasis and how their dysfunction contributes to degeneration under systemic stress. The project will investigate endothelial responses to common stressors associated with age, disease or adverse effects of treatments: inflammation, oxidative, and metabolic stress.

The student will characterise endothelial phenotypic and metabolic changes in vivo and in physiologically relevant culture models, determine how endothelial dysfunction alters tissue oxygen handling and cellular interactions, and identify pathways that support microvascular resilience and brain function. This work will provide fundamental insight into mechanisms linking systemic stress to brain health, with relevance for preserving cognitive function across the lifespan.

The work will explore how different classes of DNA-damaging agents and DDR-targeted drugs influence inflammatory signalling, immune cell recruitment, and tumour cell survival. listings.title: Evaluating challenges in global biobank-enabled multi-omic studies
listings.summary: This PhD will investigate how variability in biobank sample collection, processing, and storage influences research outcomes.
listings.description:
This PhD will investigate how variability in biobank sample collection, processing, and storage influences research outcomes.

The efficient translation of scientific discoveries from bench to bedside is a central goal of academic research and can depend heavily on robust internal infrastructure, particularly tissue‑based biobanks. Modern biobanks are often expected to provide a broader range of resources to support precision medicine initiatives and AI enabled phenotyping through access to high‑quality, clinically annotated specimens. Meeting these demands requires adherence to international best‑practice standards and strong quality management and audit systems, which improve sample integrity, enhance research reproducibility, and build confidence in clinical and regulatory translation.

This PhD will investigate how variability in biobank sample collection, processing, and storage influences research outcomes. It will evaluate the absence of universal operating procedures across institutions, inconsistencies in metadata availability, and the impact of pre‑analytical variables on downstream multi‑omic analyses and data integration. A secondary aim is to examine how population bias contributes to limited genetic diversity within biobank datasets.

Our vision is to develop interoperable frameworks for harmonisation of multi-modal biobank data across countries. As a PhD student on this project, you will gain expertise in how to design and conduct a systematic review and perform qualitative meta-analyses. You will be part of a collaborative biobanking network to develop (i) expertise in international biobanking standards and guidelines; (2) knowledge of quality management systems to directly influence reproducibility and clinical confidence and (3) experience in critically evaluating multi-omic integration challenges.

listings.summary: This project will develop an online tool that will test and ‘match’ pre-clinical models against selected patient groups using information theory, machine learning and meta-analysis techniques.
listings.description:
This project will develop an online tool that will test and ‘match’ pre-clinical models against selected patient groups using information theory, machine learning and meta-analysis techniques.

Pre-clinical models are essential to modelling diseases and treatment response in the laboratory setting. In vitro or vivo model choice can be based on personal preference or laboratory custom. However, there is limited focus as to how well these models characterise their target systems. In addition, models, such as cell lines, can be subject to mislabelling and contamination. This project will develop an online tool that will test and ‘match’ pre-clinical models against selected patient groups using information theory, machine learning and meta-analysis techniques.

The project will involve the re-use and re-analysis of curated publicly-available -omics and drug response data. Through the integration of multiple data sources, our research aims to identify similarities in patterns between pre-clinical models and different patient groups, e.g. patients who do not respond to treatment or those who develop metastatic disease. The project will develop an in silico tool to support experimental design in the laboratory, providing guidance and feedback on pre-clinical model choice. The project will span both statistical and computational fields, allowing the PhD student to develop a strong foundation in data science techniques, which are transferrable into multiple bioinformatics domains.

listings.title: Role Of The Microglia Circadian Clock In Neuroinflammation In Early Diabetic Retinopathy
listings.summary: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss driven in part by microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and vascular dysfunction. In this project the effect of circadian disruption on retina neuroinflammation will be investigated.
listings.description:
Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss driven in part by microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and vascular dysfunction. In this project the effect of circadian disruption on retina neuroinflammation will be investigated.

Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss driven in part by microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and vascular dysfunction. Microglia have robust circadian rhythms that allow optimisation of functions to the daily light/dark cycle. Bmal1 dysregulation, a main circadian clock protein, has been implicated in altered microglial function and exacerbation of neuroinflammation in neurodegenerative diseases. We have preliminary data to suggest that Bmal1 exerts key control over microglia inflammatory status under diabetic stresses. We further know that Bmal1, is elevated throughout the retina in early diabetes (T1D) before vasculopathy appears.

In this project the role of the microglia clock disruption in the context of diabetic retinopathy will be investigated. The contribution of the microglia clock vs the neuroretina clock disruption will be dissected, to understand how circadian disruption impacts neuroinflammation in the diabetic retina.

The candidate will investigate the impact of Bmal1 deletion from microglia vs the neuroretina using tissue specific Bmal1 knockout mouse models. The impact of clock disruption on diabetic retinopathy will be assessed using state of the art retinal imaging, ex vivo fluorescence microscopy, and mRNA sequencing. Finally, evaluation of clock-modulating compounds for their ability to suppress inflammation will be done using both in vitro and in vivo models.

This study will establish a mechanistic link between microglial clock disruption and retina neuroinflammation. It will also identify viable strategies targeting the clock to reprogram microglial behaviour and preserve neurovascular function, paving the way for novel therapies for early DR.

listings.title: Discovering Novel Anti-Angiogenic Strategies With In Vitro Tumour Vessel Models
listings.summary: Tumour angiogenesis drives cancer growth and metastasis but abnormal vessels hinder therapy. This project uses 3D in vitro models to test antisense oligonucleotides for regulating protein expression in endothelial cells to suppress vessel growth and improve vessel normalisation.
listings.description:
Tumour angiogenesis drives cancer growth and metastasis but abnormal vessels hinder therapy. This project uses 3D in vitro models to test antisense oligonucleotides for regulating protein expression in endothelial cells to suppress vessel growth and improve vessel normalisation.

Tumour angiogenesis, a hallmark of cancer, is a critical determinant of disease progression and malignancy. Growing solid tumours have the capacity of remodelling local vasculature to maximise contact with capillaries and thus, enhance diffusion of oxygen and nutrients required to respond to their increasing energy demands. Better access to the vasculature also facilitates the dispersion of tumour cells that can reach distant metastatic sites. On the other hand, the new tumour vessels tend to display abnormal features, which limit drug delivery and further potentiate angiogenesis.

The vascularisation of tumours is triggered by the unbalanced release of tumour-derived pro-angiogenic factors over anti-angiogenic factors, resulting in a so-called “angiogenic switch”. Much attention has been given to key signalling molecules with pro-angiogenic properties as therapeutic targets in cancer treatments. Despite the remarkable advances since the implementation of such approaches, resistance to anti-angiogenic drugs is a major hurdle. Hence, there is a pressing need to identify novel molecular mechanisms that can limit tumour angiogenesis and improve vessel normalisation.

With the rapid development of new and fascinating 3D cell culture systems, it is now possible to recreate key tumorigenic events in artificial environments. Using in vitro models of tumour angiogenesis, this project aims to discover novel ways of regulating protein expression in vascular cells to reduce blood vessel growth.

listings.title: Precision Approaches To Treatment Of Respiratory Viral Infections In Children
listings.summary: We aim to understand and reduce the impact of oral corticosteroids on children’s respiratory health. Using biomarker discovery with genomics and proteomics, we seek to identify which children benefit most, advancing precision medicine and improving respiratory care in early childhood.
listings.description:
We aim to understand and reduce the impact of oral corticosteroids on children’s respiratory health. Using biomarker discovery with genomics and proteomics, we seek to identify which children benefit most, advancing precision medicine and improving respiratory care in early childhood.

In preschool-aged children, oral corticosteroids are commonly prescribed for acute respiratory viral infections, such as virus-associated wheezing. Yet, we know surprisingly little about how these treatments influence children’s long-term respiratory health—especially in those who receive repeated courses of corticosteroids.

What we do know is that even one short course can temporarily alter the immune system, increasing the risk of pneumonia and sepsis in the weeks that follow. However, the underlying mechanisms, and the potential long-term effects on children’s respiratory health, remain a major research gap.

This creates a unique opportunity for discovery. Our research is dedicated to understanding the consequences of corticosteroid use in children and to develop tools that allow clinicians to identify which children will truly benefit from corticosteroid therapy. By improving prescribing practices, we can reduce unnecessary risks while ensuring the right children receive the right treatment.

As part of our team, you will have the chance to contribute to this important work, gaining experience in biomarker discovery and child health research, using powerful multi-omics technologies such as proteomics. Working closely with our multidisciplinary team, you will help pioneer novel methods to phenotype children with acute wheezing and translate these insights into better clinical care.

listings.summary: This PhD will investigate the early cellular and molecular changes driving retinal ischaemic diseases such as diabetic retinopathy. listings.description:
This PhD will investigate the early cellular and molecular changes driving retinal ischaemic diseases such as diabetic retinopathy. Using state-of-the-art cellular and animal models the project aims to identify mechanisms of neurovascular dysfunction and test strategies for early intervention.

Retinal ischaemia underpins many of the world’s most common causes of blindness including diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion and retinopathy of prematurity. These conditions impose a major health and economic burden globally, yet the early stages of disease pathogenesis remain poorly characterised. Current treatments often target advanced disease when irreversible damage has already occurred.

This PhD project will focus on understanding the molecular and cellular events that initiate neurovascular dysfunction in the ischaemic retina. The student will use a combination of in vitro models of endothelial and neuronal cells exposed to hypoxic and inflammatory stimuli together with in vivo experimental models of retinal ischaemia to identify pathways that drive early neurovascular injury. Advanced imaging, transcriptomic profiling and functional assays will be applied to dissect cross-talk between vascular and neural compartments.

This project offers world-class training in vascular biology, ophthalmic disease models and translational science preparing the candidate to contribute to future therapies for blinding eye disease.

listings.title: Comparative Transcriptomic Profiling Of Glymphatic And Gliovascular Cell–Cell Communication In Health And Disease
listings.summary: This project uses transcriptomics to characterise gliovascular communication in the retina and brain. By comparing data across diabetes and Alzheimer’s Disease, we aim to uncover molecular signatures driving neurovascular dysfunction and waste clearance failure in CNS diseases.
listings.description:
This project uses transcriptomics to characterise gliovascular communication in the retina and brain. By comparing data across diabetes and Alzheimer’s Disease, we aim to uncover molecular signatures driving neurovascular dysfunction and waste clearance failure in CNS diseases.

The glymphatic system plays a vital role in brain waste clearance, yet its molecular regulation—particularly via gliovascular interactions—remains poorly understood. This project will use single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to define glymphatic-related cell-cell communication signatures in the human brain, and assess how these networks are altered in aging, Alzheimer’s disease, and diabetes.

The project will also extend this analysis to the retina - an accessible CNS tissue with a similar glymphatic clearance system - comparing human and mouse retinal transcriptomes in health and disease.

This cross-species, cross-tissue systems biology approach will provide novel insight into shared and divergent glymphatic mechanisms, identifying potential therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative and retinal diseases. It is ideally suited to a student with interests in neuroscience, bioinformatics and translational medicine.

Therefore, the microbiome represents an innovative approach to develop new therapies. Our team studies how bacterial competition for nutrients and space shapes the biodiversity of the gut. This is important because gut biodiversity is a determinant of human health. Moreover, few key species can affect biodiversity, by direct competition with other bacteria.

Most microbiome bacteria contribute to homeostasis and contribute to reduce inflammation in the gut. However, like Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, some species called pathobionts have strains associated with cancer and chronic inflammation. Moreover, modern lifestyles contribute to dysregulation of the gut microbiome and establish vicious circles contributing to various metabolic diseases, obesity and cancer.

In this project, we will study genes that allow pathobiont bacterial species to stably colonize the intestinal environment in the first place using state-of-the-art techniques such as microbiome sequencing. Furthermore, we will study how do they affect acute and chronic inflammation in a colitis model. The results of this research will contribute to design strategies to manipulate the microbiome to reduce digestive tract cancer incidence, which in the UK represents ~40,000 new cases per year with an economic cost of £17.1 billion.

The successful candidate will acquire training in cell biology, microbiology, genome editing and high-throughput sequencing. The project should provide experience to pursue industrial or academic R&D in the new field of microbiome therapeutic biologicals, synthetic biology, or biotechnology.

listings.description:
PhD position available in a genetics lab to study bacterial antibiotic resistance. The project explores molecular mechanisms and aims to develop strategies to counter resistance. Applicants should have a strong background in microbiology, genetics, and bioinformatics.

Antibiotic resistance is one of the most pressing challenges in global health today. The rapid emergence and spread of multidrug-resistant bacteria threaten to undermine decades of medical progress, raising the alarming possibility of a post-antibiotic age in which common infections and minor injuries could once again become deadly. Understanding the genetic and molecular mechanisms that drive resistance is critical to developing innovative strategies to counteract it and safeguard the efficacy of existing and future antibiotics.

We are seeking motivated and talented individuals to join our research group at WWIEM to study antimicrobial resistance in bacteria causing intestinal infections.

This project will explore the genetic pathways and regulatory networks that contribute to resistance in clinically relevant bacterial species. Using a combination of molecular genetics, genomics, and bioinformatics, the student will investigate how resistance genes are acquired, expressed, and maintained, and how these processes can be disrupted.

listings.title: Understanding The Mechanism Of Extracellular Vesicle-Mediated Drug Resistance In Multiple Myeloma
listings.summary: This project will characterise the role of MM-derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) on MM progression and the development of therapeutic resistance, with a focus on alterations to the alterations to the immune microenvironment.
listings.description:
This project will characterise the role of MM-derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) on MM progression and the development of therapeutic resistance, with a focus on alterations to the alterations to the immune microenvironment.

Multiple myeloma (MM) represents around 10% of all blood cancer and while treatment options have drastically improved, almost all patients relapse and develop of drug resistance. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of resistance would provide new therapeutic options and aid precision medicine approaches. The bone marrow microenvironment performs a crucial role in supporting MM pathogenesis and promoting the development of therapeutic resistance. Exosomes, also known as small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), have been identified as a key component of cell-to-cell communication within the bone marrow microenvironment (BMM).

Using CRISPR/Cas9 whole genome screening data we have identified genes related to exosome biogenesis and release as essential for growth specifically in MM cell lines. Furthermore, patients exhibiting increased expression of these genes at relapse have significantly poorer prognosis. Using cell line models of therapy sensitive and resistant MM we have that EV secretion is altered in resistant cells and demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of exosome release blocks MM cell proliferation. Taken together this data points to a strict requirement for exosome biogenesis and a role for this in relapse and development of resistance.

This PhD aims to understand how MM-derived exosomes influence MM pathogenesis and the development of therapeutic resistance. We will use unbiased proteomics approaches to define the molecular mechanisms behind exosome-mediated effects with a focus on alterations to the immune microenvironment. The study will uncover important tools to predict or target drug resistance, representing a significant advance in our move towards personalised medicine.

listings.title: The Role Of Secondary Bile Acids In Lung Infection And Inflammation
listings.summary: This project investigates how bile acids contribute to lung infection and inflammation in respiratory diseases such as CF, COPD, and IPF. It will explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying bile acid–mediated immune responses, using experimental models to clarify their role in respiratory infection and…
listings.description:
This project investigates how bile acids contribute to lung infection and inflammation in respiratory diseases such as CF, COPD, and IPF. It will explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying bile acid–mediated immune responses, using experimental models to clarify their role in respiratory infection and disease progression.

The aspiration of bile acids (BA) into the lungs has been identified as a major co-morbidity of a range of respiratory diseases, and in some cases, has been shown to correlate with a reduction in microbial diversity and an increase in inflammation. Aspiration has been shown to be associated with severe episodes of acute exacerbations of COPD with BA in the lower airways inducing microbiota changes. The presence of BA has been reported in the lungs of patients diagnosed with a range of respiratory conditions, including CF, COPD and IPF. Moreover, BA are also a major contributor to the development of pneumonia in the elderly and have been demonstrated to promote chronic respiratory infections in CF. Despite this, the precise effect of BA on innate immune cell function and response to pathogens associated with respiratory infection currently remains unknown. This project will fulfil this knowledge gap.

Neuroinflammation, a condition associated to excessive cytokine production, promotes neuronal death. Astrocytes play a major role in neuroinflammation. Substance P stimulates neurokinin-1 receptor (NK1R) abundantly expressed by astrocytes leading to cytokine secretion. This project aim to identify the transduction mechanisms involved in NK1R-mediated cytokine secretion in the context of astrocytes.

Infection to pathogens can cause neuroinflammation, a condition associated to excessive production of cytokines promoting neuronal death. Astrocytes, a type of glial cells in the central nervous system, play a major role in neuroinflammation. These cells express neurokinin-1 receptor (NK1R) and stimulation of NK1R by the neuropeptide substance P induces cytokine secretion. Exposition of astrocytes to bacterial pathogens dramatically increases NK1R expression in astrocytes and consequently exacerbates the cytokine production by substance P. Although the role of NK1R in cytokine secretion by astrocytes is well established, the molecular mechanisms translating NK1R activation into this cellular response remains obscure as it mainly occurs at endosomes rather than at the plasma membrane.

listings.title: Estimating cancer treatment effects in patient audit data
listings.summary: Cancer treatment effects on patient survival can be estimated in population-based observational cancer audit datasets. For certain patient groups, these estimates could be their only treatment evidence-base. The PhD will explore the data conditions and the causal inference methods required for unbiased estimation
listings.description:
Cancer treatment effects on patient survival can be estimated in population-based observational cancer audit datasets. For certain patient groups, these estimates could be their only treatment evidence-base. The PhD will explore the data conditions and the causal inference methods required for unbiased estimation

Cancer patient survival in Northern Ireland lags behind other central and northern European countries. To improve patient outcomes, cancer services in NI are audited regularly by the Northern Ireland Cancer Registry providing service metrics, including the provision of timely and optimal treatment (chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery) . The audits captures a wealth of clinical information that, when coupled with causal inference (CI) statistical methods, have the potential to estimate unbiased treatment effects in the population, or in sub-groups.

The aim of the PhD study is to increase the treatment evidence-base for patients not included in conventional randomised control trials (RCTs). Such patients may have a rare cancer, or due to inclusion and exclusion criteria, are under-represented in RCTs, e.g. elderly or patients with dementia.

The objectives are to assess, in the audit data, if 1) treatments are well-defined, 2) there is sufficient information to adjust for confounding (exchangeability), 3) sufficient variety in clinical practice around treatment use (positivity). The study will also explore how best to apply CI methods. In situations where the conditions are met, the study will estimate treatment effects, thus contributing to the evidence base. Otherwise, the study will recommend if and how audits can be improved.

listings.title: Bio-based textile reinforced mortar (bio-TRM) composites for structural strengthening
listings.summary: Textile reinforced mortars (TRM) have emerged besides fabric reinforced polymers (FRP) composites for structural strengthening in the construction industry due to their better compatibility with concrete and masonry materials and lower sensitivity to high temperature.
listings.description:
Textile reinforced mortars (TRM) have emerged besides fabric reinforced polymers (FRP) composites for structural strengthening in the construction industry due to their better compatibility with concrete and masonry materials and lower sensitivity to high temperature.

This PhD project aims at manufacturing, testing, and assessing novel bio-TRM composites for strengthening masonry and concrete structures.

Textile reinforced mortar composites are particularly suited to strengthen unreinforced masonry structures such as heritage constructions and ordinary buildings subjected to seismic excitation. However, the market of these composites are currently dominated by synthetic fibres such as carbon, plastic, basalt and glass fibres, which makes it difficult for low-income countries to avail of this strengthening method. Contrary to syntetic fibres, natural fibres are affordable and readily available in most countries. The fabric manufacturing has a low environmental impact and the products are recyclable and biodegradable by the end of their life cycle.

While they have already entered the automobile sector as reinforcement for FRP composites, flax, jute and hemp are not yet used in the construction field.

This PhD project aims therefore at addressing two main goals: 1) optimising a set of bio-TRM composites by studying the mortar/fabric long term compatibility and 2) assessing the composite structural performance in real world applications. This will entail a mechanical characterization of the tensile and bonding behaviour and a demo strengthening case of a masonry member.

listings.title: Mapping urban transformations and production of space in post-socialist cities
listings.summary: Post-socialist transformation of cities has been characterised by significant changes in their built fabrics, resulting from the political, economic and societal processes of change after the fall of state socialism. This research will contribute to the understanding of the transformative processes in post-socialist…
listings.description:
Post-socialist transformation of cities has been characterised by significant changes in their built fabrics, resulting from the political, economic and societal processes of change after the fall of state socialism. This research will contribute to the understanding of the transformative processes in post-socialist cities and the mechanisms of production of space after the fall of state socialism.

Rapid political, economic and societal processes of change after the fall of state socialism led to dynamic processes of urban restructuring of cities. The sudden transformation towards a market economy and the reintroduction of land ownership required an establishment of a new decentralised system of decision-making, with direct consequences on the structure and the form of cities after the fall of state socialism. As a result, the built fabrics of post-socialist cities became a testing ground for new developments subjected to real-estate interests. This research will identify and evaluate various spontaneous and planned practices of the continuing urban transformations and production of space in post-socialist cities. Case studies will contribute to the understanding of the complex interplay between many actors, ideologies and interests that shape the experience of urban life in cities after the fall of state socialism. It is expected that the findings of this research will provide valuable insights and inform future sustainable practices and initiatives of transformation of post-socialist cities.

Architecture at Queen’s addresses the issues of architecture and urbanism in an increasingly globalised world, where factors such as sustainability and climate change, identity and heritage, and notions of craft and form create a complex context that architecture has to mediate.

This project will complement the re-purposing of FRP waste for land-based applications. With sustainability at the forefront of governmental agendas directed towards a greener, carbon-neutral future, a sustainable decommissioning plan must be put in place to promote a circular economy and reduce the levels of waste going to landfill. In the next decade, there will be a considerable number of wind farms reaching their End-of-Service-Life (EoSL) with thousands of tonnes of waste being created and needing to be managed. To mitigate climate change and enhance the decarbonisation agenda, the reuse of the marine industries composite waste can be reused to further develop the marine renewable energy industries, in line with governmental policies and global research objectives. Reuse of FRP for reinforcing cross-laminated timber and use of chopped FRP in a low pH concrete are other alternative solutions that would be investigated in the project. Such reuse would displace the use of virgin materials and reduce carbon emissions associated with refinement and production.

listings.summary: Transport of water, salts and gas into concrete leads to premature deterioration of reinforced concrete structures. Electrical resistivity of concrete indicates the ease with which concrete can conduct ions. Resistivity is a simpler and affordable property to measure. The aim of this project is to develop an…
listings.description:
Transport of water, salts and gas into concrete leads to premature deterioration of reinforced concrete structures. Electrical resistivity of concrete indicates the ease with which concrete can conduct ions. Resistivity is a simpler and affordable property to measure. The aim of this project is to develop an instrument for measuring temperature and electrical resistance of fresh concrete and use the data to predict the concrete properties. This will be an affordable instrument for concrete industry worldwide.

Concrete being a porous material will allow ions and gas to travel through its pore structure. The ease of this travel can be quantified by measuring its electrical conductivity or resistivity. Higher the resistivity, the difficult the ionic (or gas) transport. Resistivity measurement does not require sophisticated equipment and therefore is affordable and fast.

Besides the instrument development, interpretation of the data and making viable prediction of the concrete properties are the challenges to overcome. In situ data from structures are available from the previous research programmes. Student will receive training and access to an array of analytical equipment used for characterising concrete. A working prototype for the instrument is available. You will be trained by staff with expertise on instrument development and commercialisation. If you are interested in using technology to make a difference in the world, this is a project for you.

listings.summary: Alkali activated binders refers to inert powders such as calcined clay, fly ash and blast furnace slag activated to form a binding material using an engineered metal silicate solution. listings.description:
Alkali activated binders refers to inert powders such as calcined clay, fly ash and blast furnace slag activated to form a binding material using an engineered metal silicate solution. Such binders have low carbon footprint is now considered as a viable construction material for a range of Engineering applications. This project will determine the performance of mild steel as a reinforcing material for such binders.

The critical next step in adoption of alkali activated binders is to identify suitable reinforcing materials for such binders and to clearly understand the interaction these binders will have on the reinforcing material. Previous studies found that corrosion behaviour and products formed when steel reinforcement gets in contact with the high initial alkalinity and low post reaction alkalinity of such binders are causes for concern. The free ions in such concrete make the measurement inflated and non-comparable to conventional norms in addition to contributing to further corrosion. Therefore the aim of the project is to evaluate the performance of reinforcing materials in alkali activated binders. The objectives are therefore: to study the chemical interaction between alkali activated binders and a range of available reinforcing materials; to establish the short and long term structural behaviour; to define the corrosion mechanism and provide guidelines for corrosion testing; and to validate reinforcing specification, failure mechanism and load carrying capacity for selected products.

listings.summary: The project aims to investigate secure, smart building information models with real time sensor data combined with user feedback / participation. This will aid energy use tracking, gathering real time data for analysis and prediction of energy use.
listings.description:
The project aims to investigate secure, smart building information models with real time sensor data combined with user feedback / participation. This will aid energy use tracking, gathering real time data for analysis and prediction of energy use.

Smart technology is fast becoming the norm in new build construction, with widespread use of digital twins and integration of temperature, room occupancy, energy and light sensors enabling building energy management systems to track, predict and manage energy use. However, there exists a large stock of existing buildings which are, by comparison, largely ‘dumb’; very little information is gathered on their efficiency, occupancy, and energy use, and their management often uses legacy, analogue systems.

Fitting sensors to monitor existing buildings presents a number of challenges: the integration of the technology with the existing building envelope; older mechanical and electrical systems which may use a mixture of heat and energy generation and distribution networks; and the security and reliability of information gathered.

This project responds to the UK construction 2025 strategy through the development and use of innovative techniques to record the existing built environment including connecting room and building wide information.

Augmented Urbanism and Place Based Data investigates and identifies potential applications and manifestations of augmented contextual data. This will include developing appropriate platforms for data presentation and communication, understanding how they engage with and present the interface between physical and digital space and how this may affect behaviour.

The emergence of highly digitally connected environments, the promise of ubiquitous connectivity and an always on mode raises the possibility of seamless augmented environments becoming normalised. What these environments need to include/exclude, their performance, formal, physical and aesthetic characteristics, and parameters for their engagement with users at a range of scales from the individual citizen upwards requires definition. This project explores these questions and will culturally contextualise augmented urbanism from a human centric perspective, both as an overlay to current urbanism and potentially also as a replacement for elements of it.

The project connects with technology and external partners where appropriate, being developed from an architecture/spatial design/ urbanism origin to question technocentric versions of inhabited digital and smart space.

listings.description:
By 2030, UN-Habitat estimates that 3 billion people, about 40 per cent of the world’s population, will need access to adequate housing. This translates into a demand for 96,000 new affordable and accessible housing units every day. While housing is explicitly articulated in Target 11 of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), it is a key component of sustainable development across all of the goals. Good housing drives access to basic services, contributes towards inclusive growth, and supports the development of a sustainable future. The future of urbanization will therefore depend on how countries and cities position housing as a priority in the public debate around sustainable development.

Within this context, this project aims to explore both empirical and epistemological advancement in informal housing, urban transformation and international housing policy that look to address one or more of the following areas: different purpose (policy audit, project evaluation, strategic understanding and theoretical explanation), methodology (hypothesis testing, interpretation, model building, indicator development), multiple field of focus (locality, tenure, institution, household, individual, social relations, financial arrangements, organisations, welfare regimes, state’s role and neo-liberalism) and diverse contribution to theoretical debates made by comparative housing research. To this end, the project invites proposals that advocate the production of theoretical accounts from a greater diversity of urban contexts, particularly within the rapidly urbanising global south.

listings.title: Heritage and Placemaking
listings.summary: Every community has multiple cultural identities, which manifest as overlapping interpretations, histories and traditions about the space they exist in. In this way, culture is embedded in the space shared by the community, which in turn reflects and shapes culture itself. In literature everyday heritage concept as an…
listings.description:
Every community has multiple cultural identities, which manifest as overlapping interpretations, histories and traditions about the space they exist in. In this way, culture is embedded in the space shared by the community, which in turn reflects and shapes culture itself. In literature everyday heritage concept as an approach to placemaking process in the urban landscape has gained ground, as with, the instrumental use of heritage in urban design; in place-branding and in placemaking. Ultimately, placemaking creates social value, by building spaces where people want to live, work and play. This, in turn, creates economic value, by creating a need for local services and businesses. Placemaking and heritage are therefore key strategic assets in the city-making processes.

The nexus is however fraught with complexities, multiple interpretations especially when elements of heritage conservation, reconstruction, removal and new creation is involved. In part there are expected economic motivations overriding the social value. Heritage is also seen to be a powerful tool, for the ownership of heritage objects, places and practices can bestow political power as well as stimulate political struggle at both national and international levels. Equally complex is the question of who the potential beneficiaries might be – citizens, or more broadly, a process of nation-building. Proposals are invited that explore in what ways can heritage and placemaking can best be understood, conceptualised and modelled? How can placemaking contribute to processes which uncover ‘hidden’ heritages, rediscover ‘lost’ heritages, make greater use of under-explored, understand ‘entangled’ heritages and/or enable the re-valuation and re-interpretation of under-valued heritages? How can heritage and placemaking contribute to international development and the UN Sustainable Development Goals?

listings.description:
Natural disasters are becoming more frequent with far-reaching impact on cities. They disrupt lives and livelihoods through the damage they cause on both tangible and intangible heritage. Post-disaster rebuilding efforts prioritise heritage reconstruction, which is a recognition of their role in safeguarding lives and livelihoods, traditions and cultures.

Although sometimes overlooked or marginalised in scientific research, urban spaces often feature prominently in building resilience in disaster situation. As such, while much of what follows after the disaster emerges from the communities’ embodied participation and subjectivities, various forms of urban geographies play a role in enabling those actions to happen. Historic spaces and sacred spaces are commonly perceived to have restorative value. The project investigates how urban spaces are adapted and readapted in building resilience and subsequent public actions, in the face of risks and uncertainties caused by the disaster. In what ways can the urban space best be represented, conceptualised and modelled such that it is able to contribute to more rounded and reliable research on post-disaster resilience? Applications are encouraged to bring together multi-country studies and interdisciplinary knowledge and collaboration especially from global south.

listings.title: Microstructure and mechanical properties of an advanced metal matrix composite with ultrafine particle reinforcement for manufacturing aerospace components
listings.summary: Metal matrix composites have the high strength needed for advanced manufacturing, but they tend to have limited ductility, because they are almost invariably reinforced by hard ceramic particles that are brittle themselves and also have a rather brittle interface with the metal matrix. Shandong Yuanhang Ultra Light…
listings.description:
Metal matrix composites have the high strength needed for advanced manufacturing, but they tend to have limited ductility, because they are almost invariably reinforced by hard ceramic particles that are brittle themselves and also have a rather brittle interface with the metal matrix. Shandong Yuanhang Ultra Light Material Research Institute Co., Ltd., China invented a world-first metal matrix composite that is reinforced by an intermetallic compound YAl2. Because the reinforcing particles are also metals, there should be a seamless interface between the particles and the metal matrix, thus overcoming the brittle interface problem. In addition, these particles are ultrafine, down to the nanometre range, so their strengthening is more effective.

The metal matrix of this new material is an ultra-light magnesium alloy and would be suitable for manufacturing critical components for aerospace products specifically satellites, drones, and low-altitude aircrafts, where weight and strength-to-weight ratio are important. However, before the new material can be used, we need to fully understand its properties and performance, and to know the optimal processing parameters to achieve the best properties and performance. In order to accomplish these, we need to study the microstructure and metal/particle interface of the prototype composite. Then, we need to figure out where to use this top-notch material for advanced manufacturing. All these are part of this PhD project.

This project is interdisciplinary, between materials science, composite production, and mechanical, manufacturing and aerospace engineering. It will be intersectoral, between academia and industry, working directly with the company responsible for the invention of this material. It is international, because the company is in China. The combination is essential, because, without the company, we don’t have this material to study and without Queen’s University, it will take longer for this material to reach its full potential.

listings.title: Babbitt/aluminium composite material with enhanced tribological and mechanical characteristics
listings.summary: Metal matrix composites (MMCs) are essential in a wide variety of markets, including automotive, military, aerospace, energy, architecture, infrastructure, marine, sports, and recreation. Because of its commercial availability, durability, high-strength to weight ratio, and wear resistance, the aluminium alloy-based…
listings.description:
Metal matrix composites (MMCs) are essential in a wide variety of markets, including automotive, military, aerospace, energy, architecture, infrastructure, marine, sports, and recreation. Because of its commercial availability, durability, high-strength to weight ratio, and wear resistance, the aluminium alloy-based metal matrix composites (AMMCs) have attracted the focus of extensive R&D activity. The MMCs and in particular AMMCs are important choices for better performance and longer endurance in comparison to conventional metals. Usually, AMMCs are reinforced with fibres (including whiskers) and particles with various shapes and sizes offering potential to tailor materials to specific engineering design requirements. AMMCs are incorporated with different types of reinforcing phases. The most important reinforcing phases for attaining enhanced mechanical and tribological properties of the composite material are alumina, silicon carbide, zircon, and graphite. A different alloy type with improved mechanical and tribological properties is the babbitt alloy. It is widely employed in engineering and specifically as a bearing material. Two main babbitt alloys are broadly exploited, tin-based babbitt and lead-based babbitt alloys. Due to their easy bonding, very good corrosion resistance, and reduced tendency towards segregation, the tin-based alloys are more often utilised than the lead based babbitt alloys. Their microstructure consists of a solid solution of antimony and copper in tin, large cubic hard inclusions of a second phase (solid solution based on SnSb intermetallic), and more dispersed crystals of chemical compound Cu3Sn.

AMMCs (skeleton) with open porosity structure infiltrated with tin-based alloy (infiltrated skeleton) could be very suitable for frictional elements. The combination of high load-carrying capacity, fatigue strength, high chemical resistance and low-density of the skeleton is supplemented by the wear resistance properties of the babbitt to act as a lubricant by reduction of friction force and by decreasing temperature on the sliding wear surface. For fabrication of skeleton, AlSi12(Fe) alloy will be used, which combines good strength and dynamic properties with low weight and flexible post-processing possibilities. It will be reinforced with alumina particles to maintain the strength and stiffness of the skeleton. The ceramic particles will act as a load-carrying element and as an inhibitor against plastic deformation and adhesion

listings.title: Electroless high entropy alloy coatings for energy storage applications
listings.summary: Traditionally, alloys have been developed on one principal element (e.g., Fe, Al, Cu, Mg, and Ni-base alloys) to which solutes are supplementary in minor quantities for the betterment of specific properties. A new approach to alloy design involves mixing elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic proportions, to form…
listings.description:
Traditionally, alloys have been developed on one principal element (e.g., Fe, Al, Cu, Mg, and Ni-base alloys) to which solutes are supplementary in minor quantities for the betterment of specific properties. A new approach to alloy design involves mixing elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic proportions, to form multicomponent alloys (usually > 5 at. %) with no single principal element. These alloys are expected to have high configurational entropy and are named as ‘high-entropy alloys (HEAs)’. Their configuration entropy of mixing grasps its maximum for a solution phase. HEAs are among the materials with the highest strength and specific strength.

The HEAs are typically prepared by physical methods, usually through the melting-casting route (arc and induction furnace melting). Mechanical alloying and rapid solidification are other synthesis routes used for attaining bulk materials. On the other hand, HEA coatings have been produced by deposition methods including magnetron sputtering and laser cladding. Electrodeposition is a low-cost alternative for the synthesis of high entropy alloy thin and thick films, as it does not require complex and expensive equipment and uses easily available raw materials. This simple method provides the possibility of depositing thin films on substrates with a complex geometry and it can be carried out at low processing temperatures and with low energy consumption. In this project, unlike electrodeposition, the electroless route is proposed for the easy control of the composition, morphology, and thickness of the coatings through the variation of the deposition parameters. Among the HEA alloy systems, HEAs based on the Mg-TM-Ln (TM: transition metals; Ln: lanthanide) system have attracted much attention due to their high energy density hydrogen storage capacity, high specific strength, excellent corrosion resistance, good bend ductility, light-weight and low cost. Hence, it would be of immense technological importance for the scientific community if the full capability of Mg-TM-Ln is explored. The synthesis and application of high entropy alloys have been patented through other expensive routes. In this aspect we propose here low-cost preparation of these Mg-TM-Ln HEAs systems through this electroless route. This technology will have a greater impact on the energy storage sector. These materials could be beneficial from an economical point of view.

This project will be in collaboration with Dr. Jothi Sudagar, VIT-AP Uni

This interdisciplinary doctoral project explores the emerging typology of the fully online, immersive virtual museum, situated at the convergence of architecture, game design, and museum studies. It aims to investigate how digital technologies - specifically virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), artificial intelligence (AI), and game engines - are reshaping not only the design and experience of museum spaces but also their potential roles in peace-building and social sustainability.

While computer-aided design (CAD) has been integral to architectural practice since the late 20th century, recent advancements in immersive technologies have expanded the scope of architectural imagination. This research considers how such tools can be deployed beyond representational models, toward the creation of inhabitable, socially meaningful, and culturally resonant virtual environments. Guided by the reflective provocation of architect Louis Kahn "What does a building want to be?" the central research question becomes: What does a virtual museum want to be in the digital age?

listings.title: Improving the shrinkage behaviour and efflorescence formation of low carbon geopolymer concrete
listings.summary: Previous projects have developed technology for environmentally friendly geopolymer concrete. The LowCoPreCon project culminated in the production of full scale precast geopolymer concrete units including stairs, wall panels, floor panels and building blocks. This was a significant step forward towards more widescale…
listings.description:
Previous projects have developed technology for environmentally friendly geopolymer concrete. The LowCoPreCon project culminated in the production of full scale precast geopolymer concrete units including stairs, wall panels, floor panels and building blocks. This was a significant step forward towards more widescale use of low carbon concrete. Overall, the trials were successful and demonstrated that geopolymer technology can be used in the production of precast concrete elements. However, the trials also highlighted some remaining issues which still need to be addressed to allow and encourage greater uptake of geopolymer concrete by industry. There were two main issues identified. Firstly, there were microcracks on the surface of concrete elements. These are related to early age drying shrinkage. Further research is needed to assess the early age drying shrinkage of the geopolymer concrete. Modifications need to be made to the binder composition to assess if a reduction in drying shrinkage is observed. There are a few possible ways to adjust the composition of geopolymer concrete. One promising option is the addition of MgO which hydrates to form Mg(OH)2, an expansive mineral. The addition of MgO in small quantities and the subsequent formation of Mg(OH)2 may offset early age drying shrinkage and eliminate the microcracks observed on the concrete surface. The second issue identified during the factory trials was efflorescence on the surface of geopolymer building blocks. The geopolymer building blocks produced in the factory trials were competitive and often superior to conventional building blocks in every aspect including cost, mechanical properties, and environmental impact. The only problem they exhibited, was the formation of white deposits on their surface known as efflorescence. Recent studies have also identified the issue of efflorescence as a knowledge gap in geopolymer concrete technology. It may be possible to reduce the issue of efflorescence through altering the mix proportions, modifying the curing conditions or by using additives that can reduce the mobility of alkalis in the geopolymer matrix. This project will aim to address these issues, thereby eliminating remaining obstacles hindering the uptake of low carbon geopolymer concrete.

listings.title: High-Entropy Alloy-Infused Cementitious Composites: A Circular-Economy Approach to Corrosion Mitigation and Service-Life Extension (HEA-CIRC)
listings.summary: Applications are invited from Northern Ireland, Great Britain and Republic of Ireland candidates only. International candidates should NOT apply for this PhD opportunity.
listings.description:
Applications are invited from Northern Ireland, Great Britain and Republic of Ireland candidates only. International candidates should NOT apply for this PhD opportunity.

Reinforced-concrete infrastructure in Europe incurs €840 billion in corrosion-related losses each year. Up to 30% of bridges and underwater tunnels in Europe suffer from active rebar corrosion, shortening service life by 15% under future climate scenarios. In service, dissolved chlorides migrate through capillary pores by diffusion, quantified by the apparent chloride diffusion coefficient, and govern the time to steel depassivation – a 20% drop in the apparent chloride diffusion coefficient can delay corrosion onset by 5-10 years in marine environments. State-of-the-art strategies currently rely on cathodic protection, chemical inhibitors, or micro-additives such as colloidal nano-silica (which lowers permeability with no toughness gain), and steel/carbon fibres (which bridge cracks but impair workability and scale poorly). Limitations of these approaches include complex application, limited durability and costly gains, and poor scalability for mass infrastructure. HEA-CIRC addresses these gaps by embedding High Entropy Alloy (HEA) particulates at the steel-paste interfacial transition zone to combine three functions – (i) passive-film corrosion resistance, (ii) permeability reduction via tortuosity effects, and (iii) microcrack bridging for toughness – thereby extending service life, lowering maintenance costs, and cutting carbon dioxide emissions in line with the EU Circular Economy Action Plan and Green Deal. Preliminary equilibrium calculations predict robust spontaneous passive-film formation; while estimate indicates a shift in corrosion-onset potential. The multi-oxide passive films on HEAs resist alkali/chloride attack and locally limit corrosion initiation on steel, while the hard, ductile HEA cores bridge microcracks that otherwise accelerate ion ingress.

listings.title: Delay of gratification in children
listings.summary: Delaying gratification involves deciding to wait for a better reward in the future rather than taking a small reward now. Learning to delay gratification is widely assumed to be an important developmental skill, and has been linked to a variety of outcomes. Despite the large amount of research interest in this topic,…
listings.description:
Delaying gratification involves deciding to wait for a better reward in the future rather than taking a small reward now. Learning to delay gratification is widely assumed to be an important developmental skill, and has been linked to a variety of outcomes. Despite the large amount of research interest in this topic, there are still some important things that are not known about the processes underlying developmental changes.

Research with adults suggests that one important factor in deciding to delay gratification is the extent to which someone enjoys looking forward to a reward. Adults will sometimes decide to delay gratification because they know that they will enjoy the anticipation of it (e.g., they decide not to eat some biscuits now so they can look forward to eating their favourite dessert later). Very little is currently known about the extent to which children factor in ‘looking forward’ to a future reward when deciding to delay gratification.

This project will address the issue through measuring whether children anticipate they will enjoy looking forward to rewards. It will also explore whether children are more likely to delay gratification if they are encouraged to imagine this anticipation. It will use simple delay choice tasks in which children decide between a small reward now or a larger one later (e.g., between one candy now or five tomorrow). The project is suitable for a student who is interested in working on cognitive development in primary-school aged children.

listings.description:
In instances of mind wandering, people’s attention shifts away from the here-and-now towards thoughts about other times or places. Interesting, there seems to be a link between mood and mind wandering:

research with adults indicates that lower mood levels are associated with higher levels of mind wandering. Moreover, experimental manipulations of mood seem to impact on mind wandering.

Very little research to date has looked at the link between mood and mind wandering in children. We have some preliminary evidence that low mood is associated with levels of mind wandering in a primary-school aged sample (Teague et al., 2025). The aim of this project will be to follow up this work.

The project will particularly focus on whether changes in mood are associated with changes in levels of mind wandering in children. It will also examine whether it is possible to experimentally manipulate mood to alter levels of mind wandering in children, and what impact this might have on their learning in a classroom context. It is suitable for a student who is interested in applied developmental research with children.

listings.description:
The Advanced Vehicle Engineering Centre is looking for a PhD candidate to join our tyre dynamics research team. The aim of the research is to develop an understanding of aircraft tyre force and moment generation limitations on contaminated surfaces. The research will use advanced simulation techniques to predict the force and moment generation capability of aircraft tyres operating where contamination persists between the rubber and the ground surface. The research will create advanced simulations that can enable more accurate prediction of ground handling behaviour of aircraft. This research project is fully funded by Airbus and the EPSRC.

Aims to advance the understanding of the fundamental Tyre contact mechanics under different runway conditions, and to determine whether there is a relationship between lateral and longitudinal friction coefficients. The study will involve developing models and build bench tests of tyre friction cases to demonstrate the relationship between lateral and longitudinal friction coefficient on aircraft.

The project will help define future activity, in relation to the ground handling behaviour of aircraft on contaminated surfaces. The industrial sponsor will use the results from the study to advise discussions with regulation authorities with respect to the predicted forces and moments from aircraft tyres on contaminated runways

Cranfield has a long heritage of work in the area of aircraft tyre dynamics, and unique test rigs which can be made available to the project.

The successful candidate will develop a deep understanding of advanced simulation methods of aircraft tyres, aircraft tyre-ground interation and aircrfat groud handling. The study aims to support harmonised, evidence-based assessment of cerebral palsy across clinical, research, and surveillance settings.
listings.description:
This project will evaluate the diagnostic and asssessment framework of Cerebral Palsy through evidence synthesis, expert consensus, and stakeholder engagement. The study aims to support harmonised, evidence-based assessment of cerebral palsy across clinical, research, and surveillance settings.

Cerebral Palsy (CP) is a group of permanent physical disabilities caused by non-progressive injuries to the immature or developing brain. As a heterogeneous condition, CP encompasses a wide range of clinical presentations, and debate remains regarding its definition, classification, and diagnostic criteria. The Surveillance of Cerebral Palsy in Europe (SCPE) has developed a widely used reference and training manual to support the identification, classification, and assessment of children with CP.

This study aims to evaluate the uptake, applicability, and future development of specific assessment tools across clinical and research contexts.

The project will involve three interconnected work packages. First, a scoping review will examine definitions, classification systems, and assessment tools used in describing strengths and challenges of children with CP. Second, a Delphi study will establish expert consensus on the strengths, limitations, and potential refinements of existing training resources. Third, a mixed-methods study will engage clinicians, researchers, and people with lived experience of CP to explore priorities for improving the acceptability, implementation, and utility of assessment tools for children with CP.

This study will provide valuable information that will be foundational in refining and harmonising tools used in the assessment of people with CP, improving clinical practice, surveillance, while ensuring that these tools reflect the needs of people affected by CP.

The project focuses on environmental sustainability in grain storage, developing telemetric robotic sensing and predictive modelling to control mycotoxin (Ochratoxin A) risk while reducing postharvest drying energy demand. Combining applied mycology, food safety modelling, precision agriculture and Net Zero energy systems, the research will deliver energy-efficient, data-driven grain storage solutions for the UK agri-food sector.

This interdisciplinary project sits at the intersection of bioengineering, heat and mass transfer, predictive modelling, postharvest systems engineering and applied microbiology. It addresses the urgent need for energy-efficient grain storage solutions in the context of climate change and Net Zero commitments. By integrating thermal dynamics, moisture migration modelling and real-time telemetric sensing, the research responds constructively to the dual challenge of maintaining food safety while reducing the carbon footprint of postharvest cereal management across the UK supply chain.

The project aims to collaboratively design and validate an integrated engineering and biological modelling framework for carbon-efficient grain storage. It will combine heat and moisture transfer modelling, stochastic prediction of fungal growth and Ochratoxin A risk, and optimisation of in situ robotic sensing technology. Through this systems-based approach, the research will generate balanced, data-informed strategies that enable proportionate ventilation, cooling and drying decisions, reducing unnecessary energy use while safeguarding grain safety.

The research will be conducted at Cranfield University within a supportive, cross-disciplinary environment spanning energy systems engineering, computational modelling, bioinformatics and food safety science. The project is delivered in close partnership with Crover Ltd, an innovative agri-robotics SME (based in Edinburg, Scotland) developing advanced telemetric grain-monitoring systems, contributing £15,000 in cash support alongside engineering co-supervision and technology integration expertise.

listings.summary: Mangoes are highly perishable biological products travelling through complex international supply chains. listings.description:
Mangoes are highly perishable biological products travelling through complex international supply chains. Small differences in fruit maturity, temperature and ripening conditions can determine whether fruit reaches consumers at optimum quality—or is lost as waste. This PhD will develop the sensing and predictive modelling tools needed to make those supply chains smarter. By delivering research across laboratory experiments, mathematical modelling and commercial ripening facilities, you will investigate how mangoes respond to their environment, develop methods to monitor ripening in real time, and build predictive models that can be used to optimise commercial ripening while reducing energy use and food loss. The project brings together Cranfield University, the University of Birmingham and global fresh-produce company Blue Skies, giving you the opportunity to work at the interface of plant biology, engineering, data science and industry in a project supported by the EPSRC Doctoral Landscape Award.

Global fresh produce supply chains face increasing pressure to reduce carbon emissions, minimise food waste, and improve energy and resource efficiency while maintaining consistent product quality. These challenges are particularly acute for highly perishable products, where biological variability and changing environmental conditions make quality difficult to predict and control.

Mango provides an ideal model for addressing these challenges. Fruit can vary considerably in maturity and physiological state at harvest and must subsequently undergo controlled ripening before reaching consumers. During international transport, storage and ripening, fruit quality is influenced by interactions between time, temperature, atmospheric conditions and the underlying physiology of the fruit. This variability makes it difficult to predict ripening behaviour and consistently deliver fruit at the required quality while minimising energy use and waste.

Recent advances in sensor technologies, predictive modelling and digital control systems create new opportunities to address this problem. By combining real-time measurements of fruit and its environment with models capable of predicting ripening behaviour, postharvest systems could move from fixed operating protocols towards adaptive control strategies that respond to the condition of the fruit itself.

It will use signals from different sources—such as radio signals and internal sensors— to maintain robust and accurate PNT, even when satellite signals are weak or missing. listings.title: Decoding Hive Health: Using Honey, eDNA and tracking to Predict Disease and Reproductive Failure in Honey Bees
listings.summary: Honey bees (Apis mellifera) are vital pollinators of crops and wild plants, supporting biodiversity, rural economies, and sustainable food production. Their health is threatened by parasites and pathogens, pesticide exposure, habitat loss, poor weather, and queen failure. Current disease surveillance often requires…
listings.description:
Honey bees (Apis mellifera) are vital pollinators of crops and wild plants, supporting biodiversity, rural economies, and sustainable food production. Their health is threatened by parasites and pathogens, pesticide exposure, habitat loss, poor weather, and queen failure. Current disease surveillance often requires removing large numbers of bees from already weakened colonies, creating a need for sensitive, non-invasive tools that can detect declining colony health at an early stage. This PhD project will develop diagnostic and prognostic indicators of hive health by combining pathogen and environmental DNA analysis of honey with geographical and environmental metadata. Machine-learning approaches will be used to identify robust signatures of disease and colony stress, potentially enabling earlier intervention and reducing colony losses. The project will also investigate how environmental conditions affect honey bee reproduction, particularly queen and drone mating behaviour and health. Poor weather during mating periods is thought to contribute to queen failure in Ireland and Northern Ireland, yet the reproductive behaviour of native honey bees remains poorly understood. Imported bees may also threaten native subspecies through hybridisation, making improved understanding of local reproductive adaptations particularly important. These challenges will be addressed in the current project.

Methods will include RFID tagging and remote sensing of queen and drone mating flights, detailed observations at apiaries and drone congregation areas, queen and drone rearing and monitoring, molecular and genetic analyses, assessment of colony health and gut microbiota, and engagement with beekeepers. The project will examine environmental and genetic factors associated with reproductive success and identify links between mating behaviour, individual health, and colony performance.

Understanding of basic biological/ecological principles, experience of molecular biology methods, previous work with bees beneficial, clean driving licence essential.
